children.translated_text: The thesis of a purely negative inference is [advanced] on the basis of not accepting agreement in presence — such is the intent.

children.text: anumānasyetyupalakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: 'Of inference' is used illustratively [to include other <s>pramāṇas</s> as well].

children.text: svata iti ca taditarasyāpi, svataḥ parataśca prāmāṇyasiddheriti //
children.translated_text: 'Intrinsically' also [includes] by the other [i.e., extrinsically] — the meaning is: validity is established both intrinsically and extrinsically.

children.text: nanu samarthapravṛttijanakatvādityetāvataiva sādhyasiddheḥ pramāṇator'thapratipattāvityasamarthaviśeṣaṇaṃ vayadhikaraṇa cetyata āha--pravṛttijanakatvaṃ tviti /
prāmāṇyādyabhidhānadvārā hi śāstrasya niḥśreyasena saṃgatiḥ, na tu svarūpeṇa /
children.translated_text: For the connection of the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise) with the highest good is through the exposition of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, not through its own nature.

children.text: tato yathā pramāṇāditattvajñānaṃ sādhyatayā prayojanaṃ pratijñāyate tathā pramāṇādyabhidheyatayāpi pratijñeyaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as the knowledge of the true nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like is declared as the purpose, being what is to be established, so too it should be declared as what is to be expounded by the <s>śāstra</s>.

children.text: yathā athāto dharma vyākhyāsyāmaḥ (vai.sū.1.1.1) iti dharmasya vyākhyeyatvenaiva pratijñā samānatantre na ca tadabhidheyatāpratijñānamatra /
children.translated_text: Just as in 'Now, therefore, we shall expound <s>dharma</s>' (<s>Vaiśeṣikasūtra</s> 1.1.1), the declaration of <s>dharma</s> is merely as what is to be expounded within the same system, and there is no separate declaration of its being the subject-matter.

children.text: tasmādabhidheyattvāpratijñānānna pramāṇādayaḥ śāstreṇābhidhīyanta iti śrotṛbuddhacanurodhenāśaḍkya sūtrakārahṛdayānurodhena vārttikamuttarayatisyādetaditi //
children.translated_text: Therefore, lest it be suspected — from the lack of a separate declaration of the subject-matter — that <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like are not expounded by the <s>śāstra</s>, the <s>Vārttika</s> (commentary) responds to this, following the intent of the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the <s>sūtras</s>) rather than the understanding of the listener — 'this will be [addressed].'

Now, since the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) is already established by just 'because it generates effective activity,' the qualifier 'in the apprehension of an object by a <s>pramāṇa</s>' is redundant and pertains to a different locus — therefore he says: 'but the capacity to generate activity...'

children.text:
śiṣyākāṅkṣākrameṇa hi śāstramidaṃ pravṛttam, anapekṣitābhidhāne anavadheyatvaprasaṅgāt /
na ca śiṣyākāṅkṣā kiṃ vakṣyati bhavāniti /
kiṃ tu niḥśreyasaṃ kuto 'dhigamyata iti /
tatrottaram--pramāṇāditattvajñānānniḥśreyasādhigama iti /
tataḥ kathamiti? tataḥ ke, kati, kiṃlakṣaṇāḥ pramāṇādayaḥ iti /
tatroddeśavibhāgalakṣaṇānīti /
tataḥ kathamiti? tatra dvitīyādhyāyādīti /
etacca sarvamanubhavasiddham /
nātrāpi vacanāpekṣā /
uktāboddhāraṃ prati tu vyākhyātāro bhavanti, yata
children.translated_text: For this <s>śāstra</s> has proceeded according to the sequence of the student's inquiry, since without attending to what is desired [to be known], it would be disregarded. And the student's inquiry is not 'What will you say?' but rather 'From what is the highest good attained?' The answer to that is: 'From knowledge of the true nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, the highest good is attained.' Then, 'How?' Then, 'What are the <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like, how many, and what are their characteristics?' The answer to that is: 'enumeration, classification, and definition.' Then, 'How [is this elaborated]?' 'In the second chapter and so forth.' All of this is established by experience. No verbal instruction is needed here either. But for one who has not understood what has been stated, commentators exist [to explain]: 'This is what

children.text: evamayamāheti /
children.translated_text: he says.'

children.text: tadanubhavasiddhamapi pramāṇādyabhidhāyakatvaṃ yaḥ kutaścid vyāmohānna pratipadyate taṃ prati vyākhyātā śāstrasya puruṣaśreyo 'bhidhāyakatvādityāhetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And the fact that the <s>śāstra</s> expounds <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like — though established by experience — for one who, due to some confusion, does not understand it, the commentator states: 'because the <s>śāstra</s> expounds the highest good of persons.' That is the meaning.

children.text:
nanu śreyo 'bhidhānamātreṇāpi na pramāṇādyabhidhānaṃ sidhyati /
na hi pramāṇādipadārthā eva śreyaḥ /
atha svayameva vivarīṣyati--tatpadārthāḥ pramāṇādaya iti /
tathāpi tacchāstraṃ śreyo 'bhidhatta ityanene kim? atha śreyaḥśabdasya pramāṇādaya evārthaḥ, tarhi śreyaḥ punaḥ sukhamahitanivṛttiriti kimityata āha--yadyapīti /
yadyapi śāstra punaḥ puruṣaḥ punaḥ śreyaḥ punariti pratipadaṃ gṛhītvā vivaraṇaṃ prakṣayeṇetyantena sphuṭāvabhāsam /
na ca puruṣā rāgādimanta ityādāvapi
children.translated_text: Now, merely by expounding the highest good, the exposition of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like is not established. For <s>pramāṇa</s> and the other categories are not themselves the highest good. Or if [the author] himself intends to explain — 'the subjects of that are <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like' — even then, what is the point of [the statement] 'that <s>śāstra</s> expounds the highest good'? Or if the meaning of the word '<s>śreyas</s>' (highest good) is just <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like, then why [the separate explanation] '<s>śreyas</s> is again happiness and the cessation of what is harmful'? Therefore he says: 'although...' Although 'the <s>śāstra</s> again, the person again, the highest good again' — taking each word and expounding it through [the phrase] ending with 'through exhaustion' — is of clear import, and

children.text: vivaraṇatvāśaḍkā, prakṛtenāsaṃbandhāt /
children.translated_text: nor is there a suspicion of its being an exposition [of the statement] 'persons are endowed with passion and the like,' due to its lack of connection with the topic at hand.

children.text: na hi rāgādimantaṃ prati śāstraṃ na sasādhanaṃ śreyo 'bhidhatte /
children.translated_text: For the <s>śāstra</s> does not fail to expound the highest good together with its means to one endowed with passion and the like.

children.text: na ca taṃ prati na tat śreyo yena vītarāgo vivicya gṛhyatām /
children.translated_text: Nor is that not the highest good for him, merely because one who is free from passion should be distinguished and accepted [differently].

children.text: tathāpi, tasmāt tat śāstraṃ puruṣaśreyo 'bhidhatta iti madhyapatitopasaṃhāra eva vivaraṇavicchedabhramo mā bhūdityetadarthamavacchinatti--upabhogāt prakṣayeṇetyanteneti //
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, lest there be a confusion of breaking the exposition at the intermediate conclusion — 'therefore that <s>śāstra</s> expounds the highest good of persons' — he demarcates [the scope by the phrase]: 'from enjoyment, ending with exhaustion.'

children.text:
nanu samūho vyūhaviśiṣṭa ityasaṃgatam, paryāyatvādityata āha--vyūha iti /
te khalvamī samūhāḥ praṇetṛpuruṣecchānurodhinaḥ svārthānurodhino vetyata āha--eka-smṛtīti /
yadyapyekārthapratipādanāvacchinnā varṇāḥ
children.translated_text: Now, [the objection is raised that] 'a collection distinguished by arrangement' is inconsistent, since they are synonyms — therefore he says: 'arrangement.' These collections indeed follow either the wish of the author or the [natural] arrangement of their meanings — therefore he says: 'of a single recollection.' Although the definition is just this much — that sounds delimited by conveying a single meaning constitute a word,

children.text:
padamityetāvadeva lakṣaṇaṃ tathāpyetadeva lakṣaṇaṃ kṣaṇabhaḍgurāṇāṃ kathamityetaduktam--ekasmṛtisamārūḍhā iti /
samūhaḥ padamiti vārttike śeṣaḥ /
padasamūhaḥ sūtramiti vārttikam /
taccānupapannam /
vākyaviśeṣo hi sūtram /
na ca vākyasāmānyamapi padasamūhamātram, gauraścaḥ puruṣo hastītyāderapi vākyatvaprasaṅgādityata āha--evaṃ svārtheti samūho veditavyaḥ sūtratveneti śeṣaḥ /
sūtrasamūhaḥ prakaraṇamiti vārttikam /
children.translated_text: 'A collection of <s>sūtras</s> is a <s>prakaraṇa</s> (section)' — this is from the <s>Vārttika</s>.

children.text: tatra cāvāntarasamūhabhede kāraṇābhāvāt, śāstrameva sūtrasamūharūpaṃ prakaraṇamiti prāptamityata āha--evaṃ kvaciditi /
children.translated_text: Since there is no reason for sub-division of collections there, [the conclusion] follows that the <s>śāstra</s> itself, in the form of a collection of <s>sūtras</s>, is the <s>prakaraṇa</s> — therefore he says: 'thus, in some cases...'

children.text: tadyathā prayojanābhidheyasaṃbandhapratipādanamekamarthamadhikṛtya prathamadvitīyasūtrayoḥ samūhaḥ prakaraṇam /
children.translated_text: For example, the collection of the first and second <s>sūtras</s>, dealing with a single topic — the exposition of purpose, subject-matter, and connection — is a <s>prakaraṇa</s>.

children.text: evaṃ pramāṇaprakaraṇam, prameyaprakaraṇam, nyāyapūrvāṅgaprakaraṇam, nyāyāśrayaprakaraṇam, nyāyāśrayaprakaraṇam, nyāyasvarūpaprakaraṇam, nyāyottarāṅgaprakaraṇamityādyūhyam //
children.translated_text: Similarly, the <s>pramāṇa</s>-section, the <s>prameya</s>-section, the section on the preliminaries of <s>nyāya</s> (reasoning), the section on the basis of <s>nyāya</s>, the section on the essence of <s>nyāya</s>, the section on the consequent parts of <s>nyāya</s> — and so forth should be understood.

nevertheless, 'how can this definition [apply] to things that are momentarily perishing?' — this is addressed by: 'mounted on a single recollection.' 'A collection [of such sounds] is a word' — this is the completion from the <s>Vārttika</s>. 'A collection of words is a <s>sūtra</s>' — this is from the <s>Vārttika</s>. But that is untenable. For a <s>sūtra</s> is a particular kind of sentence. And even a sentence in general is not merely a collection of words, since even 'a bull, and, a person, an elephant' would absurdly be a sentence — therefore he says: 'thus, its own meaning' — a collection should be understood as a <s>sūtra</s> [only when its components convey their own meaning]; this is the completion.

children.text:
prakaraṇasamūhaścāhnikamiti vārttikam /
tadidaṃ prakaraṇānāmavāntaraikavākyatāyāmasatyāṃ na sidhyatītyata āha--prakaraṇānāmiti /
asti hyamīṣāṃ prakaraṇānāṃ saparikaranyāyalakṣakatvamekamiti /
tatsamūha āhnikam /
uttarasmiścāhnike nyāyanyāyābhāsavivekopāyalakṣaṇamekam /
tatrāpi kathāprakaraṇam, hetvābhāsaprakaraṇam, chalaprakaraṇam, puruṣāśaktiliṅgaprakaraṇamityevaṃ prathame lakṣaṇamadhyāyārthaḥ /
dvitīye pramāṇaparīkṣā /
tṛtīye kāraṇarūpaprameyaṣaṭkaparīkṣā /
caturthe kāryarūpaprameyaṣaṭkaparīkṣā /
pañcame puruṣāśaktiliṅgaviśeṣalakṣaṇamiti /
evaṃ dvitīyādhyāyādāvāhnikaprakaraṇasaṃgatīstatraiva darśayiṣyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: Similarly, at the beginning of the second chapter and so forth, we shall show the arrangement of <s>āhnikas</s> and <s>prakaraṇas</s> there.

children.text: tadidamuktam--evaṃ tatra tatra veditavyamiti /
children.translated_text: This is what is meant by: 'thus, in each case, it should be understood.'

children.text: tatra tatretyāhikādāvityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'In each case' means 'at the beginning of each <s>āhnika</s> and so forth.'

children.text: nanu ca tatra ekaprakāro 'pi na darśitaḥ, kathaṃ tatra tatra veditavyamityata āha--etāśceti //
children.translated_text: Now, since not even one example has been shown there, how can it be said 'it should be understood in each case'? — therefore he says: 'these...'

'A collection of <s>prakaraṇas</s> is an <s>āhnika</s> (daily lesson)' — this is from the <s>Vārttika</s>. Now, this is not established when there is no sub-sentential unity among the <s>prakaraṇas</s> — therefore he says: 'of the <s>prakaraṇas</s>...' For these <s>prakaraṇas</s> share a single [feature], namely, characterizing <s>nyāya</s> (reasoning) together with its accessories. Their collection is an <s>āhnika</s>. And in the second <s>āhnika</s> too, there is one [unifying feature]: the characterization of the means of distinguishing <s>nyāya</s> from <s>nyāyābhāsa</s> (semblance of reasoning). Therein too: the <s>kathā</s>-section, the <s>hetvābhāsa</s>-section, the <s>chala</s>-section, and the section on marks of personal incapacity — thus the first [<s>āhnika</s>] is the meaning of the chapter on definitions. The second is the examination of <s>pramāṇas</s>. The third is the examination of the six <s>prameyas</s> (objects of knowledge) in the form of causes. The fourth is the examination of the six <s>prameyas</s> in the form of effects. The fifth is the characterization of the particular marks of personal incapacity.

children.text: nanu śāstrasya sasādhanapuruṣaśreyo 'bhidhāyakatvaṃ pratijñāya śāstrasvarūpadarśanaṃ kkopayujyata ityata āha--tadevamiti /
children.translated_text: Now, having declared that the <s>śāstra</s> expounds the highest good of persons together with its means, where is the demonstration of the nature of the <s>śāstra</s> itself relevant? — therefore he says: 'thus, indeed...'

children.text: śāstrasvarūpākhyānapūrvakaṃ tadarthakathanaṃ sugamaṃ bhavatītyabhiprāyaḥ //
children.translated_text: The intention is: the exposition of the <s>śāstra</s>'s content becomes easy when preceded by a description of the <s>śāstra</s>'s own nature.

children.text: nanu pratītisiddhaṃ pramāṇādīnāṃ ṣoḍaśatvaṃ kimityanūdyata ityatastannirākaraṇīyām āśaḍkāmāha--nanviti /
children.translated_text: Now, since the sixteen-fold [classification] of <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like is established through common experience, why is it [merely] stated? — anticipating the objection to be refuted, he says: 'now...'

children.text:
sāmānyaviśeṣaḥ sādharmyaviśeṣaḥ /
yato 'syeti padasamūhasya śāstrasya /
padārthāḥ padānāṃ samūhinām arthāḥ pramāṇādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'General and particular' [means] commonality and distinction. 'Of which' — of the <s>śāstra</s>, which is a collection of words. '<s>Padārthas</s>' — the meanings of the words that form the collection — [namely] <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like.

children.text:
tasmāt śāstraṃ vākyarūpaṃ puruṣaśreyo vākyārtharūpamabhidhatte /
samādhānamiti śeṣaḥ /
kathaṃ niḥśreyasāya kalpanta ityāpātataḥ /
paramārthato teṣāṃ kālpanikatve niḥśreyasamapi kālpanikam /
tatastadarthaṃ prayāso viphalaḥ tasyāyatnasiddhatvādityāśayaḥ /
kalpanākośasyānantaprasaratvādanantātmāna ityāpātataḥ /
parakārthato nirātmāna ityāśayaḥ /
pratyakṣānumāneti pramāṇadvayopanyāsaḥ svasiddhāntaviruddho vāttikakṛta ityāha--pramāṇādaya iti /
nopamānaviṣayā iti /
yadyapyupamānasya saṃjñāsaṃjñisaṃbandhaparicchedaphalasya śabde pramāṇe 'styevopayogaḥ, agṛhītasamayasya śabdasyāpramāpakatvāt /
samayasya ca prāyaśa upamānenākalanāt /
tathāpi na tena te sākṣād viṣayīkriyante pramāṇādaya ityarthaḥ /
nanu yadi sākṣādupamānasya prakṛtānupayogādanabhidhānam, tarhi śabdo 'bhidhīyatām /
sa hi sākṣādupayogītyata āha--yadyapīti /
tatrāpītyāgamaviṣayaparāmarśaḥ /
āgamo hi yatra pravartate tadviṣayameva pratyakṣamanumānaṃ vā apekṣate /
te tu samūle api na sviṣayapravṛttaṃ pramāṇamapekṣete /
tato mūlāsaṃplutaviṣayatvāt te eva darśite ityarthaḥ /
vainayiketi viśiṣṭo nayaḥ śāstraṃ nyāyaśāstram, tajjanyabuddhivirahiṇa ityarthaḥ /
naitāna viviñcate samāropitād rūpāditi śeṣaḥ /
śuśrūṣādirityādigrahaṇena śravaṇādau pāṭavam /
saṃdigdhasyāpi jijñāsā na bhavatyevānabhimatāpavargasyetyata uktam"--śiṣyasyeti /
śiṣyatayā mumukṣutādisaṃpattimupalakṣayati /
vipratipanno 'pi kathāmārabhamāṇo 'pyamumukṣurgalite 'haṅkāre na sāpekṣo bhavatītyato niṣphalo jalpavitaṇḍārambha ityata āha-- śiṣyamāṇasyeti /
mohādapi mokṣamicchata ityarthaḥ /
jalpavitaṇḍābhyāṃ vigalite 'haṅkāre iti yojanā /
children.translated_text: The construction is: 'when the ego has dissolved through <s>jalpa</s> (debate) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive criticism).'

children.text: sāpekṣasya sataḥ pratipādyateti vākyaśeṣāgre /
children.translated_text: 'Of one who is attentive, what is to be taught' — this is the remainder of the sentence, [to be supplied] later.

children.text: kenacit pramāreṇeti /
children.translated_text: 'By some <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)' —

children.text: prathamasūtrapāṭhaprakāreṇetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: means: by the method of reading the first <s>sūtra</s>.

Therefore, the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise), having the form of sentences, expresses the highest good of man, which has the form of sentence-meaning. 'Resolution' is the remainder [to be supplied]. 'How do they conduce to the highest good?' — this is the surface meaning. In ultimate reality, if those [categories] are merely constructed, then the highest good too would be merely constructed. Therefore, effort toward it would be fruitless, since it would be accomplished without effort — this is the intention. 'Because the scope of construction is endless, they are of endless nature' — this is the surface meaning. From the opponent's standpoint, 'they are without self' — this is the intention. 'By <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference)' — the mention of only two <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) contradicts the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>'s (commentator's) own doctrine — to this he says: '<s>pramāṇas</s> and the rest.' 'They are not the objects of <s>upamāna</s> (analogy)' — although <s>upamāna</s>, whose result is the ascertainment of the relation between name and named, has utility indeed for verbal testimony as a <s>pramāṇa</s>, since a word whose conventional usage is not grasped is not a valid indicator, and since conventional usage is mostly ascertained through <s>upamāna</s>; nevertheless, the <s>pramāṇas</s> and the rest are not directly made the objects by it — this is the meaning. Now, if <s>upamāna</s> is not mentioned because it has no direct utility for the present subject, then let verbal testimony be mentioned, for it has direct utility — to this he says: 'Although.' 'In that case too' — this is a reference to the domain of <s>āgama</s> (scriptural authority). For <s>āgama</s>, wherever it operates, requires perception or inference regarding that very domain. But those [<s>pramāṇas</s>] do not require a <s>pramāṇa</s> operating in their own domain, even when their root [i.e. <s>āgama</s>] exists. Therefore, since they pertain to a domain not contaminated by [dependence on] their root, they alone have been demonstrated — this is the meaning. '<s>Vainayika</s>' means one who lacks the understanding produced by the distinguished method (<s>naya</s>), that is, the science of reasoning (<s>nyāyaśāstra</s>). The remainder is: 'does not distinguish these from superimposed form and the like.' By the word 'etc.' after '<s>śuśrūṣā</s>' (desire to hear), proficiency in hearing and the like [is indicated]. Even one who is in doubt may not have the desire to inquire if he does not desire liberation — therefore it is said: 'of the student.' By the word 'student,' he indicates the possession of qualifications such as the desire for liberation. Even one who holds a contrary view, who begins a discussion, if he does not desire liberation, when his ego dissolves he becomes indifferent — therefore the initiation of <s>jalpa</s> (debate) and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive criticism) is fruitless — to this he says: 'of the one being taught.' Even one who desires liberation out of delusion — this is the meaning.

children.text:
nanvasaṃdigdhasyāpi saṃdigdhīkaraṇe kimasya prayojanamityata āha--asaṃdigdho 'pīti /
tathā ca pramātaṇāṃ
children.translated_text: Now, even for one who is not in doubt, what is the purpose of creating doubt? To this he says: 'Even one who is not in doubt.' And thus, of the <s>pramāṇas</s>

children.text:
sāpekṣāṇāmiti śeṣaḥ /
te 'bhī durlalitāḥ śiṣyā yadi mokṣādāvapi indriyādyapekṣante, tadā kathaṃ pratipādyā ityato
children.translated_text: 'who are attentive' is the remainder. If those difficult students, even regarding liberation and the like, depend on the senses and so forth, then how are they to be taught? To this

children.text:
vārtikaṃ pūrayati--kañciditi /
dṛṣṭaprayojanopayoginaṃ pratyakṣopalabhyamānamityarthaḥ /
dṛṣṭaprayojanopayoginamevānumeyaṃ
children.translated_text: he completes the <s>vārttika</s>: 'some' — meaning: something that is perceptually apprehended and serves an observed purpose. Something inferable that serves an observed purpose —

children.text:
jijñāsava ityuttaratrāpi pūraṇīyamityāha--evamuttaramapīti /
nanvetāvatāpi jijñāsava ityuttaratrāpi pūraṇīyamityāha--evamuttaramapīti /
nanvetāvatāpi sāpekṣā anenaiva śāstreṇa pratipādyāḥ pratyakṣānumānābhyāṃ ceti
children.translated_text: they wish to investigate — this is to be supplied in the subsequent [passage] too, he says: 'thus the subsequent also.' Now, even with this much, the attentive ones are to be taught by this very <s>śāstra</s> and also by <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference) —

children.text:
parasparavyāhatamityata āha--ayamabhisandhiriti /
paramapuruṣārthasādhanaṃ tu jijñāsava iti śeṣe nyāyeneti śeṣaḥ /
iha yadyapi sukhaṃ dṛṣṭameva vidhāyakapramāṇagocara eva ahitanivṛttiradṛṣṭaiva niṣedhakapramāṇagocara eveti yathāsaṃkhyamapi saṃbhavati /
tathāpi śreyaḥ punaḥ sukhamahitanivṛttiśceti ato na kiñcidadhikamuktaṃ bhavatīti pramāṇāviśeṣasaṃbandhakathanameva param /
na ca tenedānīmasti prayojanam /
na cābhimataśreyoviśeṣanirdhāraṇe kartavye vidhiniṣedhagocaratvopavarṇanamupayujyata ityabhisaṃdhāyānyathā vyācaṣṭe--tatrāpīti /
tacchreyaḥ sukhamahitanivṛttiśceti tacchabdena dvayamapi śreyastvena parāmṛśyata ityarthaḥ /
yathāsaṃkhyaṃ śaḍkāṃ nivārayati--na vyāsajyeti /
dṛṣṭaṃ sukhamityatra
children.translated_text: this is mutually contradictory — to this he says: 'this is the intention.' But they should investigate through reasoning the means to the supreme human goal — 'by reasoning' is the remainder. Here, although pleasure is indeed directly perceived and falls within the scope of injunctive <s>pramāṇa</s>, and the cessation of harm is indeed unperceived and falls within the scope of prohibitive <s>pramāṇa</s>, and although a sequential correlation is also possible; nevertheless, since the highest good is again pleasure and cessation of harm, nothing additional is stated — therefore the statement merely establishes a general connection with <s>pramāṇa</s>. And there is no purpose for that now. Nor is the description of being the object of injunction and prohibition useful when determining the specific nature of the desired highest good — with this intention, he explains otherwise: 'in that case too.' By the word 'that,' both [pleasure and cessation of harm] are referred to as the highest good — this is the meaning. He removes the objection of sequential correlation: 'it is not to be applied.'

children.text: drṛṣṭādṛṣṭaśabdayorarthamudāharaṇamukhena spaṣṭayati--srakcandaneti /
aihikamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Meaning: pertaining to this world.

children.text: svargādīti āmuṣmikamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Heaven and so forth' — meaning: pertaining to the next world.

children.text: uktamanyatrāpīti diśati--evamiti /
children.translated_text: 'It has been stated elsewhere too' — he indicates: 'thus.'

children.text: ahitanivṛttirapyaihikyāmuṣmikī cetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The cessation of harm too is both of this world and of the next world — this is the meaning.
He clarifies the meaning of the words 'perceived' and 'unperceived' by way of examples: 'garlands, sandalwood, and so forth.'

children.text:
naivaṃ vāttike rūyata ityata āha--cakāralopāditi /
cakārayorloparadityarthaḥ /
tena dṛṣṭaṃ sukhamadṛṣṭaṃ ca /
tathā
children.translated_text: Since it is not read thus in the <s>vārttika</s>, to this he says: 'due to the elision of the <s>ca</s> (and).' The meaning is: there is an elision of the two <s>ca</s>-particles. Thus: 'perceived pleasure and unperceived [pleasure].' Likewise,

children.text:
ahitanivṛttiśceti vāttikārthaḥ /
tadayaṃ saṃkṣepaḥ dṛṣṭaṃ śreyaḥ /
tacca sukhamahitanivṛttiśca /
sukhamapyaihikamāmuṣmikaṃ ca /
duḥkhanivṛttirapyaihikyāmuṣmikī ceti /
tatra sukhalakṣaṇaṃ śreyo dṛṣṭamadṛṣṭaṃ vā /
naitacchāstrasādhyam, tasya sragādiyāgādisādhyatvāt /
ātyantikasya ca tasyābhāvāt /
ahitanivṛttirapyanātyantikī dṛṣṭādṛṣṭabhinnā naitacchāstrasādhyā, tasyāḥ prasaktakaṇṭakādihisādiparihārasādhyatvāt, tadaprasaktau tvasādhyatvāt /
ata
children.translated_text: 'and cessation of harm' — this is the meaning of the <s>vārttika</s>. This is the summary: The perceived highest good — that is both pleasure and cessation of harm. Pleasure too is both of this world and of the next world. Cessation of suffering too is both of this world and of the next world. Among these, the highest good characterized by pleasure, whether perceived or unperceived, is not to be accomplished by this <s>śāstra</s>, since it is accomplished by [means such as] garlands and sacrifices. And because an absolute [pleasure] does not exist. Cessation of harm too, being non-absolute and divided into perceived and unperceived, is not to be accomplished by this <s>śāstra</s>, since it is accomplished by avoiding thorns and other encountered dangers, and in the absence of such encounters, there is nothing to accomplish. Therefore,

children.text:
ātyantikīmahitanivṛtti nirdhārayituṃ punarbhinattītyāha--ahitanivṛtteriti /
nanu yadi nivṛttiriti nanu yadi nivṛttiḥ prāgabhāvo duḥkhasya, sa kathamātyantikaḥ? uttarāntānavacchedo hi ātyantikatvam /
prāgābhāvasya ca tathātve prāgityeva na syāt /
children.translated_text: And if prior absence were such [i.e. absolute], then it would not be 'prior' at all.

children.text: atha nivṛttiḥ pradhvaṃsaḥ, sa ca sarva evātyantika iti kuto nivṛtterātyantikatvavyutpādanamityata āha--ātyantikatvamiti /
children.translated_text: If, on the other hand, cessation means destruction (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>), and all destruction is absolute, then why the need to establish the absoluteness of cessation? To this he says: 'absoluteness.'

children.text: nivṛttasya nivṛttajātīyasya punaranutpādaḥ /
children.translated_text: The non-re-arising of what has ceased — that is, of what belongs to the class of the ceased.

children.text: tatraivātmanīti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: The remainder is: 'in that very self.'

in order to determine the absolute cessation of harm, he further analyzes — he says: 'of cessation of harm.' Now, if cessation means the prior absence of suffering, how can it be absolute? For absoluteness means having no delimitation by a later boundary.

children.text:
nanvekaviṃśatiprabhedabhinnaduḥkṣahānireva ātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttiḥ, tatkathaṃ hānyeti vāttikamityata āha--sa ceti /
nivṛttyā nivṛttisvarūpeṇa lakṣyate /
atra ca kāryaśabdena duḥkhamuktam /
kāraṇaśabdena śarīrendriyaviṣayabuddhayaḥ /
anuṣaḍgi sukhaṃ duḥkhenaikakāraṇatvāt /
atha śarīrādiṣu nivṛtteṣvapi dukhaṃ kiṃ na bhavet? mā bhūd duḥkham, sukhaṃ kiṃ na bhavet? na
children.translated_text: Now, the absolute cessation of suffering is just the removal of suffering divided into twenty-one kinds — then how [is it stated as] 'removal'? — this is the <s>vārttika</s> — to this he says: 'and that.' It is characterized by cessation, by the very nature of cessation. And here, by the word 'effect,' suffering is meant. By the word 'cause,' body, senses, objects, and cognitions [are meant]. Concomitant pleasure [is included], because it shares the same cause as suffering. Now, even when body and the rest have ceased, would suffering not arise? Let there be no suffering — but would pleasure not arise? No,

children.text:
hyanyasminnatyantanivṛtte anyanna bhavati /
tathā cānuṣaḍgāsukhinivṛttiḥ kimupavarṇyaya ityata āha--na hīti /
kāraṇa vinā bhavatkāryaṃ kāryatāmava jahyāt /
atḥ śarīrādiṣvasatsu duḥkhavat sukhamapi na bhavati, tasyāpi tatkāryatvāt /
bhavadvā śarīrādiṣu satsveva bhavet /
children.translated_text: Or, it would arise only when body and the rest exist.

children.text: tathā ca duḥkhamapi bhavet kāraṇasadbhāvādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: And thus suffering too would arise, due to the existence of [its] cause — this is the meaning.

children.text: atraivārthe vāttikaṃ yojanayati--tadidamuktamiti /
children.translated_text: He construes the <s>vārttika</s> for this very point: 'this is what has been stated.'

children.text: anenaiva kāraṇamavidyātṛṣṇe, kāryāpravṛttiranuṣaḍgiṇau dharmādharmāviti ṭīkāvyākhyānam apahastitam, śarīrādīnāṃ duḥkhatvamanubhavabādhitamityata āha-- gauṇeti //
children.translated_text: By this alone, the commentary's (<s>ṭīkā</s>'s) explanation that the cause is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving), and the effects are the concomitants <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), is set aside — since the suffering-nature of body and the rest is contradicted by experience, to this he says: 'figurative.'

for when one thing has absolutely ceased, another does not fail to arise [on that account alone]. And thus, what is the point of describing the cessation of concomitant pleasure? To this he says: 'for.' An effect cannot abandon its character as an effect without [its] cause. Therefore, when body and the rest do not exist, pleasure too, like suffering, does not arise, since it too is their effect.

children.text:
nuna ghrāṇādisūtre(1.1.12) pañcendriyāṇi prasiddhāni /
na ca pradeśāntare 'pi ṣaḍityata āha--ṣaṣṭhamiti /
tantrayuktyeti bhāvaḥ /
nanu viṣayā apyanitaretarasādhanasādhyāḥ pajcaiva vibhāge parīkṣāyāṃ ca siddhāḥ, na tu ṣaḍityata āha--tasyeti /
yadyapi buddhisukhaduḥkhānyapi manaso viṣayaḥ, tathāpi, tasyaiva viṣayatvena duḥkhatvopacāro cadviṣayīkriyamāṇaṃ duḥkhamupajanayati /
vakṣyati hi--viṣayā bodhyatvāditi /
na ca buddhirbudhyamānā duḥkhahetuḥ /
vakṣyati hi--buddhayastu sākṣāditi /
sukhaduḥkhayostu duḥkhahetutvameva nāsti, sukhasya vijātīyārambhakatve 'pi rāgamātrāmbhakatvāt /
duḥkhasya tu vijātīyārambhakatvādeva /
icchādveṣaprayatnāstu pratīyamānā eva sākṣād duḥkha janayanti /
tathā hi, mumukṣustāvadicchāmi dveṣmi yogābhyāsādanyatra prayata iti pratītyaiva duḥkhī bhavati, ahitasādhanatvenecchādveṣaprayatnānāṃ tenāvadhāritatvāt /
children.translated_text: For example, one who desires liberation, perceiving 'I desire, I am averse, I exert effort elsewhere than in <s>yoga</s>-practice,' becomes miserable through that very perception, because he has ascertained that desire, aversion, and effort are means to harm.

children.text: anyo 'pīṣyamāṇālābhe bubhukṣito 'smi pipāsito 'smīti pratītya duḥkhī bhavati /
children.translated_text: Another too, not obtaining what is desired, perceiving 'I am hungry, I am thirsty,' becomes miserable.

children.text: hitamevāhitamupalabhya dviṣato nivṛttabhramasya hitameva dveṣmi, dhiḍ māmiti duḥkham /
children.translated_text: One who hates what is actually beneficial, having perceived the beneficial itself [as harmful], when his delusion ceases and [he realizes] 'I hate what is beneficial — shame on me!' — that is suffering.

children.text: evamaniṣṭa evārthe iṣṭabuddhyā prayatamānasya nivṛtte bhrame tathā alasasya prayatnamupalabhyaiva duḥkhamityetāvataita eva manaso viṣayatvena nirdiṣṭāḥ //
children.translated_text: Likewise, when one who exerts effort toward an undesirable thing with the notion that it is desirable has his delusion removed, or when a lazy person perceives his own effort — suffering arises from that very [perception]. By this much, these [desire, aversion, and effort] alone are designated as objects of the mind.

Now, in the <s>sūtra</s> on smell and the rest (1.1.12), five sense-organs are well known. And nowhere else either are there said to be six — to this he says: 'the sixth.' The implication is: by the reasoning of the system (<s>tantrayukti</s>). Now, the objects too are established as just five, being mutually distinct means and ends, by division and examination, not six — to this he says: 'of that.' Although cognition, pleasure, and pain are also objects of the mind, nevertheless, suffering is figuratively attributed to them only by virtue of being its object — that which is made into an object generates suffering. For it will be said: 'objects, because they are to be known.' And cognition, while cognizing, is not a cause of suffering. For it will be said: 'but cognitions, directly.' As for pleasure and pain, they are simply not causes of suffering — pleasure, even though it initiates something of a different kind, only initiates attachment. But pain, precisely because it initiates something of a different kind. Desire, aversion, and effort, however, being directly apprehended, directly generate suffering.

children.text:
nanu jarākuṣṭādyupahatadehasyopalabhyamānameva śarīraṃ duḥkhahetuḥ, tatrāpi viṣayatvenaiva duḥkhatvopacāraḥ syādityata āha--yadyapīti /
anyathāsya duḥkhahetubhāvo 'sādhāraṇa iti śeṣaḥ /
viṣayatvena puraridaṃ na ṣaḍbhyo bhidyate /
children.translated_text: Now, for one whose body is afflicted by old age, leprosy, and the like, the perceived body itself is a cause of suffering — would not the figurative attribution of suffering apply there too by virtue of being an object? To this he says: 'although.' Otherwise, its being a cause of suffering is distinctive — this is the remainder. By virtue of being an object, this [body] is not different from the six [objects].

children.text:
asādhāraṇendriyasaṃbandhāttu bhidyate /
na tu svarūpeṇa, viṣayāṇāmanantatvādityarthaḥ /
iha yadyapi anuṣaḍgo 'vinābhāva iti vakṣyati vāttikakāraḥ, tadupapattaye ca samānanimittatāsāmānādhāratāsamānopalabhyatāḥ, tathāpi na
children.translated_text: But it is different due to its connection with a distinctive sense-organ. Not, however, in its own nature, since objects are infinite in number — this is the meaning. Here, although the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> will say 'concomitance means invariable co-occurrence,' and for establishing that, [he adduces] commonality of cause, commonality of substratum, and commonality of apprehension; nevertheless,

children.text:
tāvanmātreṇāvinābhāvo nirvahati /
sādhāraṇanimittāyāmapi hyanyatarāsādhāraṇanimittanivṛttāvekataranivṛttau itarānavṛttisaṃbhavāt /
ata eva ādhārasyopalabdhisādhanasya ca sāmye 'pyekatarasya kāraṇābhāvenābhāve 'pyanyatarasabhdāvenāvinābhāva ityāśaḍkya sukhasya duḥkhānuṣaḍgopapattaye duḥkhahetvanuṣaṅgamevāha--sādhaneti /
ato na dvitīyasūtravārtikaṭīkābhyāṃ virodhaḥ /
sādhanapāratantryaṃ kāryātvāt /
akāryasya ca sukhasyābhāvāt /
pāratantryaṃ ca daṃḥkhahetuḥ /
yadāha--
children.translated_text: invariable co-occurrence is not established by those alone. For even when the cause is common, if the distinctive cause of one ceases, one may cease while the other does not — this is possible. Therefore, even when substratum and means of apprehension are the same, when one is absent due to absence of [its] cause while the other is present, [there is no invariable co-occurrence] — anticipating this doubt, in order to establish the concomitance of pleasure with suffering, he states the concomitance with the cause of suffering itself: 'of means.' Therefore there is no contradiction with the second <s>sūtra</s>, <s>vārttika</s>, and <s>ṭīkā</s>. Dependence on means [constitutes suffering], because of being an effect. And because there is no pleasure that is not an effect. And dependence is a cause of suffering. As it is said:

children.text: sarva paravaśaṃ duḥkham /
children.translated_text: Everything dependent on another is suffering.

children.text: iti /
children.translated_text: Thus.

children.text: kṣayitvaṃ ca sukhasya samavāyikāraṇavattvāt /
children.translated_text: And the perishability of pleasure, because it has a material cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>),

children.text: tadapi duḥkhahetuḥ, iṣṭaviyogo hi duḥkhaṃ janayatīti /
children.translated_text: that too is a cause of suffering, for separation from the desired generates suffering.

children.text: kṣayitvaṃ kāme satīti tu vyākhyānaṃ duḥkhahetava iti bahuvacanaviruddham, ataḥ svatantramevedaṃ hetutrayam //
children.translated_text: But the explanation 'perishability when there is desire' contradicts the plural in 'causes of suffering' — therefore this triad of causes is independent.

children.text:
kāma icchā /
sāca sukhatatsādhanayorvyāpikā /
na hi sukha tatsādhanaṃ vā anicchataḥ sukhaṃ nāma sukhasādhanaṃ ca /
tadapi sulabhaṃ durlabhaṃ ca /
tatra durlabhecchā duḥkhaikaphalaiva /
sulabhecchātvaniṣiddhasādhanagocarā niṣiddhasādhanagocarā ca /
tatra niṣaddhasādhānagocarāpi svarūpataḥ kāryataścādharmajananadvāreṇāvaśyaṃ duḥkhaphaleti /
aniṣiddhasulabhasādhānagocarāpi śarīrapāṭave satsati vā /
tatrāsati duḥkhahetureva /
śarīrādipāṭave 'pi savighnā nirvighnā ca /
tatra savighnā duḥkhameva prasūte /
nirvighnāpyaniṣṭasaṃbhinnaviṣayā tadviparītā ca /
tatra prathamā avaśyaṃ
children.translated_text: <s>Kāma</s> (desire) means wish. And that pervades both pleasure and its means. For one who does not desire pleasure or its means has neither pleasure nor means to pleasure. And that [means] is either easily obtainable or difficult to obtain. Among these, desire directed toward what is difficult to obtain has suffering alone as its fruit. Desire directed toward what is easily obtainable pertains either to permitted means or to prohibited means. Among these, [desire] pertaining to prohibited means, both in its own nature and in its effects, necessarily has suffering as its fruit through generating <s>adharma</s> (demerit). [Desire] pertaining to easily obtainable permitted means [depends on] whether bodily fitness is present or not. When it is absent, it is a cause of suffering alone. Even when bodily fitness exists, [desire] is either obstructed or unobstructed. Among these, obstructed [desire] produces suffering alone. Unobstructed [desire] too pertains either to an object mixed with the undesirable or to its opposite. Among these, the first necessarily

children.text:
duḥkhahetuḥ /
dvitīyā tu viphalā saphalā ca /
tatra prathamā duḥkhahetureva /
dvitīyā tu savilambaphalā avilambphalā ca /
tatra prathamā avaśyameva duḥkhahetuḥ /
dvitīyāpyanāyativiśuddhā tadviparītā ca /
tatra prathamā duḥkhahetureva /
dvitīyā tu viṣayasya piriṇativirasatvād duḥkhameva prasūte, ativyāmohād viṣayeṣveva magnasyecchāntarameva vā, ubhayathāpyanarthamūlamiti /
evaṃ sukhānuṣaktaḥ kāmo 'pi duḥkhaheturiti /
children.translated_text: Thus, even desire (<s>kāma</s>) conjoined with pleasure is a cause of suffering.

children.text: iha yadyapi rāgadveṣamohapravṛttayo 'pi duḥkhatadanuḍgisādhanabhāvādindriyādivat duḥkhatvena parisaṃkhyātumucitāstathāpi na śarīrendriyādivyatirekeṇāmūṣāmātmalābho duḥkhaṃ prati vyāpāro vā, indriyādīnāṃ punardeṣapravṛttyabhāve 'pi duḥkhaṃ prati vyāpāro jīvanmuktasyāstyeva /
children.translated_text: Here, although the activities of attachment, aversion, and delusion too are fit to be enumerated as suffering — like the sense-organs and the like — by virtue of their being causes of suffering and its accompaniments, nevertheless, apart from the body, sense-organs, and the like, these [mental afflictions] have neither independent existence nor an operation toward suffering. But the sense-organs and the like have an operation toward suffering even in the absence of the activity of defects, as is the case for one who is liberated while living (<s>jīvanmukta</s>).

children.text: pravṛttiphalaṃ tu dharmādharmau yadyapi sukhaduḥkhahetū, tathāpyekaviṃśatividha duḥkhamayasaṃsāranṛtyaśālā mūlastambhatvādanayornātra parisaṃkhyānam /
children.translated_text: But <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), which are the fruits of activity — although they are causes of pleasure and suffering, nevertheless, because they are the foundational pillars of the twenty-one-fold dance-hall of suffering that is <s>saṃsāra</s>, they are not enumerated here.

children.text: na hi bhāvini janmāntare śarīrendriyāviṣayabuddhisukhaduḥkhānyāhatya vyāpriyante yathā dharmādharmau //
children.translated_text: For in a future birth that is to come, body, sense-organs, objects, cognition, pleasure, and suffering do not operate in conjunction [with each other] in the way that <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> do.

[it] is a cause of suffering. The second, however, is either fruitless or fruitful. Among those, the first is itself a cause of suffering. The second, however, either has delayed fruit or immediate fruit. Among those, the first is necessarily a cause of suffering. The second too is either impure with respect to the future or the opposite. Among those, the first is itself a cause of suffering. But the second, due to the insipidity of the object upon transformation, produces only suffering — or, due to extreme delusion, [the person] remains immersed in objects alone, or merely [arises] another desire — in either case, it is the root of harm.

children.text:
etadevābhisaṃdhāya kāraṇarūpadharmādharmocchedakrameṇa kāryarūpaikaviṃśatividhaduḥkhasyocchedovārttikakṛtā darśita iti tathaiva vāttikamavatārayati--uktaprakāreti /
iha cāgāmidharmādharmanivṛttāvupāyastatsādhanapravṛttiparityāgaḥ, utpannanivṛtau tūpabhoga iti
children.translated_text: Intending precisely this, the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> has shown that through the sequential elimination of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> in their causal form, the elimination of the twenty-one-fold suffering in its effect-form [is achieved] — thus he introduces the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'uktaprakāra' (in the manner stated). And here, the means for the cessation of future <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> is the abandonment of the activity that produces them; for the cessation of [those] already arisen, however, it is experience (<s>upabhoga</s>) — thus

children.text:
darśitam /
tadubhayamapyanupapannam, vāgbuddhiśarīrāmbhaṃ parityajya jīvitumaśaktayatvāt /
mṛte 'pi śadīrādyantarajralepasya dupaneyatvāt, upabhāgaścāśakyaḥ, aniyatavipākasamayatvāt, anantatvādanantaphalatvācca /
bhogāvasthāyāmapyanantakarmāntarotpādanatāyā avarāmāt /
atha kathañcidupabhogānutpādābhyāmutpannānutpannayoḥ śakyaḥ prakṣayaḥ, tarhi śāstravaiyarthyaprasaṅgaḥ, tata eva tatsiddherityāśaḍkya vārttikasyopaskurūte--saṃśayādīti /
saṃśayādītyādipadena caturdaśāpi nyāyaparikaratvena saṃgṛhītāḥ /
paramanyāyetyanene mūlamūlībhāvavyavasthitāni catvāryapi pramāṇāni /
nyāyo mārga iva nyāyamārgaḥ, niḥreyasabhūmeḥ prāptihetutvāt /
dvādaśavidhetyātmādi prameyam /
tadanena śāstrasyāvasaropayogau darśitau /
tattvaparibhāvanetyanenābhyāsasya /
tadevaṃ pūrvoktena nyāyena mokṣamāṇasya śāstre pravṛttiḥ /
tataḥ parikaraparijñānam /
tato nyāyamārgapariśodhanam /
tatastena dvādaśavidhaprameyāsādanam, tato 'bhyāsaḥ, tataḥ prasaṃkhyānam /
tataḥ samūladoṣānuṣaṅganirmokṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: from that, release from the attachment of defects together with their root;

children.text: tato 'pravṛttiḥ /
children.translated_text: from that, cessation of activity;

children.text: tata āgāminordharmādharmayorasaṃcayaḥ /
children.translated_text: from that, non-accumulation of future <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>;

children.text: ityevamanāgataḥ pravāho nivāritaḥ //
children.translated_text: thus the future stream [of saṃsāra] is prevented.

it has been shown. Both of those are untenable, since it is impossible to live while abandoning all activity of speech, mind, and body. Even upon death, the stain within the body and so forth is difficult to remove. And experience [of all karmic results] is impossible, because the time of maturation is indeterminate, and because [karmic impressions] are infinite and produce infinite results. Even in the state of experiencing [results], there is no cessation of the production of further karmic actions. Now, if somehow through both experience and non-production, the exhaustion of arisen and un-arisen [karma] is possible, then there would follow the uselessness of the <s>śāstra</s>, since liberation would be accomplished by that alone. Anticipating this, he augments the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'saṃśayādī' (from doubt, etc.). By the word 'ādi' in 'saṃśayādī,' all fourteen [categories] are included as accessories of the <s>Nyāya</s> [system]. By 'paramanyāya' (supreme method), the four <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) are [included], as established in their hierarchical relation. <s>Nyāya</s> (method) is like a path — the <s>nyāya</s>-path, because it is the means of reaching the ground of the highest good. 'Dvādaśavidha' (twelve-fold) refers to the objects of knowledge beginning with <s>ātman</s>. By this, the occasion and utility of the <s>śāstra</s> have been shown. By 'tattvapari-bhāvana' (contemplation of truth), [the utility] of practice [has been shown]. Thus, by the aforementioned method, the activity [is as follows]: of one who seeks liberation, engagement with the <s>śāstra</s>; from that, knowledge of the accessories; from that, purification of the <s>nyāya</s>-path; from that, through that [purified path], attainment of the twelve-fold objects of knowledge; from that, practice; from that, <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (discriminative contemplation);

children.text: yadyapi ca yāvaccharīrādibhāvinī pravṛttistathāpi doṣānuṣaṅgasahakārivirahānnāsau pravṛttiḥ
children.translated_text: And although activity persists as long as there is the body and so forth, nevertheless, due to the absence of the cooperation of the attachment of defects, that is not [karmically productive] activity,

children.text:
tatkāryāsamarthatvāditi /
utpannabhogamupapādayati--anādīti /
yadyapi yathānādau bhāvaparamparāyāṃ karmāṇi pracīyante tathāpacīcante 'pi /
na hyārambhe paraṃ bhavasyānāditā /
nanūpabhoge karmārambho hyadhikāriṇi śarīre /
tacca śarīrakoṭimadhyapatitamekaṃ śarīraṃ
children.translated_text: because it is incapable of producing that effect. He establishes the experience of arisen [karma]: 'anādī' (beginningless). Although, just as in a beginningless series of existents karmic actions accumulate, so too they diminish. For the beginninglessness of existence does not pertain only to the beginning [of accumulation]. Now, the undertaking of [new] karma during experience [of results occurs] in a qualified body. And that body, falling within the series of bodies, is one body

children.text:
kadācit kiñcit kvacideva /
bhogastu nāstyeva taccharīraṃ yatra nāsti, bhogasya tadāyatanatvāt /
tasmādāyavyayaparyālocanayā parimitameva karma /
ata eva niyavipākasamayamapi /
tasya ca kramabhāvibhirapi kiyadbhiḥ
children.translated_text: at some time, of some kind, in some place only. But experience is never absent from any body where it is present, because experience has that [body] as its basis. Therefore, by calculation of income and expenditure, karma is indeed finite. And for that very reason, the time of its maturation is also determinate. And through experience by even a few

children.text: kaiścideva śarīrairūpabhogāt prakṣayo 'pi na durūpapādaḥ /
children.translated_text: particular bodies arising in sequence, exhaustion [of karma] too is not difficult to establish.

children.text: tathāpyāgamaprāmāṇyāt kāyayaugapadyasyāpi prasaṃkhyānaphalatayā siddhatvādanantāmaniyatavipākasamayatāṃ cābhyupagamyaiva parihṛtam /
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, since the authority of scripture [establishes that] even the simultaneity of bodies is a result of <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s> (discriminative contemplation), the objections of infinite [karma] and indeterminate time of maturation have been answered by accepting [that possibility].

children.text: vibhūtimatā anekakālopabhogyamapyekadā bhujyata ityatra samudrapānamudāharaṇam /
children.translated_text: For one endowed with supernatural power, even what is to be experienced over many lifetimes can be experienced at once — here the drinking of the ocean is cited as an example.

children.text: yogardhiprabhāvasampanno vividhaphalabhogino vicitrasvabhāvānekadaiva bahūn kāyān icchāmātreṇaiva nirmimīta ityatra daṇḍakāraṇyasṛṣṭirūdāhaṇamiti //
children.translated_text: One endowed with the power of yogic supernatural ability creates many bodies of diverse natures at once by mere will, for the experience of various fruits — here the creation of <s>Daṇḍakāraṇya</s> is cited as an example.

children.text:
iha kecid āhuḥ, duḥkhanivṛtti puruṣārtha eva svarūpato na bhavati sopādhitvāt /
sukhaṃ duḥkhābhāve satyeva bhavatīti sukhasādhanāntaravat duḥkhābhāvo 'pi mṛtyate /
na nu sa eva puruṣasya samīhita iti /
taduktam,
children.translated_text: Here some say: the cessation of suffering is not in itself a human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), because it is conditional. Pleasure occurs only when there is an absence of suffering — hence the absence of suffering is desired just like any other means to pleasure. Is it not the case that this itself is what a person desires? To this it is said:

children.text: varaṃ vṛndāvane 'raṇye kroṣṭatvamabhivāñchitum /
children.translated_text: 'Better to wish for the state of a jackal in the forest of <s>Vṛndāvana</s>,

children.text: na tu vaiśeṣikī muktiṃ gautamo gantumicchati //
children.translated_text: than for <s>Gautama</s> to desire the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> liberation!' —

children.text:
iti /
tadanupapannam, viparyāsasyāpi saṃbhavāt, bhojanādisukhe satyeva hi bubhukṣādiduḥkhaṃ nivartata iti duḥkhanivṛttyarthameva bhojanādisukhaṃ mṛgyate /
na punastadeva tasya samīhitamiti kiṃ na kalpayate /
kvacid duḥkhabhāve 'pi sukhasyeṣyamāṇatvā diti cet--na, duḥkhanivṛtterapi kvacit sukhābhāve 'pīṣyamāṇatvādeva /
duḥkhanivṛttau satyāṃ sukhameva bhaviṣyatītyabhisandhistāvadastīti cet-na, sukhāvasthāyāṃ niyamato duḥkhaviraho bhaviṣyatītyabhisandhestatrāpi saṃbhavāt /
tasmād yadyapi duḥkhahānau sukham, sukhe ca duḥkhahānirniyatā, tathāpi
children.translated_text: thus. That is untenable, because the reverse is also possible. For it is only when there is pleasure such as eating that the suffering of hunger and the like ceases — thus pleasure from eating and the like is sought only for the purpose of cessation of suffering. Why does one not suppose that this [cessation of suffering] itself is what is desired? If it is said that even in the absence of suffering, pleasure is desired — no, because the cessation of suffering too is desired even in the absence of pleasure. If it is said that there is an underlying intention: 'when there is cessation of suffering, pleasure itself will arise' — no, because even in the case of pleasure, the underlying intention 'when there is a state of pleasure, there will necessarily be freedom from suffering' is equally possible. Therefore, although pleasure [arises] from the removal of suffering and removal of suffering [arises] from pleasure in a determinate manner, nevertheless

children.text: parasparanirapekṣameva puruṣārthatvamanayoricchayoḥ apyasaṃkīrṇaviṣayatvāt //
children.translated_text: the status of being a human goal belongs to each of these independently of the other, since the desires for them have non-overlapping objects.

children.text:
anyastvāha--bhavatyeva hi duḥkhahāniḥ puruṣārthaḥ, kiṃ tvanubhūyamānatayā /
na hi viṣādijanyamohāvasthāyāṃ duḥkhanivṛttiriti tadarthaṃ prekṣāvantaḥ pravartante /
tasmāt mokṣe duḥkhahānerananubhūyamānatvānna puruṣārthatvamiti /
taduktam,
children.translated_text: Another, however, says: the cessation of suffering is indeed a human goal, but only insofar as it is experienced. For in a state of stupor caused by poison or the like, the cessation of suffering does not [function as a goal], and discerning persons do not act for that purpose. Therefore, since in <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) the cessation of suffering is not experienced, it is not a human goal. To this it is said:

children.text: duḥkhābhāvo 'pi nāvedyaḥ puruṣārthatayeṣyate /
children.translated_text: 'Even the absence of suffering, if not experienced, is not accepted as a human goal;

children.text: na hi mūrcchādyavasthārthaṃ pravṛtto dṛśyate sudhīḥ //
children.translated_text: for a wise person is not seen to act for the purpose of attaining a state of unconsciousness.' —

children.text:
iti /
tadapyanupapannam, putrādiviyogajanyaduḥkhahānimicchato keṣāñcid viṣaśastrodūndhanadāvapi pravṛttidarśanāt /
prekṣāvanto naivaṃ kurvantīti cet--na, puruṣārthatvāvirodhāt /
na hi paradāreṣu śāstraniṣedhāḍkuśanivāritāḥ prekṣāvanto na pravartanta iti /
na tatra kāmaḥ puruṣārthaḥ, api tvalpīyaḥ sukhaṃ mahānanartha iti nivṛttiḥ /
tathā viṣādāvapi pravṛttasya śāstragarhitatvādalpīyānanartho nivartate /
mahīyān pravartata iti na te pravartanta iti /
iyameva hi prekṣā yat puruṣārthatve 'pi lokaśāstravirodhaparāmarśaḥ, na tu apuruṣārthatvādeva svarūpeṇeṣyamāṇatāmātranibandhanatvāt puruṣarthatāyāḥ /
ataeva na yatra lokaśāstravirodhaḥ, tatra vyādhyādiparipīḍitāḥ prayāgavaṭaprapātānaśanādināpi dehaṃ tyajantaḥ prekṣāvanto dṛśyante /
na hi kaścid duḥkhanivṛttimanubhaviṣyāmīti tatsādhane pravartate, api tu duḥkha hāsyāmīti /
api ca duḥkhanivṛtteranubhūyamānatāmātraṃ vivakṣitam,
children.translated_text: thus. That too is untenable, because we see some who desire the cessation of suffering caused by separation from sons and the like engaging even in poison, weapons, and drowning. If it is said that discerning persons do not act thus — no, because there is no contradiction with [its] being a human goal. For it is not the case that discerning persons, restrained by the goad of scriptural prohibition, do not engage with others' wives, and therefore desire for them is not a human goal. Rather, the cessation [of that engagement] is because the pleasure is minor while the harm is great. Similarly, even for one who has engaged with poison and the like, the minor harm is averted because it is censured by scripture; the greater [harm of continued suffering] drives [him] to act — thus they do not [truly] act [wrongly]. For this very thing is discernment: the consideration of conflict with worldly and scriptural norms even when something is a human goal — not that it is not a human goal by its own nature, since being a human goal is grounded merely in being desired in itself. And for this very reason, where there is no conflict with worldly and scriptural norms, discerning persons are seen to abandon their bodies even through hurling themselves from the banyan tree at <s>Prayāga</s>, fasting unto death, and the like, when tormented by disease and so forth. For no one acts toward the means [of cessation] thinking 'I shall experience the cessation of suffering,' but rather thinking 'I shall abandon suffering.' Moreover, is the mere experienceability of the cessation of suffering what is intended,

children.text:
duḥkhanivṛttisattāvadhirvā? ādyaścet, tuṣyatu durjanaḥ carame janmanyanubhūyata eva samādhiprabhāvāt /
ātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttiranāgatā vartamānāpyaciramanubhūyata eva /
dvitīye tu prasaktakaṇṭakādihetukadaḥkhanivṛtterapuruṣārthatvaprasaṅgaḥ, sarvadānanubhūyamānatvāt /
tathātve vā viṣayāntarasaṃcārābhāvaprasaṅgāt, nivṛtteḥ sarvadā tādavasthyāditi /
tasmāt sarvadānanubhūyamānāpi yathā kaṇṭakādijanyaduḥkhanivṛttiḥ puruṣārthatayā puruṣaṃ prayojayati, tathā śāstrārthabhūtāpi /
tadidaṃ duḥkhanivṛtterapuruṣārthatvamananubhūyamānatayaiva cāpuruṣārthatvamiti pakṣadvayamatinirvalamityetadityupekṣya tṛtīyaṃ śaṅkate--syādetaditi /
taduktam,
children.translated_text: or is it the actual existence of the cessation of suffering? If the first — let the wicked be satisfied! In the final birth, it is indeed experienced through the power of <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption). The ultimate cessation of suffering, though pertaining to the future, even when present, will be experienced before long. If the second, then there would follow that the cessation of suffering caused by thorns and the like that are in contact [with the body] is not a human goal, since it is never experienced [as such]. Or, in that case, there would follow the absence of movement toward any other object, since the cessation [of suffering] would always remain in the same state. Therefore, just as the cessation of suffering caused by thorns and the like, even though never experienced [as a distinct experience], motivates a person as a human goal, so too does [the cessation of suffering] that is the subject-matter of the <s>śāstra</s>. Thus, this — that the cessation of suffering is not a human goal, and that it is not a human goal because it is not experienced — these two positions are exceedingly weak. Setting them aside, he raises a third objection: 'syādetad' (this may be so). To this it is said:

children.text: asatyāni durantāni samavyayaphalāni ca /
children.translated_text: 'Things that are non-existent, interminable, of equal cost and benefit,

children.text: aśakyāni ca vastūni nārabheta vicakṣaṇaḥ /
children.translated_text: and impossible — a wise person should not undertake [them].' —

children.text:
iti /
siddhāntavārttikamuddīpayati--yadyapīti /
tadanena madhuviṣasaṃpṛktānnabhojanadṛṣṭāntena samavyayaphalatvamapavargasya nirākṛtam /
yathā hyatrānarthasya bhūyastvamarthasya tu kṣudratvam, na tathāpavarge 'pīti /
children.translated_text: thus. He illuminates the settled doctrine of the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'yadyapī' (although). By this, through the illustration of eating food mixed with honey and poison, the objection that <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) has equal cost and benefit is refuted. For just as in that [case] harm predominates while benefit is trifling, it is not so in the case of <s>apavarga</s>.

children.text: etenaitadapi nirastaṃ yaduktam, yathā duḥkhaśabalaṃ saṃsārasukhamanādeyam, tathā sukhaśabalatayā duḥkhamapyupādeyaṃ kiṃ na syāt? dṛśyante hi sukhārthino yagādiduḥkhamanubhavanta iti /
children.translated_text: By this, the following [objection] too is refuted: 'Just as the pleasure of <s>saṃsāra</s>, being mixed with suffering, is not worth taking, so too suffering, being mixed with pleasure, should be worth taking — why not? For we see those who desire pleasure undergoing the suffering of sacrifices and the like.'

children.text: yasya duḥkhamupādeyaṃ heyaṃ tasya kimucyatām /
children.translated_text: 'For one for whom suffering is worth taking — what should be called worth avoiding for him?

children.text: heyahīnasya kā muktiḥ kena vāpyupadiśyate //
children.translated_text: For one who has nothing to avoid, what liberation [is there]? And by whom would he be instructed?' —

children.text:
iti /
yastu ghanataraduḥkhatimiranirantarāt saṃsārakāntārāt sukhakhadyotikāsu dyotamānāsvapi bibheti taṃ prati ayaṃ nirastatamaskatayā sugamo mārga upadiśyata iti /
tadidamuktam-tena mā bhūdatadityādi /
children.translated_text: Thus it is said: 'tena mā bhūd atad' (therefore let it not be otherwise), etc.

children.text: nanvevaṃ sati nāsya sarvārthatā /
children.translated_text: Now, if this is so, this [śāstra] does not serve all purposes.

children.text: tathā ca jagataḥ śamāyetyanena virodha ityata āha--avivekināmapīti /
children.translated_text: And thus there would be a contradiction with [the statement that it is] 'for the peace of the world' — to this he says: 'avivekināmapī' (even of the undiscerning).

children.text: yadyapi kasyacidapravṛttāvapi na sarvārthatā asya hīyata iti prapañcitamadhastāt, tathāpi heyaṃ heyatvenāgṛhṇanto mandāḥ kāruṇikeṇa grāhayitavyā ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Although it has been elaborated below that even if someone does not engage, the [śāstra's] serving of all purposes is not diminished, nevertheless, the dull-witted who do not apprehend what is to be avoided as to-be-avoided should be made to apprehend it by the compassionate one — this is the meaning.

thus. But for one who fears the wilderness of <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is filled with the unbroken darkness of dense suffering — even as the fireflies of pleasure glimmer [within it] — to him this path is taught as easy to traverse, being free from that darkness.

children.text:
nanu śāstreṇa tattvajñānād vairāgyam, vairāgyācca śāstre pravṛttiriti durūttaramitaretarāśrayatvamityata āha--śāstre pravṛttīti /
duḥkhādudvijato bhogavaimukhyamātramiha vairāgyaṃ vivakṣitam, na tu rāgābhāva evetyarthaḥ /
iṣṭāniṣṭaprāptiparihārārthatayā dvaividhyaśaḍkāmapanayati--aikarūpyaṃ dvairūpyaṃ ceti /
nanu puruṣabhede 'pi pravṛtteḥ dvaividhyameva /
na hi kaścit sukhaṃ prāptumiva duḥkhamapyāptuṃ pravartate /
nāpi kaścit duḥkhahānāyeva sukhahānāyāpītyata āha--puruṣabhedo rāgavairāgyābhyāmiti /
children.translated_text: nor does anyone [act] for the removal of pleasure as for the removal of suffering — to this he says: 'puruṣabhedo rāgavairāgyābhyām' (the difference of persons is by attachment and dispassion).

children.text: nanu sukhasya heyatvameva kuta ityata āha--prāptavyasyeti /
children.translated_text: Now, whence the to-be-avoided nature of pleasure? — to this he says: 'prāptavyasya' (of what is to be attained).

children.text: avivekināṃ tu pravṛttirdvirūpetyuktam /
children.translated_text: But the engagement of the undiscerning is of two kinds — thus it is said.

children.text: vārttikakṛtā iti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'By the author of the <s>Vārttika</s>' is to be supplied.

Now, from the <s>śāstra</s> [arises] knowledge of truth, from knowledge of truth [arises] dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>), and from dispassion [arises] engagement with the <s>śāstra</s> — thus there is the difficult-to-answer fault of mutual dependence. To this he says: 'śāstre pravṛttī' (engagement with the śāstra). What is intended here as dispassion is merely the aversion to enjoyments arising from recoiling from suffering, not the complete absence of attachment (<s>rāga</s>) — this is the meaning. He dispels the doubt of a twofold nature [of engagement] based on the purposes of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired: 'aikarūpyaṃ dvairūpyaṃ ca' (uniformity and duality). Now, even with the difference of persons, the engagement is of two kinds only. For no one acts to obtain suffering in the way one acts to obtain pleasure;

children.text:
prakṛtamupasaṃharannevāprakṛtopanipātaśaḍkāmapyapanetuṃ vṛttavartiṣyamāṇe anukīrtayati--tadaneneti /
tadavayavaṃ vivarītumuktatātparyasphoraṇārthamiti śeṣaḥ /
alaukikatvāt /
lokasyāsmadādernityaparokṣatvāt /
ayuktam aprāmāṇikam /
vipratiṣiddhaṃ mitho vyāpakaviruddham /
pravṛttyai niṣkampapravṛttyai /
kiṃ tarhi? pramāṇamiti /
gṛhītamityanuvartate /
rajatajñānamidaṃ śuklabhāsvararūpavad dravyaṃ rajatamityevaṃ jñānamityarthaḥ /
paricchinatti uktamarthamālambya paricchittirūpaṃ jāyata ityarthaḥ /
śuktikājñānamapīti /
idaṃ śuklabhāsvararūpaṃ śuktikādravyaṃ na rajatamiti jñānamityarthaḥ /
yadyevaṃ kathamanayorbādhyabādhakabhāva ityata āha--kevalamiti /
rajatasamāropāpavādābhyāmiti /
children.translated_text: Summarizing the topic at hand and also removing the suspicion of an irrelevant intrusion, he recapitulates what has been said and what is about to be said: 'By this...' The remainder is: 'in order to elucidate the stated purport by analyzing its components.' Because it is beyond ordinary experience. Because for ordinary people like us, it is always directly perceptible. 'Improper' means lacking valid authority. 'Contradictory' means mutually opposed to the pervading. 'For action' means for unhesitating action. 'What then? A <s>pramāṇa</s>' — 'is apprehended' is to be supplied. 'The cognition of silver' means the cognition 'this substance having a white lustrous form is silver' — this is the meaning. 'Determines' means a cognition of the nature of determination arises taking the stated object as its basis — this is the meaning. 'The cognition of nacre also' — this means the cognition 'this white lustrous substance is nacre, not silver' — this is the meaning. If so, how is there a relation of sublation between these two? To this he says: 'Merely...' Through the superimposition and negation of silver.

children.text: samāropāpavādasvabhāvatayetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: by virtue of having the nature of superimposition and negation.

children.text:
tadevaṃ paricchedadvāreṇa paricchedakamunnīyata iti paricchedasyaiva sāmānyaviśeṣayoḥ paricchedatvāparicchedatve darśite /
na caikasyaiva jñānasya viruddhadharmasaṃsargaḥ /
jātyā hi buddhiranubhavaḥ smṛtiśca /
tatra smutirapramaiva /
anubhavastu svarūpānubhavo 'svarūpānubhavaśca /
so 'yaṃ viṣayakṛto viśeṣaḥ /
nānāviṣayā caikā buddhirbhavatyeva /
tataśca saiva buddhiḥ svarūpāvasthitenārthena nirūpyamāṇā pramā /
asvarūpāvasthitena nirūpyamāṇā tvaprameti tathābhūtāvacchinnānubhavatvameva pramāṇatvam /
atathābhūtena tvavacchinnamapramāṇatvamiti bhavati apramāṇasyāpi sāmānyaparicchedakatvamiti /
racitā bhūmiḥ /
kimetāvatetyāha --asti tāvadasādhāraṇaṃ kāraṇamasamarthāyāḥ pravṛttestathaivonnīyamānam /
tasya ca vyāpāro viparītārthapariccheda evāsādhāraṇaḥ /
taccaivaṃbhūtavyāpāropakaraṇamapramāṇamiti vyavahniyate /
evaṃ ca pravṛttisāmarthyāsāmarthyasaṃdehe 'pi yadi tajjanakamapramāṇamasamarthaiva sā /
children.translated_text: And thus, even when there is doubt about the competence or incompetence of an action, if its cause is an invalid means of cognition, the action itself is incompetent.

children.text: atha na tadapramāṇam, tajjanyā pravṛttirapi nāsamarthetyapramāṇānniyataḥ samarthapravṛttivyatirekaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if it is not an invalid means of cognition, then the action produced by it too is not incompetent — thus the invariable exclusion of competent action from an invalid means of cognition is established.

children.text: pramāṇaṃ cātrobhayavyatirekagrāhakaṃ viruddhakāryatvaṃ liṅgam /
children.translated_text: And the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) here is the inferential mark of 'being a contrary effect,' which apprehends both exclusions.

children.text: prakṛtakāryasya tadvyatirekagrāhi ca pratyakṣamadhyavaseyamiti nāpramāṇādarthavyabhicāriṇor'thavyabhicārijñānavyāpārādityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And direct perception is to be understood as that which apprehends the exclusion of the effect in question — thus from an invalid means of cognition, through the operation of cognition that deviates from the object and is itself object-deviating,

Thus, through the door of determination, the determiner is inferred; and in this way, both the determination and non-determination of the general and particular aspects of determination have been shown. And contradictory properties do not belong to one and the same cognition. For cognition is by its class either experience or memory. Among these, memory is indeed not valid cognition. But experience is either of the real form or of the unreal form. This distinction is caused by the object. And a single cognition can indeed have multiple objects. Therefore, that very cognition, when evaluated in relation to the object as it truly is, is valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>); when evaluated in relation to the object as it is not, it is invalid — and thus being valid means being an experience delimited by that condition; being invalid means being delimited by the contrary condition. Thus even an invalid cognition can be a determiner in the general sense. The ground has been prepared. What follows from all this, he says: There exists, to begin with, an uncommon cause of incompetent action, which is inferred in just this way. And its operation, specifically the determination of a contrary object, is what is uncommon. And that which is the instrument of such an operation is designated as an invalid means of cognition (<s>apramāṇa</s>).

children.text:
siddho vyatirekaḥ, ki cāta ityata āha--tathā ceti /
arthavattvamarthāvyabhicāritvam, arthāvyabhicāryanubhavajanakatvamityarthaḥ /
nanu tasyā ityatra kathamanantaratvena prakṛtāmasamarthāṃ vihāya vyavahitvenāprakṛtāpi samarthaiva pravṛtti /
parāmṛśyata ityata āha--asamarthā tviti /
pūrvaprakāntaṃ yogyameva prakṛtamucyate, na tvanantaroktamityarthaḥ /
nanvanuditasyānuvādaḥ kkopayujyata ityata āha--saṃpratīti /
pūrvaṃ vyākhyātumidānīmākṣeptumityarthaḥ /
ākṣepasamādhānayoḥ sphuṭāvabhāsitve 'pi saṃgrahavivaraṇayoḥ paunarūktyaṃ pariharannāha--ākṣipatīti /
children.translated_text: the exclusion is established. What follows from this? To this he says: 'And thus...' 'Meaningfulness' means non-deviation from the object, i.e., the capacity to generate experience that does not deviate from the object — this is the meaning.

children.text:
saṃdehādapi pravṛttestatra tatra darśanāt nirūcchvāsamākṣepamujjīvayati--na tāvaditi /
amumevārthaṃ bhāṣyeṇa saṃvadati--seyamiti /
uktā bhāṣyakuteti śeṣaḥ /
kimato yadyevamityata āha--na ceti /
arthaviniścaya uktarūpaḥ śreyohetutānumānasahita iti yāvat /
prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇaṃ śreyohetutāliṅgaparāmarśaprasavocitamantareṇetyarthaḥ /
evaṃrūpatā ca
children.translated_text: Reviving without pause the objection from the observation that action occurs even from doubt, as seen here and there, he says: 'Not at first...' He corroborates this very point with the <s>bhāṣya</s> (commentary):

children.text:
prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇasya vyāptismaraṇasāhityameveti tasyāpi bījaṃ samuccinoti--śreyohetutānumānanimittavyāptigrahaṇaṃ ceti /
tābhyāṃ vineti /
svarūpaniścayaśreyohetutānumānābhyāṃ vinetyarthaḥ /
vyāptigrahaṇānantarye 'pi tatphalasyaivānumānasya yogyatayā prakrāntatvāt /
imameva vārtikārthaṃ pariśodhayan sphuṭayati--tadidamuktamiti /
niścayānumāne na prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇānumānabījabhūtavyāptigrahaṇābhyāṃ vinā /
te ca na pravṛttyā vinā /
pravṛttiśca na niścayānumānābhyāṃ vinetyākṣepasaṃkṣapaḥ /
iha ca dvidhā pravṛttiḥ, aihikaphalā āmuṣmikaphalā ca /
children.translated_text: Here action is of two kinds: having results in this life and having results in the next life.

children.text: tatrāmuṣmikaphalā prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇapūrvikaiva /
children.translated_text: Among these, action having results in the next life is indeed preceded by the ascertainment of validity.

children.text: aihikaphalā tu apekṣitopāyatājñānamātrādhīnā arthaniścayamapi nāpekṣate, prāgeva pramāṇasrūpajñānam /
children.translated_text: But action having results in this life depends merely on knowledge of the required means and does not even require ascertainment of the object, let alone knowledge of the nature of the means of valid knowledge.

children.text: kutastarāṃ tadviniścayam? yatrāpi pravṛtteḥ prāgeva pramāṇatattvaviniścayaḥ, tatrāpyasau svahetubalādāyato na pravṛttiṃ prati prayojakaḥ, anyathaikāntikavijayāniścaye prāmāṇyākṣepaka eva vijigīṣuḥ kathāyāṃ na pravarteta //
children.translated_text: Much less does it require the determination of that. Even where the determination of the true nature of <s>pramāṇa</s> precedes action, that determination, arising by the force of its own causes, does not depend on action.

'The ascertainment of validity being accompanied by the recollection of invariable concomitance' — he also gathers the seed of that: 'and the apprehension of the invariable concomitance that is the basis of the inference of being a means to the good.'

children.text:
na hi jalpato vitaṇḍayato vā avaśyamaikāntiko vijayaḥ /
tasmādarthāniścaye 'pi pravṛttirityubhayavādisiddhaṃ hṛdi nidhāya siddhāntamupakramate--tatra brūma iti /
dṛṣṭārtheṣviti adṛṣṭārthāgamādivyudāsaḥ, tatra pravṛtteḥ phalābhisaṃbandhāniścayāt /
anabhyāsadaśāpanneṣvityabhyāsadaśāpannāpitṛvacanādivyudāsaḥ /
te hi pramāṇatayā pravṛtteḥ prāgava niścīyante /
abhyāsaśvāviparīto vivakṣitaḥ /
tena svātmanyabhyāse 'pi pravṛttisāmarthyādeva tanniścayo viparītābhyāsavirahāt /
sa ca viṣayagocarastannāntarīyakārthagocaro vā tajjātīyatvāvadhāraṇopāyo yatra svarūpato 'pi nāsti tatra pravṛttisāmarthyādeva tadgocarasya prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇam, yathā vaidyavacanādanarthanivṛtti saṃbhāvayato 'saṃstutapradeśasthiteṣu mūleṣu /
yatra tu svarūpābhyāso 'styeva tadgataṃ tu śreyaḥsādhanamabhyastam, tatra pravṛttisāmarthyena tatsādhanatvagrāhiṇaḥ prāmāṇyam /
yathā angiḥ pākādisamartha iti saṃbhāvitāptatvasya vacanādupalabhya svayaṃ pacataḥ /
yatrāpi śreyaḥsādhanatve 'bhyāsaḥ svarūpe tvanabhyāsastatrāpi svarūpagocarasyaiva prāmāṇyaṃ pravṛttisāmarthyādavasīyate /
children.translated_text: even where there is practice with regard to the means of attaining the good but no practice with regard to its intrinsic nature, even there the validity of what pertains to the intrinsic nature is ascertained from the competence of action.

children.text: yathā agniḥ pākādisamartha eveti niścitavato 'pariśīlitavanavahnau /
children.translated_text: Just as one who is certain that fire is capable of cooking and so forth, even regarding an unexamined forest fire.

children.text: sarvatraivārthabhūyastvam, viparyaye tvanarthamāndyaṃ saṃbhāvayataḥ pravṛttiḥ /
children.translated_text: Everywhere the preponderance of meaningful results explains the action of one who considers harm to be slight in the contrary case.

children.text: svarūpaśreyaḥsādhanatvaniścaye 'pi phalasaṃdeha ivetyāha--no khalviti //
children.translated_text: Even when there is certainty about the intrinsic nature and its being a means to the good, there is still, as it were, doubt about the result — to this he says: 'Not indeed...'

For neither the debater nor the caviler necessarily achieves a decisive victory. Therefore, keeping in mind the proposition, accepted by both parties, that action occurs even without certainty about the object,

children.text:
tadamī saṃśayānā apipravartamānāḥ phala iva svarūpaśreyaḥsādhanatvayoriti śeṣaḥ /
pramāṇasya svarūpagrāhiṇaḥ śreyaḥsādhanatvagrāhiṇaścetyarthaḥ /
tattvaṃ pramāṇatvam, arthāvyabhicāripramāsādhanatvamiti yāvat /
viniścityārthāvyabhicāripramāviniścayadvāreṇeti śeṣaḥ /
tajjātīyasyānyasyaitāvataiva samarthatve abhyāsadaśāpannasyeti dṛṣṭārthapramāṇasaṃgrahārtham /
pravṛttisāmarthyāt prāgeva samarthāyāḥ pravṛtteḥ pūrvameveti /

tenāyamarthaḥ, yadyapi dṛṣṭārtheṣu abhyāsadaśāpanneṣvapi pravṛttisāmarthyamasti, tenāpi ca prāmāṇyamavadhārayituṃ tatra śakyate, tathāpi tajjātīyatvalakṣaṇenaiva liḍgena pravṛtteḥ prāgevāvadhārite prāmāṇye tatpramāturūttarakālaṃ pramitsaiva nāsti /
children.translated_text: Therefore the meaning is this: although even in the case of objects of direct experience that have reached the stage of habituation there is competence of action, and although validity can be ascertained even through that,

children.text: tannibandhanatvācca anumānapravṛtteḥ /
children.translated_text: and because inferential activity is based on that.

children.text: yadi punaḥ pramitsānapekṣameva samarthapravṛttijanakatvaṃ parāmṛśyate, tadā kā kṣatiḥ? tenāpyanumīyatāṃ prāmāṇyam /
children.translated_text: But if what is intended is the capacity to generate competent action independently of the desire to know, then what harm is there? Let validity be inferred through that as well.

children.text: pramāṇasaṃplavasyāpi vyavasthāpanāditi //
children.translated_text: Because even the total dissolution of means of valid knowledge can be resolved thereby.

The remainder is: 'Thus these people, even though doubting, still act — with regard to both the intrinsic nature and the means to the good, as with the result.' Of the <s>pramāṇa</s> that apprehends the intrinsic nature, the means to the good...

children.text:
nanu kimidaṃ tajjātīyatvam? na tāvat pramāṇajātīyatvam, sādhyāviśiṣṭatvaprasaṅgāt /
nāpi samarthapravṛttijanakajātīyatvam /
taddhi samarthapravṛttisaṃbandho vā syāt? tadupahito vā niyataprāgabhāvaḥ? na tāvadādyaḥ, pravṛtteḥ prāgeveti vacanāt /
nāpyuttaraḥ, tasyātīndriyasya liḍgaṃ vinā pratyetumaśakyatvāt /
liḍgaṃ ca tasya prāmāṇyaikaniyatasya yadyasti tadā prāmāṇyameva tenānumīyatām, kiṃ tajjātīyatvānumānena? prāmāṇyāniyatasya tu tasyānumānena kim? nāpi pratyakṣasiddha eva kaściddharmastajjātīyatvam /
pratyakṣatve tu tasyānabhyāsadaśāpananagocare 'pipramāṇe pratītiprasaṅgāt /
tathā ca
children.translated_text: Now, what is this 'being of the same type'? It is not being of the same type as a means of valid knowledge, for there would follow the fault of being indistinguishable from what is to be proved. Nor is it being of the same type as what generates competent action...

children.text: tatrāpi pravṛtteḥ prāgeva prāmāṇyāvadhāraṇaṃ syāt, vyāpterapi prāgeva pratītatvāt /
children.translated_text: Even there, the ascertainment of validity would precede action, since the invariable concomitance too is cognized even earlier.

children.text: na hyayaṃ kvacidapi tajjātīyatvena prāmāṇyaṃ nānumitavāt /
children.translated_text: For no one has ever inferred validity anywhere by means of 'being of the same type.'

children.text: tatra nāstyeva tajjātīyatvam, kiṃ pratyakṣeṇa pratīyatāmiti cet--na, abhyāsadaśāpanneṣu tajjātīyatvena prāmāṇye 'numīyamāne pravṛttisāmarthyānumitaprāmāṇyasya sādhanavikalatayā dṛṣṭāntābhāsatvaprasaṅgāt /
children.translated_text: If one says that being of the same type simply does not exist there, and let it be cognized through perception — no, because in cases that have reached the stage of habituation, validity is inferred through being of the same type.

children.text: tasmāt tajjātīyatvamatiriktaṃ na paśyāma iti //
children.translated_text: Therefore we do not see that 'being of the same type' is anything over and above this.

children.text:
satyam, tathāpi jñānasya viṣyanibandhanatvāt tattadviṣayopādhaya eva te te jñānopādhayastaistairūpādhibhirūpādhīyamānaṃ jñānameva tajjātīyaṃ tasya bhāvastattvaṃ bhavati /
te copādhayaḥ pratibhedaṃ svasaṃjñābhirabhidhātumaśakyā iti tajjātīyatvamityanayā vācobhaḍgyā darśitāḥ /
ata evātra vīpsā draṣṭavyā
children.translated_text: True, nevertheless, since cognition is dependent on its object, the very conditions pertaining to the respective objects are the conditions of the respective cognitions, and the cognition qualified by those conditions

children.text:
tattajjātīyatvamiti /
tathā hi, anubhavastāvat svarūpaprakārāvālambate /
tatra dharmisvarūpeṇopadhīyamāno 'nubhavaḥ pramaiveti tena rūpeṇānubhūte tasmin pramātvamevānubhūtaṃ bhavatītyagre sphuṭībhaviṣyati /
prakāraviṣayastvanubhava ubhayathā /
kaścit svarūpaprakāreṇopādhīyate, kaścidasvarūpaprakāreṇāpītyataḥ kvacit saṃśayaḥ /
tatra svarūpaprakāreṇopahitamanubhava vivektuṃ viśiṣṭāḥ prakāropādhayo bhavanti /
te ca niyamena vibhramaviṣayavirodhitayā nirdhāritasvabhāvabhedā guṇādaya eva /
tadidaṃ sāmānyatastāvallakṣaṇasahacaritalakṣyaviṣayajñānatvameva jñānagataṃ tajjātīyatvamiti pratyakṣe gatiḥ /
yadā tvapratyakṣe lakṣye lakṣaṇena jñānaṃ janyate tadānumānaṃ taditi tasyānyathaiva gatirbhaviṣyatīti /
tatra dravye gandhavati pṛthivījñānamityādi sāmānyataḥ /
karacaraṇādimati śarīrajñānam ityādi viśeṣataḥ /
guṇeṣu ketakyādau saurabhajñānam, śaḍkhādau śvetajñānamityādi /
karmaṇi tu avātulena tiṣṭhatā tīvravegāsaṃskṛtena calajjalādisvacchavilokanādivirahiṇā yad dravyaṃ calatītyupalabhyate tat tatheti /
evaṃ teṣu teṣu viśeṣeṣu te te viśeṣā vyabhicāravirodhino na pratipadamanukramituṃ śakyante /
tadevaṃ tattadupādhiviśiṣṭatattadviṣayānubhavatvameva tajjātīyatvamiti mantavyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, being of the same class should be understood as nothing but being an experience of that particular object, qualified by that particular qualifying condition.

children.text: tadevaṃbhūtasya jñānasya viṣayanāntarīyakatvenopādhyabhyāsa evābhyāsadaśāpannatvam /
children.translated_text: Thus, for cognition of such a nature, having reached the stage of repeated practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is nothing but the repeated practice of qualifying conditions, due to their being inseparable from the object.

children.text: yatra tu sa evārtho bhūyo bhūyo 'bhyastaḥ, tatra saṃvādakatvameva tajjātīyatvam /
children.translated_text: But where that very object has been repeatedly practiced again and again, there concordance (<s>saṃvādakatva</s>) alone constitutes being of the same class.

children.text: evaṃ tāvad bāhyapratyakṣaṃ samarthitam //
children.translated_text: Thus, external perception (<s>bāhyapratyakṣa</s>) has been so far established.

[It means] being of the same class as that particular [cognition]. For, experience first apprehends the essential form and the qualifier.
