The <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion) too [includes] the doctrine of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) and the like for the opponents. And for us, [conclusions] such as "darkness is the absence of light" [<s>Vaiśeṣika Sūtra</s> 5.2.19] and so forth. For all, <s>apavarga</s> is the absence of suffering. But the components — <s>tarka</s> (reasoning), <s>nirṇaya</s> (determination), <s>vāda</s> (discussion), <s>jalpa</s> (disputation), and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil) — have real distinctions only. <s>Hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious marks) are of two kinds — for example, "sound is non-eternal because it is devoid of existence," "because it is visual" and so forth. <s>Chala</s> (equivocation) and <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinders) also have real distinctions only. Among <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat), the varieties of disagreement have real distinctions, while the varieties of non-apprehension have non-real distinctions. This is what is said: "Thus, in each case it should be understood." Now, since in the <s>bhāṣya</s> there is not even a mention of non-real distinctions — therefore he says: "Here..." Of the two mutually contradictory [alternatives] — statement and non-statement — ultimate reality is not possible [for both]. Which of these is ultimately real? — therefore he says: "In the second alternative, [the non-statement] is ultimately real."

children.text: // avatāraṇābhāṣyādivyākhyānam //
children.translated_text: // Explanation of the introductory <s>bhāṣya</s> and so forth //

children.text:
dvandvasvarūpamāha tattātparyābhidhānāyeti śeṣaḥ /
dvigvavyayībhāvau prayogamātranirākṛtatvāt nopanyastau /
saṃbhāvitaprayogān bahuvrīhikarmadhārayatatpuruṣān nirākaroti--bahuvrīhīti asaṃbhavādarthāsaṃbhavāt /
ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa iti saṃbhāvitatatpuruṣopalakṣaṇaparam /
iti hi ityādi hītyarthaḥ /
tenārthanirdeśaṃ samupādāya saṃśaye 'pi bahuvacanaṃ draṣṭavyam /
tatrāpi sādharmyavaidharmyavipratipattijanyānāṃ saṃśayānāṃ parasparanirapekṣāṇāmeva nyāyapravartakatvamiti tātparyam /
children.translated_text: He states the nature of the <s>dvandva</s> (copulative compound) — the completion being: "for the purpose of stating that and its import." The <s>dvigu</s> (numeral compound) and <s>avyayībhāva</s> (indeclinable compound) are not presented because they are excluded by usage alone. He refutes the <s>bahuvrīhi</s> (possessive compound), <s>karmadhāraya</s> (descriptive compound), and <s>tatpuruṣa</s> (determinative compound) as having possible usage: "<s>Bahuvrīhi</s>..." — because of impossibility, i.e., impossibility of meaning. "<s>Ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa</s> (genitive compound)" — this is intended as an indication of the possible <s>tatpuruṣa</s>. "<s>Iti hi</s>" and so forth — "<s>hi</s>" has the meaning [of emphasis]. Therefore, taking the specification of meaning into account, the plural should be seen even in the case of doubt. And there too, the import is that only doubts arising from agreement, difference, and disagreement — being mutually independent — serve as the initiators of <s>nyāya</s> (reasoning).

children.text:
dṛṣṭānte 'pi viśeṣalakṣaṇakaraṇāvasare dvivacanameva /
tasyāpi parasparanirapekṣodāharaṇasaṃpratipattiḥ prayojanam /
evaṃ
children.translated_text: In the case of <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration) too, when there is occasion for specifying the particular definition, the dual number alone [is used]. Its purpose too is the apprehension of [the two] illustrations that are mutually independent. Similarly,

children.text:
siddhāntānāmapi svaprayojane parasparānapekṣatvemeva /
tacca bahuvacanasamānārthena saṃkhyāvacanena pratipāditam /
avayavānāṃ tu yadyapyekasmin vākyārthe pratipādayitavye mithaḥ sāpekṣatvam, tathāpi parasparāsaṃpratyayitamarthamabhidadhatāmeveti bahuvacanaprayojanam /
children.translated_text: As for the components (<s>avayavas</s>), although there is mutual dependence when they are to establish a single meaning of a sentence, nevertheless, since they express a meaning not [yet] communicated by one another — that is the purpose of the plural.

children.text: hetvābhāseṣvapi bahuvacanasya svavyāpāre parasparanirapekṣatvapratipādanameva tātparyam /
children.translated_text: In the case of <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious marks) too, the import of the plural is precisely the indication of mutual independence in their own respective functions.

children.text: tathā chalajātinigrahasthāneṣvapi /
children.translated_text: Likewise in the case of <s>chala</s> (equivocation), <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinders), and <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) as well.

children.text: yatra tu nirdeśo nāsti tatra lakṣaṇe yathāvacanaṃ vigrahaḥ, sāmānyamātrasyaiva prayojakatvāditi bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: But where there is no [specific] enumeration, the analysis of the definition follows the wording as it is, since it is generality alone that serves as the motivating factor — that is the purport.

of the <s>siddhāntas</s> (established conclusions) too, mutual independence obtains precisely in respect of their own purposes. And this is conveyed by the numeral expression, which is synonymous with the plural.

children.text: kārakasyārtharūpatvānna tasyābhidheyamastītyata āha--kārakārthaḥ pradhānakriyeti /
children.translated_text: Since the <s>kāraka</s> (grammatical agent/case-relation) is of the nature of meaning, it has no [separate] thing to be expressed — therefore he says: "The meaning of <s>kāraka</s> is the principal action."

children.text: arthaśabdaḥ pradhānakriyāvacano na kvacid dṛṣṭa itya āha--yaduddeśeneti /
children.translated_text: The word "<s>artha</s>" (meaning) is nowhere seen as denoting the principal action — therefore he says: "That for the sake of which..."

children.text: kārakāṇāmavivakṣetyetāvataiva susthe pradhānakriyāyā avivakṣā kimarthamityata āha--kārakagrahaṇeti //
children.translated_text: "The non-expression of the <s>kārakas</s>" alone being sufficient, what is the purpose of [mentioning] the principal action? — therefore he says: "The word <s>kāraka</s>..."

children.text:
nanu kārakāṇāmavivakṣā śeṣalakṣaṇa tadā syād yadi tatra kārakatvaṃ saṃbhavet, tadeva tu nāstītyata āha--yadyapīti /
atra codayati śaiṣikyāṃ ṣaṣṭhyām /
ṣaṣṭhī cānarthikā niṣprayojanā /
avyatireke tadanupapatteḥ ṣaṣṭyarthasya saṃbandhasyānupapatteḥ /
ekadeśitve bījam--aniyamavādīti /
tasyāsvatantratvāt pramāṇādayo gamyanta iti kiṃ kena saṃgatamata āha--bhāvasyeti /
na pramāṇādimātramucyate tattvaśabdena atha ca nārthāntaraṃ tattvamiti parasparavyāhatamityata ekadeśinaṃ kiñciduddīpayati--abhede 'pītīti /
anāropitarūpeṇa svarūpataḥ pratīyantāṃ pramāṇādaya ityetadarthamanatiriktārthamapi tattvagrahaṇaṃ kṛtamityarthaḥ /
dṛṣṭāntamasiddhaṃ mattvā sopapatti vyācaṣṭe--dvitvaikatvayoriti /
children.translated_text: Considering the example to be unestablished, he explains with justification: "Of duality and unity..."

children.text: vyavahāragativastugatyoḥ samānayogakṣematvaṃ manyamāno hyabhāvamapahnotuṃ na śaknotyeva, abhāvavyavahāragateḥ sarvavādisiddhatvāt /
children.translated_text: For one who holds the equal standing of conventional practice and the course of reality cannot deny absence at all, since the conventional practice of absence is accepted by all disputants.

children.text: yastu vastunirapekṣo 'pi vyavahāro 'stīti manyate, tanmatamavaśiṣṭa ityāśayavānāha--kṣaṇabhaṅgabhaḍgeti /
children.translated_text: But one who holds that conventional practice exists even independent of reality — his view is what remains [to be addressed]. With this intention he says: "The breakdown of momentariness..."

children.text: nivedayiṣyate vāttikakṛteti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: The completion is: "will be shown by the <s>Vārttikakṛt</s> (author of the <s>Vārttika</s>)."

Now, the non-expression of the <s>kārakas</s> would be the <s>śeṣa</s>-definition (residual relationship) only if <s>kāraka</s>-hood were possible there; but that very [possibility] does not exist — therefore he says: "Even though..." Here he raises an objection regarding the <s>śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī</s> (the genitive in the residual relation). And the genitive is meaningless, purposeless — because of non-distinction, [i.e.,] because the meaning of the genitive, namely relation, is impossible. The seed of the one-part view is: "the proponent of non-restriction." Since from its non-independence <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like are understood — what is connected with what? — therefore he says: "Of the entity..." It is not mere <s>pramāṇa</s> and the like that are denoted by the word "<s>tattva</s>" (reality), nor is <s>tattva</s> something different — [these two claims] are mutually contradictory — therefore, illuminating the partial view somewhat, [he says]: "Even in non-difference..." Let <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like be cognized in their own nature, without superimposed form — for this purpose, the word <s>tattva</s> is used even though it does not convey a different meaning. That is the meaning.

children.text: yathārthajñānotpatti prati svarūpalakṣaṇā śaktirāropahitattvameva sahakārilakṣaṇadoṣavirahīndriyādiḥ //
children.translated_text: The intrinsic definitional capacity for the generation of veridical cognition is precisely freedom from superimposition — [while] the sense-faculties and the like are [defined by] freedom from auxiliary-definitional defects.

children.text:
nanu dṛṣṭāniḥśreyasadūṣaṇe kiṃ tātparyam? na hi tadasmānna siddhyatītyata āha--etaduktaṃ bhavatīti /
adṛṣṭameva niḥśreyasamabhiprataṃ śāstraphalatveneti śeṣaḥ /
anyathā ātmādiprameyaviśeṣapratipādanaṃ na kuryāt, tattattvajñānamantareṇāpi dṛṣṭaniḥ- śreyasasiddheriti bhāvaḥ /
aprāmāṇikaṃ darśanābhāvāditi darśanaphalaikonneyaṃ pramāṇa kathaṃ
children.translated_text: Now, what is the import of the refutation of visible highest good? For it is not the case that it is not established by us — therefore he says: "This amounts to saying..." The completion is: "The unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) alone is intended as the highest good that is the fruit of the <s>śāstra</s>." Otherwise, [the <s>śāstra</s>] would not undertake the teaching of particular knowable objects such as the self and the like, since the visible highest good would be attained even without knowledge of their reality — that is the purport. [The objection:] "It is without valid authority, because there is no perception" — how is the <s>pramāṇa</s>, whose sole import is to be inferred from [its] perception-fruit,

children.text:
tadabhāve 'pyastīti bhāvaḥ /
āgamānumānayoḥ sahakāritā pakṣādya1panākatvena /
tatrātmalakṣaṇadharmisiddhāvāgamaḥ,
children.translated_text: [established] even in the absence of that — that is the purport. <s>Āgama</s> (scripture) and <s>anumāna</s> (inference) have auxiliary cooperation in the capacity of removing the thesis and the like. Among these, <s>āgama</s> [serves] in establishing the <s>dharmin</s> (subject) characterized by the definition of the self:

children.text:
ayamātmā [bṛha 4.4.3], apahatapāpmā [chāndogya 1.2.9], ajaro 'maraḥ [bṛha 4.4.25], sa eṣa neti netyādi [bṛha 3.9.26] /
anumānaṃ cecchādi [sūtra-1.1.10] samuttham /
janmābhāvarūpaliṅgasiddhau tu,
children.translated_text: "This is the self" [<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.3], "free from evil" [<s>Chāndogya</s> 1.2.9], "unaging, immortal" [<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.4.25], "that is described as not this, not this" [<s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 3.9.26] and so forth. And inference arises from desire and the like [<s>Sūtra</s> 1.1.10]. But in establishing the mark of the nature of absence of birth,

children.text: aśarīraṃ vāva santam
children.translated_text: "Verily, one who is bodiless,"

children.text: chāndogya 8.12.1
children.translated_text: <s>Chāndogya</s> 8.12.1

children.text:
ityādyāgamaḥ /
anumānaṃ tu pravṛttyabhāvaḥ /
pravṛttyabhāve 'pi,
children.translated_text: — such is the <s>āgama</s>. And inference is the absence of activity. Even in the absence of activity,

children.text: yastvātmatireva syādātmatṛptaśca mānavaḥ /
children.translated_text: "But one whose delight is in the self alone, who is self-satisfied, a human being,

children.text: ātmanyeva ca santuṣṭastasya kāryaṃ na vidyate //
children.translated_text: and who is content in the self alone — for him there is no duty to perform."

children.text: gītā 3.1.7
children.translated_text: <s>Gītā</s> 3.17

children.text:
ityevamādi /
anumānaṃ tu doṣābhāvaḥ /
doṣābhāve 'pi,
children.translated_text: — and so forth. And inference is the absence of <s>doṣa</s> (defect). Even in the absence of defect,

children.text: raso 'pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate /
children.translated_text: "Even <s>rasa</s> (taste/attachment) turns away, having seen the Supreme."

children.text: gītā 2.49
children.translated_text: <s>Gītā</s> 2.59

children.text:
ityevamādi /
anumānaṃ tu mithyājñānābhāvaḥ /
atrāpi
children.translated_text: — and so forth. And inference is the absence of false cognition. In this case too,

children.text: bhidyate hṛdayagranthiśchidyante sarvasaṃśayāḥ /
children.translated_text: "The knot of the heart is cut, all doubts are destroyed,

children.text: muṇḍaka 2.2.8
children.translated_text: <s>Muṇḍaka</s> 2.2.8

children.text:
ityādi /
anumānaṃ tu tattvajñānasadbhāvaḥ /
ātmatattvajñāne 'pi
children.translated_text: — and so forth. And inference is the existence of knowledge of reality. Even regarding the knowledge of the reality of the self,

children.text: ātmā vā are dṛṣṭavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: "The self, verily, is to be seen,"

children.text: bṛha 4.5.8
children.translated_text: <s>Bṛhadāraṇyaka</s> 4.5.6

children.text:
ityevamādi /
anumānaṃ tūpāyābhyāsaprakarṣa ityevamādi /
upalakṣaṇaṃ tvāgamānumānagrahaṇam /
pratyakṣamapi draṣṭavyam, evaṃ śarīrādiṣvapyūhyam, anumānamevātrārthe pramāṇamiti vipratipannaṃ pratipipādayiṣatāmiti śeṣaḥ upaniṣadāpi
children.translated_text: — and so forth. And inference is the excellence of the practice of means, and so on. But the mention of <s>āgama</s> and <s>anumāna</s> is illustrative. Perception also should be considered; similarly, it should be reasoned in the case of the body and the like as well. The completion is: "for those who wish to establish that inference alone is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for this matter, regarding which there is disagreement." And by the <s>Upaniṣad</s> also,

children.text: tameva viditvātimṛtyumeti /
children.translated_text: "Having known that very one, one passes beyond death,"

children.text: śvetā 3.8
children.translated_text: <s>Śvetāśvatara</s> 3.8

children.text:
ityādīnāṃ prāmāṇyāt /
santānānumānasya ca pṛthagupadeśācca prameyasya pramāṇādibhyaḥ prathamasūtre etadvivaraṇādvacavacchetturagranthamevāvatārayati--yadi ceti /
vihitatvādādyena sūtreṇeti /
śrutyarthābhyāmiti śeṣaḥ /
tadiyatā
children.translated_text: — and so forth — because of their authority. And because of the separate teaching of inference-by-continuity and of the knowable from the <s>pramāṇas</s> and the like, since this is the elaboration in the first <s>sūtra</s>, like [the method of] word-splitting he introduces the text itself [directly]: "And if..." "Because it is enjoined, by the first <s>sūtra</s>." The completion is: "by the meaning and the scripture." That same extent —

children.text: prabandhena vārttikakṛtā kiṃ kṛtamityata āha--tadaneneti //
children.translated_text: what was accomplished by the <s>Vārttikakṛt</s> through the continuous exposition? — therefore he says: "By this..."

children.text:
uttaravārttikaviṣayībhūtabhāṣyaṃ tāvad vyācaṣṭa--atha kimiti /
nanu dvitīyasūtrārtho nātroditaḥ, tat kathaṃ tatrānūdyata ityata āha-- niḥśreyaseti /
atra ca hetvādyanuvādatrārttikaṃ nāstyevetyanāśaṅkanīyam, ṭīkākṛtā siddhavadutthāpitatvāt /
kvacillipyabhāvasya lekhakadoṣeṇāpyupapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: Because the absence of [a passage] in certain manuscripts can also be explained by scribal error.

children.text: anyathā bhāṣyatātparyārthānuvādakatvāt /
children.translated_text: Otherwise, because [the <s>vārttika</s>] restates the intended meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s>.

children.text: vyācaṣṭa iti tu yad vyākhyātam, tadabhiprāyaṃ tena taccaitaduttarasūtreṇānūdyate ityasyānuvādānantaramavyākhyāne 'pi na doṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: As for "he explains" — [it means] that which was explained; with that intention, [the statement] "that is restated by that subsequent <s>sūtra</s>" — even without explanation after the restatement, there is no fault.

children.text: evaṃ cārthaṃ dvitīyasūtra ityādinā pūrvameva vyākhyātatvāt tu nehedaṃ vyākhyātamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And thus, because it was already explained earlier by [the passage beginning] "the meaning of the second <s>sūtra</s>" and so forth, the meaning is: "therefore it is not explained here."

He first explains the <s>bhāṣya</s> that has become the subject of the following <s>vārttika</s>: "Now, what..." Now, the meaning of the second <s>sūtra</s> has not been stated here; then how is it restated there? — therefore he says: "The highest good..." And here one should not suspect that there is simply no <s>vārttika</s> restating the inferential marks and the like, since the <s>ṭīkākṛt</s> (sub-commentator) has raised it as if established.

children.text:
nanu dveṣaḥ kiheya eva na vā pravṛttiheturityata āha--upalakṣaṇamiti /
nanu hānapadamātyantikapadasamabhivyāhārādapavarge vartate, tat kathaṃ tattvajñānamityucyata ityata āha--hīyate hīti /
karaṇavyutpattimāśrityānena tattvajñānaṃ vivakṣitam /
bhāvavyutpattyā tvātyantikapadasamabhivyāhārādapavarga ityarthaḥ /
tattvajñānapadasya vyutpattisaṃdehamapanayannevāha-- tasya pramāṇasyeti /
etenādivākyavirodhaḥ parihṛtaḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, the contradiction with the opening statement is resolved.

children.text: arthapadānīti bhāṣyagatasyārthapadasya tvanyathārtho bhaviṣyatīti yaduktaṃ tadāha--puruṣārthasthānānīti /
children.translated_text: "The words for objects" — the different meaning of the word "<s>artha</s>" occurring in the <s>bhāṣya</s> will be [explained] otherwise. What was stated [about that], he says: "The loci of human purpose (<s>puruṣārtha</s>)..."

children.text: tātparyamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: "the import."

children.text: vārttikasyeti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: The completion is: "of the <s>Vārttika</s>."

Now, is <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion) itself what is to be abandoned, or is it a cause of activity? — therefore he says: "It is illustrative." Now, the word "abandonment" (<s>hāna</s>), being co-expressed with the word "absolute" (<s>ātyantika</s>), refers to <s>apavarga</s> (liberation); then how is it called "knowledge of reality"? — therefore he says: "<s>Hīyate</s> (is abandoned)..." By relying on the derivation of the verbal root (<s>karaṇa-vyutpatti</s>), knowledge of reality is intended by this. But by the derivation of the state (<s>bhāva-vyutpatti</s>), together with the co-expression of the word "absolute," it means <s>apavarga</s> — that is the meaning. He says this precisely to dispel the doubt about the derivation of the word "knowledge of reality": "Of that <s>pramāṇa</s>..."

children.text:
prasthānaṃ prakāra itthambhāvaḥ tathā cetthambhūtatvādānvīkṣikyā iti yadyapyabhimatameva, tathāpi nirūpapattika itthambhāvaḥ syādityata āha--prasthānaṃ vyāpāraḥ /
tadanena bhāṣyagatasya prasthānapadasya prakṛtyartho 'bhihitaḥ, pratyayārthastu saṃśayādibhiḥ padārthaiḥ pṛthak prasthāpyate iti vadatā bhāṣyakāreṇaiva darśitaḥ /
tadetaduktaṃ bhavati, nyāvyutpādane vyāpāravattayā hi iyamānvīkṣikī vidyāntarād bhidyate /
sa ca saṃśayādyaḍgopāṅgavyutpādanenaiva vyutpādito bhavati /
children.translated_text: <s>Prasthāna</s> means manner, i.e., the state of being thus. Although it is indeed accepted that <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> (logic/philosophy of inquiry) is of such a nature, nevertheless, that nature-of-being-thus would be without justification — therefore he says: "<s>Prasthāna</s> means operation." By this, the meaning of the root (<s>prakṛtyartha</s>) of the word <s>prasthāna</s> occurring in the <s>bhāṣya</s> is stated; but the meaning of the suffix (<s>pratyayārtha</s>) has been shown by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> himself, who says that [<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>] is separately set forth through the categories such as doubt and the like. This amounts to saying: this <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> differs from other disciplines precisely by possessing operation. And that [operation] is established precisely by the elucidation of the limbs and sub-limbs such as doubt and the like.

children.text:
tato 'syāḥ saṃśayādayo 'pi viṣayabhūtāḥ tānantareṇa nirviṣayatayā vidyaiva na syāt /
viṣayāntaravattayā vidyāntarameva vā syāditi /
atreva śaṅkate--na ca vācyamiti /
na hyanyā vidyāḥ svaṃ svamarthaṃ pratipādayantyo 'pi kathametadityaśraddhāmalamapanetumīśate vinaināmānvīkṣikīmityāśayavān pariharati--etasyā eveti /
vārttikāntaraviṣayaṃ bhāṣyaṃ darśayati--sa cācamityādibhāṣyamiti /
nirdalaṃ deśyaṃ dīpayati jñānamiti /
upalabdho 'nirṇotaśceti vyāghāto 'nupapanna eva upalabdhernirṇayaparyāyatvasyānantarameva nirākṛtatvāt /
nāpi pramāṇapravṛttiviṣaya upalabdho bhavannirṇota eva bhavedityata ākṣepturabhiprāyantaraṃ darśayati--pañcarūpa iti /
yathā pratyakṣamāgamo vā ajñāte 'pyavatarati, tathā asandigadhe 'pi /
anumānaṃ tu yathā nājñāte tathā asaṃdigdhe 'pi tasmādasyānyaiva rītirityarthaḥ /
samānaviṣayatvam ekaviṣayatvam /
samāmānādhikāraṇyaṃ na samarthayasa iti, na tādātmyamiti bhāvaḥ /
parasparasamānenādhikaraṇena saṃbandhamātra sāmānādhikaraṇyam /
na tu tādātmyamityabhipretya parihāraṃ vivṛṇoti--sāmānya viśeṣayoriti /
saṃdigdhe pravartave ityasya yogyatāparatāṃ darśayati-asaṃdigdha iti /
children.translated_text: He shows the sense of 'eligible for engagement' in the phrase 'engages when in doubt': 'of what is not in doubt.'

children.text: saṃśayānarhaśca prakāradvayena, sarvathā ajñāto viśeṣato vā nirṇātaḥ, tadviparītastu saṃdigdhaḥ saṃśayārhaḥ /
children.translated_text: And that which is ineligible for doubt is so in two ways: either entirely unknown, or determined in a specific respect. The opposite of these is what is in doubt, eligible for doubt.

children.text: tatra nyāyaḥ pravartata iti tātparyam /
children.translated_text: Therein <s>nyāya</s> (reasoning) operates — this is the purport.

children.text: ata eva vyatirekapradhānāmupalakṣaṇatayaikāṃ vidhāmudāharati--nahīti //
children.translated_text: For this very reason, he illustrates one type, predominantly characterized by exclusion, as an indicator: 'for not.'

Therefore, doubt and the like are also the subject-matter of this [discipline]; without them, it would have no subject-matter and thus would not even be a discipline. Or, by having a different subject-matter, it would simply be a different discipline. Here itself he raises the objection: "Nor should it be said..." For other disciplines too, while teaching their own respective subjects, are unable to remove the faithlessness [of one who asks] "how is this [so]?" — without this <s>ānvīkṣikī</s>. With this intention he resolves [the objection]: "Of this very [discipline]..." He shows the <s>bhāṣya</s> that is the subject of another <s>vārttika</s>: "And that — [the <s>bhāṣya</s> beginning with] 'and examine' and so forth." "<s>Nirdalam</s>" means colloquial — he illuminates [the meaning]. "Cognition" — [the objection that] what is apprehended and not determined [involves] a contradiction is itself untenable, since the identification of apprehension with determination has been refuted just before. Nor would what is apprehended as the object of <s>pramāṇa</s>-operation become thereby determined — therefore, showing another intention of the objector, he says: "Fivefold..." Just as perception or scripture operates even regarding what is unknown, so too regarding what is not doubted. But inference, just as it does not [operate] regarding the unknown, likewise does not [operate] regarding the undoubted — therefore, its procedure is different. That is the meaning. "Having the same object" means having one [and the same] object. "You do not establish co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>)" — that is, [you do not establish] identity. That is the purport. <s>Sāmānādhikaraṇya</s> is merely the relation through a common substratum that is mutual. Not identity — with this understanding, he elaborates the resolution: "Of the universal and the particular..."

children.text:
nanu kiṃ punaḥ prayojanamiti praśne yena prayuktaḥ pravartata ityuttaraṃ vaiyātyādityata āha--sphuṭataramevaitaditi /
nanu vayaṃ
children.translated_text: Now, to the question 'what then is the purpose?', the answer 'that by which one is impelled to act' is a truism — to this he says: 'this is all the more clear.' Now, we

children.text:
nviti svābhimatapradarśanamekadeśimate aparitoṣaṃ sūcayitum, na cāparitoṣabījamupalabhāmaha ityatastadvījaṃ praśnapūrvakameva tāvad darśayati--tatreti /
sarveṣāmeva kāmyatvāt dharmādīnāmiti /
tathā ca dharmādiviṣayastātsādhanaviṣayo vā kāmastatrāpi pravartaka ityarthaḥ /
na ca tadviṣayatvenāpi dharmādīnāmupādānam, srakcandanādīnāmapyupādānaprasaṅgāditi /
sarakaḥ pānam /
nanu tathāpi naiteṣāṃ prayojanatvakṣatirityata āha--dharmamokṣayoriti /
upalakṣaṇa caitat /
kākārthayorapi viraktān pratyaprayojakatvamiti draṣṭavyam /
tenaitaduktaṃ bhavati, na hi dharmādiṣu dharmatvādikameva pravṛttiṃ prati prayojakam /
kiṃ nāma? iṣyamāṇatvam /
anyathā aviśeṣeṇa sarvasya sarvatra pravṛttiprasaṅgāditi /
nanu yathāśrute ko doṣo yena viṣayeṇa viṣayiṇaṃ pratyayamupalakṣayatīti vyākhyetyata āha--asatyoriti /
satyorveti saptamī /
uttaravārttikaṃ grahītumetat /
yathāśrutaṃ dūṣayati--tathāpīti /
iha phalajñānamanyatra pravartavat tatsādhana eva pravartayatīti ato nātiprasaṅga ityevaṃ yadyapi śaṅkitumucitam, tathāpi
children.translated_text: say — this display of his own view, to suggest dissatisfaction with the one-sided position; and since we cannot identify the seed of that dissatisfaction, he first shows that seed through a question: 'therein.' Since <s>dharma</s> and the rest are desired by all. And thus, desire directed toward <s>dharma</s> and the rest, or toward the means of attaining them, is itself the motivator — this is the meaning. And yet <s>dharma</s> and the rest are not included by virtue of being objects of that [desire], since there would follow the absurd consequence that garlands, sandalwood, and the like would also have to be included. <s>Saraka</s> means drink. Now, even so, there is no impairment of their being a purpose — to this he says: 'of <s>dharma</s> and <s>mokṣa</s>.' And this is merely illustrative. It should be understood that [the same applies] regarding <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) and <s>artha</s> (wealth) too — they are not motivators for those who are detached. Thus what is stated amounts to this: it is not <s>dharma</s>-ness and so forth in <s>dharma</s> and the rest that is the motivator of action. What then? Being desired. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that everyone would act toward everything without distinction. Now, what is the fault with the reading as it stands, where the object characterizes the cognition that is the subject? — why should it be interpreted [otherwise]? — to this he says: 'when the two are absent.' 'When the two are present' is the locative. This is to capture the subsequent <s>vārttika</s>. He criticizes the literal reading: 'even so.' Here, although it is fitting to object that knowledge of the result, motivating action elsewhere, motivates only toward the means of that [result], and hence there is no over-extension, nevertheless

children.text:
tatsadhanatvenājñāne pravṛttireva nāsti ityatastajjñānamantarbhāvya āśaṅkate--tatsādhanatvajñānāditi /
sāmānādhikaraṇyena ekaviṣayatayā, saṃpratipatteravirodhataḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvasiddherityarthaḥ /
evaṃ tarhi
children.translated_text: since in the absence of knowledge of something being a means, there is simply no action [toward it] — therefore, subsuming that knowledge [of means], he raises the objection: 'from the knowledge of being a means to that.' By co-reference, i.e. by having the same object, and because there is no contradiction with common acceptance, the causal relation is established — this is the meaning. If so, then

children.text:
sukhaduḥkhāptihānibhyāmiti vārttikamasaṅgatameva kimityata āha--etaduktaṃ bhavatīti /
vivakṣitu prasthalīkarotiteneti /
children.translated_text: the <s>vārttika</s> 'through the obtaining and avoiding of pleasure and pain' is simply incongruent — why? To this he says: 'this is what is stated.' What he intends to say, he makes explicit — this is the meaning.

children.text: pravṛttiviṣayatayeṣyamāṇatvamupādeyatā, svarūpeṇeṣyamāṇatvamuddeśyatā, ubhayorapi jñānaṃ prayojayatīti ubhayamapi prayojanam /
iyāṃstu viśeṣo yadupādeyajñānaṃ sākṣāt pravartaṃyati /
children.translated_text: But this is the distinction: knowledge of what is to be adopted directly motivates action.

children.text: etadeva ca tasya sākṣātpravartakatvaṃ yat sākṣāt prayatnajananasamarthāmicchāṃ prasūte /
children.translated_text: And this very direct motivating power of it consists in this — that it directly generates a desire capable of generating effort.

children.text: saivādyā pravṛttirityucyate /
children.translated_text: That itself is called the primary activity.

children.text: uddeśyajñānaṃ tu tadviṣayāmicchāṃ janayat tathābhūtatatsādhanajñānajananadvāreṇa ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: But knowledge of the goal, generating desire directed toward it, does so through the intermediary of generating knowledge of the appropriate means to that end — this is the meaning.

Desirableness in the sense of being an object of action is eligibility for adoption (<s>upādeya</s>); desirableness in its own form is being a goal (<s>uddeśya</s>). The knowledge of both motivates — therefore both are purposes.

children.text:
nyāyaparīkṣāśabdayorekārthatvamapaśyata ākṣepa ityāha--nyāyeti /
nanu parīkṣāśabdasya vicāraṇārthatve prayojanāpekṣitvaṃ kadācid yujyate, sa cet nyāyārthastasya ca vyutpattibalena pramāṇamātramarthaḥ, tasya ca na prayojanāpakṣeti sarvaṃ samākulamityākṣepāvatāraṭīkārthāḥ /
nanvetāvatāpi codyaṃ tadavasthamevetyata samādhānaṃ vibhajate--pratyakṣādīti /
nanu avayavairarthasya parīkṣaṇamadhigatiryadi nyāyaḥ, tarhi kiṃ tasya phalamityata āha--arthasya
children.translated_text: Seeing the synonymy of the words <s>nyāya</s> and <s>parīkṣā</s> (examination), the objection is raised — he says: '<s>nyāya</s>.' Now, if the word <s>parīkṣā</s> has the meaning of investigation, then requiring a purpose would sometimes be appropriate; but if it is synonymous with <s>nyāya</s>, and if, by force of etymology, its meaning is merely <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), and if that does not require a purpose, then everything becomes confused — these are the meanings of the introductory <s>ṭīkā</s> to the objection. Now, even with this much the objection remains unresolved — therefore he divides the resolution: '<s>pratyakṣa</s> and the rest.' Now, if <s>nyāya</s> is the examination, i.e. the apprehension, of an object by means of its components, then what is its result? To this he says: 'of the object,

children.text:
liṅgasyeti /
atha yadi parīkṣāparanāmā nyāyo nānumeyaviṣayaḥ, kutastadadhigamo bhaviṣyatītyata āha--parīkṣitaṃ tviti /
atha yathā pramāṇamūlairavayavairliḍgāṃ pratipādyate tathānumeyameva kiṃ netyata āha--na tviti /
nanu saṃdigdhatvāviśeṣe 'pi kuta etadityata āha--tasyeti /
parīkṣānāspadatvālliṅgapratipādanamantareṇa tadapekṣiṇa pratyāhatya pratipādayitumaśakyatvādityarthaḥ /
na tarhi pramāṇairiti /
tathā cārthasya liṅgasya parīkṣādhigatirna pramāṇphalaṃ syāt /
atha pramāṇaireva, niṣphalāstarhi avayavā ityāśayaḥ /
na sākṣādityādinā liṅgādhigatāvavayavānāṃ svātantryaṃ nirākurvatā adhigaterapramāṇaphalatvamapāstam, avāntaravyāparatvaṃ cāvedayatā avayavānāmānarthakyamapāstamiti /
pramāṇatvāviśeṣai'pi tasyaiva vipratipannapuruṣapratipādakatvaṃ nānyasyetyatrāpi hetuṃ paraḥ prakṣyatītyatastathaivāha--samasteti /
tadayaṃ vārtikārthaḥ so 'yamitthaṃbhūtasamastapramāṇopakaraṇātmā yatastasmāda vipratipannapuruṣapratipādakaḥ tataśrva parama iti
children.translated_text: of the inferential mark.' Now, if the <s>nyāya</s>, another name for <s>parīkṣā</s>, does not have the inferable as its object, how will that [inferable's] apprehension occur? To this he says: 'but what is examined.' Now, just as the inferential mark is established by the components that are grounded in <s>pramāṇa</s>, is not the inferable [established] in the same way? To this he says: 'but not.' Now, even though there is no difference in being doubtful, how is this [distinction] established? To this he says: 'of that.' Because the inferential mark, not being the domain of examination, cannot be established without first establishing what depends on it, by overcoming [the doubt] and then establishing [the mark] — this is the meaning. Then it is not 'by means of <s>pramāṇas</s>.' And thus, the apprehension of the object and the inferential mark through examination would not be a result of <s>pramāṇa</s>. If, on the other hand, it is by <s>pramāṇas</s> alone, then the components would be purposeless — this is the intention. By saying 'not directly' and so forth, while denying the independence of the components in apprehending the inferential mark, he has set aside the view that apprehension is not a result of <s>pramāṇa</s>, and by indicating the subsidiary operation [of the components], he has set aside the purposelessness of the components. Even though there is no distinction in being a <s>pramāṇa</s>, the opponent will ask for the reason why only this [nyāya], not another, teaches the person holding a contrary view — therefore he says likewise: 'the composite.' This then is the meaning of the <s>vārttika</s>: this, being of such a nature, consisting of the composite instrument of all <s>pramāṇas</s>, is therefore the teacher of the person holding a contrary view, and therefore is called supreme.

children.text: vyavahriyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: This is the meaning.

children.text: nanu nāviruddhatvamevāśritatvamāśritasyāpi aviruddhatvād viruddhasyāpyāśritatvāt, ata eva nāvinābhāvo 'pyanayoḥ, tatkathamāha--āśritatvamityavirodhīti? na caiva tatprakṛtamityata āha--pajcāvayave iti /
children.translated_text: Now, non-opposition is not the same as dependence, since even what is dependent may be non-opposed, and even what is opposed may be dependent; for this very reason there is no invariable co-occurrence between these two — then how does he say 'dependence is non-opposition'? And this is not the topic at hand — to this he says: 'in the five-membered [syllogism].'

children.text: nyāyamūlaphalayorekaviṣayatvaṃ vastutaḥ, taccāvirodhe sati nirvahati nānyatheti /
children.translated_text: The identity of object between the root and the result of <s>nyāya</s> is factual, and that is sustained when there is non-opposition, not otherwise.

children.text: tadetadbhāṣyakāreṇārthataḥ kathintaṃ vārttikakāreṇākṣaraireva vivṛtamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: This very thing was stated in substance by the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) and made explicit in words by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> — this is the meaning.

children.text: yadyapi agniśabdastejoviśeṣavacanaḥ sūryālokādāvagnivyavahārādarśanāt, tathāpi tejāmātre 'pi kvacit prayujyaje /
children.translated_text: Although the word <s>agni</s> (fire) denotes a specific kind of radiance (<s>tejas</s>), since the conventional usage of <s>agni</s> is not seen for sunlight and the like, nevertheless it is sometimes used for radiance in general.

children.text: tadabhiprāyeṇa paramāṇunā bhāgāsiddhatāpi mā bhūdityāśayavānāha"--agniravayavīti //
children.translated_text: With that intention, he says — lest there be the fault of unestablished part even with respect to the atom: 'fire is a composite entity.'

children.text:
nanu viruddhārthaṃpariccheda eva pramāṇavirodhaḥ, sa cātra pratyakṣeṇa sphuṭatara eveti kimartha praśnaḥ kaḥ punarityata āha--idamatreti /
tata eva rūpatrayāsaṃpattereva /
tadanumānamābhāsamiti vyavahartavyamiti śeṣaḥ /
na ca rūpatrayasaṃpannamevedam, sādhyasiddhiprasaṅgāditi /
atra śaṅgate--atheti /
nanu yadi rūpatrayasaṃpattireva avinābhāvaḥ tadā kathaṃ bādhayā saha saṃbhavaḥ? ihaiva saṃbhavādityata āha--bādhāyāmiti /
pakṣadharmatvaṃ svīkṛtyānaikāntikatvavyupādanam /
ato na ca sapakṣetyādiśaḍkā na niravakāśā bhavati /
yatredaṃ tatredamityākāreṇa pakṣasyāpi sādhanavataḥ sādharmyavattāpratītiḥ sarvopasaṃhāraḥ /
ayaṃ ca yatra nedaṃ sādhyamasti tatrāpyetat sādhanamabhimatamastītyetāvanmātreṇaiva bhajyate /
eṣa ca vyabhicāraprakāraḥ pakṣe 'pi na nivārayituṃ śakya ityarthaḥ /
na bādhasya svātantryeṇa dūṣaṇatvaṃ vyabhicārāt pakṣadharmatāvirahiṇi tadabhāvāt /
yatra ca bādhasaṃbhavastatra tayorevānyatrāvagatasvātantryayorvidyamānatvādanumānamābhāsatāṃ gatam, vyabhicārādyutthāpanena tu viroghaḥ caritārtha iti
children.translated_text: Now, contradiction with a <s>pramāṇa</s> is precisely the determination of a contradictory meaning, and here that is all the more clear through perception — so what is the point of the question 'what then?' — to this he says: 'this is the point here.' For that very reason — precisely because the three conditions are not fulfilled. The remainder is: that inference should be declared to be fallacious. And it is not the case that these three conditions are indeed fulfilled, for there would follow the consequence of proving what is already established. He raises the doubt here: 'now then.' Now, if the fulfillment of the three conditions is itself invariable concomitance, then how is it compatible with sublation? Because it is compatible right here — to this he says: 'in the case of sublation.' Having accepted the property of being present in the subject (<s>pakṣadharmatā</s>), the designation as inconclusive is made. Therefore, the doubt beginning with 'and not in the similar case' is not without scope. The cognition in the form 'wherever this is, there that is,' being a cognition of the similarity of the subject too as possessing the probans, constitutes a universal generalization. And this is violated merely by this much — that wherever the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) is absent, there too the <s>sādhana</s> (probans) that is accepted [by the proponent] is present. And this type of deviation cannot be prevented even in the subject — this is the meaning. Sublation does not independently constitute a fault, [being distinct] from deviation, since where there is no property of being present in the subject, sublation is absent. And where sublation is possible, there, since the very two [perception and inference] whose independence has been established elsewhere are present, the inference has become fallacious — and the objection is fully addressed by raising [the fault of] deviation and so forth.

children.text: pūrvapakṣārthaṃḥ //
children.translated_text: This is the meaning of the prima facie view.

children.text:
anumānāviṣaye prayoga iti yathāśrute vārttike parābhimatamapakṣadharmatvameva sphuṭamapakṣasyaivānumānāviṣayatvāt, ato 'nyathā vyācikhyāsurbhūmimāracayati--vakṣyate hīti /
atiprasaṅgādativyāpterityanumānādhikāre vakṣyate hīti yojanā /
kimato yadyevamityata āha--sa ceti /
ārdrendhanamekopādhirekavyabhicārāt,
children.translated_text: In the <s>vārttika</s> 'application in a domain beyond inference,' what is manifest according to the literal reading is the opponent's view — namely, the absence of the property of being present in the subject, since it is the subject itself that is beyond the domain of inference. Therefore, wishing to interpret it otherwise, he prepares the ground: 'for it will be said.' The construction is: 'for it will be said in the section on inference — because of over-extension, because of excessive scope.' What follows from this? To this he says: 'and that.' Wet firewood — [an example of] a single adventitious condition, a single deviation.

children.text: adhyayanamubhayopādhirūbhayavyabhicārāt /
children.translated_text: Study — [an example of] both adventitious conditions, both deviations.

children.text: so 'yamityādinā nāstītyantena pratyakṣasyākāro darśitaḥ /
children.translated_text: By 'this is' and so forth, up to 'does not exist,' the form of perception has been shown.

children.text: yadyabhaviṣyaditi tarkasya /
children.translated_text: 'If it were to exist' — [the form] of reasoning (<s>tarka</s>).

children.text: nāstyevati phalabhūtasya niśrvayasya //
children.translated_text: 'Simply does not exist' — of the resultant certainty.

children.text:
nanu kṛtakasya tejaso baddhau viparivartānatve yo yaḥ kṛtakaḥ sarvo 'nuṣṇa iti sarvopasaṃhāro na saṃbhavatyeva /
aparisphurati ca tasmin na tarām /
na hi yadyatra na sphurati tadapi tasya viṣaya ityata āha--sāmānyena yo yaḥ kṛtaka iti /
anenākāreṇa so 'pi buddhau viparivartata eva, na tu viśeṣākāreṇa vyāptigrahaṇaviṣayatāmagniragādityata āha--na tu nirvimajya viśeṣato jñātvā tejo 'vayavini eva saṃbandho 'vadhārita ityarthaḥ /
atha sāmānyākāreṇāpi tejo 'vayavinaḥ kimityavakāśo deyo yāvatā pṛthivyādāveva vyāptiravadhāryatāmityata āha--na hīti /
na hi samānyākāreṇa vyāptaugṛhyamāṇāyāṃ pratyakṣabādhāt prāgeva tejo 'vayaviparityāge kācidupapattirasti, anyatrādarśanāt /
tathā ca na kevalaṃ sa eva na dṛṣṭaḥ, pṛthivyādayo 'pi kecinna dṛṣṭā eveti te 'pi parityājyāḥ /
evaṃ ca gṛhītvā gṛhītvā vyāptirgrahītavyā /
adṛṣṭeṣu vyabhicārāśaṅkayā na vetyubhayathāpi sarvānumānocchedaprasaṅga ityarthaḥ /
svayameva paraḥ pakṣaṃ gṛhṇātvityabhisandhinā sukumāraprakāramāha--na tāvaditi /
na hi vyāptyanapavāde vyabhicārāvakāśaḥ samastīti hṛdayam /
tarhi tadapavāde satyeva hetoranaikāntikatvamastvityāśayavānāśaṅkate--pratyakṣeṇeti /
iha vyāpterapavādaḥ pakṣatāmaparibhūya, tatparibhave vā? tatrādyaṃ tāvad dūṣayati--neti /
pravṛttānumānāpratirodhe vyāpterapavāda iti kutaḥ? tatpratirodhaṃ tu viparītapratyakṣaṃ na cet karoti, ko 'paraḥ kariṣyatītyāśayaḥ /
nanu yadi pakṣe 'pi vyabhicāraḥ saṃbhavati, sa nodbhāvya iti kasyāyaṃ daṇḍa ityata āha--anyatheti /
na na pakṣadharmatāmaparibhūya pratyakṣeṇa vyabhicāraḥ śakyagrahaḥ, na hyasti saṃbhavaḥ saṃdigdhasādhyadharmā dharmo tadviraheṇa nirṇotaśceti śūnyahṛdayaṃ prati tu pratibandirityarthaḥ /
pratyakṣeṇa pakṣadharmatāparibhavād vyabhicāro bhaviṣyatītyāśaṅgate--pratyakṣeṇeti /
nirākaroti--tarhīti /
yathā hi sādhyaviparītapravṛttireva sādhyanivṛttiḥ, tathā viparītapramāṇapravṛttireva sādhananivṛttiḥ /
anyathā viparītapramāṇapravṛttāvapi yadi sādhakaṃ na nivartate tadā tadāyattaṃ sādhyamapi na nivarteta, tadanivṛttau tu na pakṣatvakṣatiriti na vyabhicārāvakāśa
children.translated_text: Now, when manufactured radiance (<s>tejas</s>) is revolving in the cognition at the time of sublation, the universal generalization 'whatever is manufactured is non-hot' is simply impossible, since not all [manufactured things] are perceived [as non-hot]. And when something does not clearly appear in it [the cognition], it does not appear even more so. For it is not the case that what does not appear somewhere is also the object of that [cognition] — to this he says: 'in general, whatever is manufactured.' With this form, that too does revolve in the cognition, but not with a specific form — to this he says: 'but not after discriminating specifically' — meaning: having specifically known that the connection is established only in composite entities of radiance, [the fire-atom] did not enter into the domain of the apprehension of invariable concomitance. Now, even with the general form, why should an opening be given to the composite entities of radiance? Rather, let the invariable concomitance be established only in [composites of] earth and the like — to this he says: 'for not.' For when the invariable concomitance is being grasped with the general form, there is no justification, prior to perceptual sublation, for excluding composite entities of radiance, since it is not seen elsewhere [that such exclusion is warranted]. And thus, not only is that [fire] alone not observed [as non-hot], but some earth-composites and the like are also not observed [to be so] — therefore they too must be excluded. And thus, the invariable concomitance would have to be grasped after grasping and grasping [individual cases]. And in the case of unobserved [instances], there would be the suspicion of deviation — and thus, either way, the absurd consequence of the destruction of all inference — this is the meaning. With the intention that the opponent should himself accept the thesis, he presents the subtle approach: 'not to begin with.' For when the invariable concomitance is not contravened, there is simply no scope for deviation — this is the heart of the matter. Then, when there is contravention, let the probans be inconclusive — with this intention, he raises the doubt: 'by perception.' Here, is the contravention of the invariable concomitance without overriding the property of being present in the subject, or with overriding it? As to the first, he refutes it: 'no.' When the ongoing inference is not obstructed, how can there be contravention of the invariable concomitance? And if contrary perception does not obstruct that [inference], who else will? — this is the intention. Now, if deviation is possible even in the subject, it is not brought out [explicitly] — whose fault is that? — to this he says: 'otherwise.' Deviation cannot be grasped by perception without overriding the property of being present in the subject — for there is no possibility that a property whose possession by the subject is in doubt could be ascertained as absent from it [without such overriding] — but against one with an empty heart, [this reasoning serves] as a check — this is the meaning. He raises the doubt that deviation would occur through perceptual overriding of the property of being present in the subject: 'by perception.' He refutes: 'then.' For just as the operation of a contrary [pramāṇa] is itself the cessation of the probandum, so too the operation of a contrary <s>pramāṇa</s> is itself the cessation of the probans. Otherwise, if, even when a contrary <s>pramāṇa</s> operates, the probans does not cease, then the probandum too, being dependent on it, would not cease; and if that does not cease, then there is no impairment of being the subject — and hence no scope for deviation.

children.text: ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: This is the meaning.

children.text:
siddhamarthaṃ vārttike samarpayati--tadidamuktamiti /
nanu yadi nāmānumānanivṛtteḥ pūrvamapakṣadharmatvaṃ vyabhicāro boddhārayituṃ na śakyastathāpi taduttarakālaṃ tāvacchākyata eva, tatastāveva stām, kṛtamapahṛtaviṣayatvenetyata āha--evaṃ ceti /
yāvaddhi pratyakṣavirodhenānumānaṃ na dūṣyate, tāvad vyabhicārādyavakāśo nāstyeva /
tataḥ sāvakāśāvetau
children.translated_text: He assigns the established meaning to the <s>vārttika</s>: 'this is what was stated.' Now, even if, prior to the cessation of inference, the absence of the property of being present in the subject — i.e. deviation — cannot be made known, still, at a subsequent time it surely can be; then let those [faults] stand, and [the inference] is finished by virtue of its domain being removed — to this he says: 'and thus.' For as long as the inference is not invalidated by contradiction with perception, there is simply no scope for deviation and so forth. Therefore, these two [deviation and sublation] have scope [only]

children.text: pratyakṣavirodhamupajīvataḥ /
children.translated_text: of one who relies on contradiction with perception.

children.text: tena ced dūṣitamanumānam, kimābhyām? na hi mṛto 'pi māryata iti siddhāntasaṃkṣepaḥ //
children.translated_text: If inference has been refuted by that, what use are these two? For even the dead are not killed again — this is the summary of the established position.

children.text:
nanvaśrāvaṇaḥ śabda ityevaṃ bruvāṇaḥ kathaṃ śabdāsattvamabhipreyāt, yāvatendriyāntaragrāhyameva kimiti nāmipraiti?
atha tatra virodho 'sti, tat kiṃ svarūpāpalāpe sa nāsti? tasmādabhiprāyaḥ parasya niyantuṃ na śakyata ityata āha--na hīti /
indriyāntaravyāpāravyabhicārāt tadagrāhyatvaviniścayapakṣe svarūpāpalāpa evābhipretaḥ /
tatraivedamudāharaṇamityarthaḥ /
balitapūrvapakṣādalanādalagnakaṃ vārttikaṃ niveśayituṃ pīṭhamāracayati--saviśeṣaṇe hīti /
viśiṣṭavidhānapi ityupalakṣaṇaṃ viśiṣṭaniṣedho 'pi draṣṭavaya iti /
agatiḥ pramāṇāntarādalābhaḥ /
lauhityaviśiṣṭamuṣṇīṣaṃ
children.translated_text: Now, when one says 'sound is non-auditory,' how would one intend the non-existence of sound? — rather, why does one not simply proceed to say it is apprehended by another sense-organ? If there is a contradiction in that, is there not also one in denying its very nature? Therefore, the opponent's intention cannot be controlled — to this he says: 'For not...' When one is certain that sound is not apprehended by another sense-organ due to the deviation of the operation of other sense-organs, the very denial of its nature is intended — and this is the example for that — this is the meaning. He constructs the platform to install the <s>vārttika</s>, which is stuck fast from not having crushed the previous strong objection: 'For when there is a qualifier...' This is illustrative: 'Even a qualified injunction' should be understood as including also a qualified prohibition. 'Impossibility' means the failure to obtain from another <s>pramāṇa</s>. A turban qualified by redness

children.text:
vidhīyate /
jīrṇatāmalavattāviśiṣṭaṃ vāsaḥ pratiṣidhyate /
na samasitaśrāvaṇapadaśravaṇaṃ śrutiḥ /
viśeṣaṇāviśeṣyabhāvāvasthitapadasamūho vākyam, tayoḥ sāmarthyāt /
etaduktaṃ bhavati, samāse na uttarapadārthaniṣedhārthaḥ,
children.translated_text: is enjoined. A garment qualified by being old and dirty is prohibited. Hearing is not the hearing of the word 'non-auditory' along with its associated word. A sentence is a collection of words that stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified, by the capacity of those two [relations]. What is stated is this: in a compound, the purpose is not the negation of the meaning of the latter member,

children.text: tatraivāsya sāmarthyaṃ vācakatvaṃ yataḥ /
children.translated_text: since the capacity, i.e., the denotative power, of the [negative particle] applies precisely there [to the qualifier].

children.text: asamāsapakṣe 'pi samānādhikāraṇayorviśeṣaṇaviśeṣyayormadhye viśeṣaṇenaiva na saṃbadhyate, tatraivāsya sāmarthyamanvayayogyatā yataḥ /
children.translated_text: Even in the non-compound alternative, among two co-referential terms in the relation of qualifier and qualified, [the negative] is connected only with the qualifier, since its capacity, i.e., syntactic fitness, applies precisely there.

children.text: tadihobhayathāpi saḍketabalādanvayayogyatābalād vā na naḥ śabdapadena saṃbandha iti //
children.translated_text: Therefore, here in both cases, by the force of convention or by the force of syntactic fitness, we have no connection with the word 'sound.'

children.text:
syādetat /
śrūyamāṇasya naḥ śrāvaṇapadenaivāstu saṃbandhaḥ, śabdaniṣedhastvarthādāpadyata ityata āha--nāpīti /
children.translated_text: One might say: let the connection of what is heard be with the word 'auditory' itself, and the negation of sound will follow as a consequence — to this he says: 'Nor...'

children.text:
śrūyamāṇo hyartho yena vinā nopapadyate sa tenākṣipyamāṇor'thād āpadyata ityucyate /
na copapādako virodhī nāma /
sa hyanupapādaka evetyarthaḥ /
virodha meva dyotayati--śrāvaṇatveti /
nanu kalpitenāpyadhikaraṇena niṣedhanirūpaṇamupapadyate, tasya
children.translated_text: For a meaning that is heard is said to 'follow as a consequence' when it is entailed by something without which the heard meaning would be untenable. And that which establishes is not something contradictory. For that [the contradictory] is precisely what does not establish — this is the meaning. He illustrates the contradiction itself: 'Auditoriness...' Now, even with an imagined substratum, the formulation of a negation is tenable, since that

children.text:
tucchatvāt /
tathā ca nāsattvādhikaraṇatvayorvirodha ityata āha--na ceti /
evaṃ vyavasthite vārttikārtha
children.translated_text: is empty. And thus there is no contradiction between being a substratum and non-existence — to this he says: 'And not...' When this has been established, the meaning of the <s>vārttika</s>

children.text: dyotayati--na ca śrāvaṇatvamiti /
children.translated_text: is illustrated: 'And auditoriness...'

children.text: śabdaśrotrayoḥ saṃbandha śabdagrahaṇopāyabhūtaḥ //
children.translated_text: The connection between sound and the ear is the means of apprehending sound.

children.text:
nanu yadi saṃbandhaḥ, kathaṃ vārttikakāro vṛttirityāhetyata āha--vṛttiriti /
nanu na sākṣād vede naraśiraḥ
children.translated_text: Now, if it is a connection, how does the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> call it a 'function' (<s>vṛtti</s>)? To this he says: 'Function...' Now, the Veda does not directly state the impurity of a human skull.

children.text:
kapālāśaucaṃ śrūyate /
pratyuta,
children.translated_text: On the contrary,

children.text:
rudro ha vā mahāvrataṃ cacāra /
sa eva naraśīrṣamaṃpasaṃdadhāra iti viparitaiva śrutiḥ /
ataḥ kathamāgamavirodha ityata āha--manvādimiriti /
yadyapyasminnarthe na sākṣāt śrutiḥ pratīyate, tathāpi tanmūlā smṛtireva sphuṭatarā pramāṇam /
rudro havetyādi tvarthavādamātraṃ naramedhādau prāśastyapratipādanārtham, nāsya śucitāyāṃ pramāṇaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: '<s>Rudra</s> indeed performed the great observance. He himself held the human head' — the <s>śruti</s> is quite the opposite. So how is there contradiction with scripture? To this he says: 'By <s>Manu</s> and others...' Although no direct <s>śruti</s> is found on this matter, nevertheless <s>smṛti</s> based on it is an even clearer authority. The passage '<s>Rudra</s> indeed...' and so forth is merely an <s>arthavāda</s> (laudatory passage) intended to convey the praise of the human sacrifice (<s>naramedha</s>), and is not an authority regarding its purity — this is the meaning.

children.text:
nanūpadarśitamāgamaṃ dṛṣṭvāpi kutaḥ pṛcchatītyata āha--nāsmākamiti /
atra vastuti śabdetarapramāṇagocare āgamāntarāṇāmapramāṇyādityarthaḥ /
kutaḥ punarasya nirghṛṇasya kapālaśaucābhimāna ityata āha--avigītā hīti /
na hyāgamādeva dharmādiviniścayo 'pi tvavigītād vyavahārādapi /
sa cāsmākamapyasti /
children.translated_text: And that [practice] exists for us too.

children.text: na ca vācyaṃ sārvatriko vyavahāraḥ pramāṇam /
children.translated_text: Nor should one say that universal practice is the [sole] authority.

children.text: yathā kanyāpariṇayanavidhau purandhrīṇāmācāraḥ /
children.translated_text: Just as the practice of married women in the matter of marriage of girls [is not universal authority].

children.text: prādeśikastvayamityāśaḍkyodāharaṇaṃ kṛtam--dākṣiṇātyānāmiveti //
children.translated_text: Anticipating [the objection] that this is merely regional, an example is given: 'As of the southerners...'

Now, even having seen the cited scripture, why does he ask? To this he says: 'Not for us...' Here the real point is: regarding matters within the scope of other means of knowledge, other scriptures are not authoritative — this is the meaning. Whence comes this merciless one's conviction about the purity of a skull? To this he says: 'For undisputed...' For the determination of <s>dharma</s> and the like is not from scripture alone, but also from undisputed practice.

children.text:
upahāse bījamāha--śrutismutīti /
āhnenaivukādikriyā āmnāyamūlā avigītavedārthānuṣṭhātṛvyavahāratvādagnihotrādivaditi prayogaḥ /
atha śreyohetutaivāsyāḥ kuto nāvasīyata ityata āha--na khalviti /
yadyapi śakyata evaitadāpātataḥ, tathāpi nirmūlatvaśaḍkālakaḍkitatvenānuṣṭhānaparyantatāṃ na yāyāt /
ato mūlānumānameva sādhīya ityarthaḥ /
na vedānumāne mūlaṃ liṅgamityarthaḥ /
kimuktaṃ bhavati śucītyanena punaruktatāṃ pariharannāha--api ceti /
atha trayīvidveṣāditi /
na ca vācyam, yāvati vivādastāvānevārthaḥ pakṣaḥ /
gomayādestu śucitvamubhayavādisiddhamatastāvadeva dṛṣṭāntayiṣyata iti /
tasyāpi śucitvaṃ nāgamaprāmāṇyamanabhyupagamya śakyamabhyupagantumiti codayati--atheti /
vyutthitābhisandheḥ praśna ityarthaḥ /
abhisandhimāha--na khalviti /
nanvekasminnanumānadvayasamāveśo virodhaścarastyeva tat kathamabhāvādityata āha--ayamabhisandhiriti /
na hi pūrvapravṛttena yadeva tadeva bādhyate, aniyamaprasaṅgāt, ata uktam--tabdalabhāvīti /
children.translated_text: For what is subverted by a previously operative [inference] is not necessarily that very same thing, since there would follow the consequence of indeterminacy. Therefore it was said: 'that which does not obtain it...'

children.text: svasiddhyarthaṃ svāśrayasiddhyarthaṃ svasyāpakasiddhyarthaṃ ca tadapekṣamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: it depends on that for its own establishment, for the establishment of its own basis, and for the establishment of its own pervader.

children.text: svavyāpakasādhakena bādhitamudāharati--evamiti /
children.translated_text: He gives an example of what is subverted by a prover of its own pervader: 'Thus...'

children.text: svasādhakena bādhitaṃ tu yathaikasantatipatitāni jñānāni ekapratipattṛvirahe 'pi pratisandhānayogyāni kāryakāraṇabhāvādityapi draṣṭavyam //
children.translated_text: But an example of what is subverted by its own prover would be: 'Cognitions belonging to a single continuum are fit for mutual recognition even in the absence of a single cognizer, because of the causal relation [between them]' — this too should be considered.

He states the basis for ridicule: '<s>Śruti</s> and <s>smṛti</s>...' The procedure is: domestic rites such as the <s>ukādi</s> rituals, being rooted in tradition, are like <s>agnihotra</s> and the like, because they are the practice of those who perform undisputed Vedic duties. But how is the means-to-the-good nature of this not ascertained? To this he says: 'Not indeed...' Although this may seem tenable at first glance, nevertheless, due to being tainted by the suspicion of groundlessness, it would not reach the point of practice. Therefore, inference of a [Vedic] root is more reliable — this is the meaning. Inference from the Veda is not the root-evidence — this is the meaning. What is said by 'pure'? Removing the redundancy he says: 'Moreover...' Then, from hostility to the three Vedas... Nor should one say that the dispute extends only as far as the thesis. For the purity of cow-dung and the like, being accepted by both parties, will be used as an example precisely to that extent. He raises the objection that even its purity cannot be accepted without accepting the authority of scripture: 'Now then...' The question is that of one who has understood the real intention — this is the meaning. He states the intention: 'Not indeed...' Now, the combination of two inferences with respect to a single subject and the existence of a contradiction — how then can one say 'from non-existence'? To this he says: 'This is the intention...'

children.text:
na hyatra kāryakāraṇabhāva ekapratipatrabhāve siddhyati /
kva tarhi asamāveśo yadabhisandhāyāha--samāveśābhāvādityata āha--tasmāditi /
samastarūpopapattiḥ sāmarthyam /
samāveśapakṣe 'vaśyamantata ekatarasyānyatararūpahānyā bhavitavyam /
anyathā tadekaṃ vastūbhayātmakamanubhayātmakaṃ vā syāt /
tasmād
children.translated_text: For the causal relation here is not established in the absence of a single cognizer. Where then is there non-combination, intending which he says 'because of the absence of combination'? To this he says: 'Therefore...' 'Capacity' means the tenability of the complete form. On the view of combination, ultimately there must be the loss of one or the other's form. Otherwise, that one entity would be either of both natures or of neither nature. Therefore

children.text: vastutastulyabalayorviruddhayoḥ samāveśo nāsti /
children.translated_text: in reality, there is no combination of two contradictories of equal strength.

children.text: samāviṣṭayośca na vāstavī tulyabalatetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And of two that have combined, there is in reality no equal strength — this is the meaning.

children.text:
tat kimidānīṃ satpratipakṣatā nāstyevetyata āha--na hīti /
evametad vastutaḥ satpratipakṣatā nāstyeva, kiṃ tvagṛhyamāṇaviśeṣavasthāyāṃ pramānutpādakatvaṃ parasparapratikṣepeṇa /
ataḥ sa eva doṣatvenopanibaddho muninetyarthaḥ /
etadeva vārttikamukhena darśayati--kasmāt punariti /
anumānayoruktarūpayoranvayavyatirekasaṃpannayorapi samāveśadarśanāt yathāśrutavārttikamasaṃgatamityata āha--iheti /
abādhitaviṣayeṇa saha pratyakṣādīnāmapi samāveśo nāsti /
tatastebhyo na
children.translated_text: Then does the condition of having a valid counter-argument (<s>satpratipakṣa</s>) not exist at all? To this he says: 'For not...' This is indeed so in reality — the condition of having a valid counter-argument does not exist at all. But in a state where the distinguishing feature is not apprehended, there is the non-production of valid cognition by mutual cancellation. Therefore, that very condition has been attached as a fault by the sage — this is the meaning. He shows this very point through the <s>vārttika</s>: 'Why then...' Since even when two inferences of the described form possess both positive and negative concomitance, combination is observed, the <s>vārttika</s> as literally read seems inconsistent — to this he says: 'Here...' Even perception and the like have no combination with one whose object is unsublated. Therefore no

children.text: kaścidanumānasya viśeṣa uktaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: specific distinction of inference from those [other means of knowledge] would have been stated.

children.text: atastadrūpaparihāreṇopalakṣaṇam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is illustrative, with the avoidance of that form [being understood].

children.text:
nanu yathā agṛhyamāṇaviśeṣāvasthāyāmanumānayoḥ satpratipakṣatvaṃ tathā pratyakṣānumānayorapyastu tataḥ kva bādhyabādhakabhāvaḥ? atha viśeṣeṇa gṛhīte pratyakṣamanumānasya bādhakamiṣyate, anumānamapyevamiṣyatām /
tathā ca parasparanirapekṣayoranumānayorapi bādhyabādhakabhāvo 'stvityāśayavān codyābhiprāyamāha--pratyakṣamapīti /
parihārābhiprayamāha--tulyabalau hīti /
pratyakṣaṃ hi nānumānasyānyathāsiddhyananyathāsiddhī pratīkṣate /
kiṃ tu svayamananyathāsiddhaṃ sadanumānamāskandatyeva, yathoṣṇatvagrāhiṇānanyathāsiddhena pratyakṣeṇānuṣṇatvānumānamanaupādhikatayā bādhakajñānāt pūrvamananyathāsiddhamapyāskanditam /
tadetadanayorhenādhikabalatvam /
anumānaṃ tu svayamananyathāsiddhamapi satpratipakṣānumānasyānyathāsiddhiṃ pratīkṣate /
na hyananyathāsiddhaṃ tattvena bādhituṃ śakyate aviśeṣāt /
tadetadanayostulyabalatvam /
na cānanyathāsiddhenāpyanyathāsiddhaṃ bādhyatāmiti yuktam, tasyānyathāsiddhatvenaiva dūṣitatvāt /
na ca yatra pratyakṣamanyathāsiddhaṃ tatrānumānenāvaśyamanyathāsiddhena bhavitavyam, ubhayorananyāsiddhau vastu
children.translated_text: Now, just as in the state where the distinguishing feature is not apprehended there is the condition of having a valid counter-argument between two inferences, so too let it be between perception and inference — then where is the relation of sublating and sublated? But if, when the distinguishing feature is apprehended, perception is accepted as sublating inference, let inference too be accepted likewise. And thus let there be a relation of sublating and sublated even between two mutually independent inferences — with this intention he states the purport of the objection: 'Even perception...' He states the purport of the reply: 'For of equal strength...' Perception does not await the otherwise-establishment or non-otherwise-establishment of inference. Rather, being itself non-otherwise-established, it directly assails even a well-established inference — just as a non-otherwise-established perception that apprehends heat assails the inference of non-heat, which, being non-conditional, was itself non-otherwise-established before the sublating cognition. This is the superiority in strength of the former over the latter. But inference, even when itself non-otherwise-established, awaits the otherwise-establishment of the counter-inference. For what is non-otherwise-established cannot truly sublate [another], since there is no distinction. This is the equal strength of the two. Nor is it proper that what is otherwise-established should be sublated by what is non-otherwise-established, since the former is already vitiated by being otherwise-established. Nor is it the case that wherever perception is otherwise-established, inference must necessarily be otherwise-established too — if both were non-otherwise-established, the entity

children.text:
dustaraṃ vyasanamāsādayet, tatastadapi tenaiva paribhūtam, kiṃ tatra pratyakṣabādhayeti vācyam /
tadanyathāsiddheḥ pratyakṣabādhotthāpyatvāditi viśeṣaḥ /
tasmād yāvat pratyakṣasyānanyathāsiddhatvaṃ nāvadhāryate, tāvatkālameva tatra
children.translated_text: would encounter an irresolvable predicament. Therefore that [inference] too is defeated by that very [perception] — what is the point of talking about perceptual sublation there? The distinctive point is that the otherwise-establishment of that [inference] is brought about by perceptual sublation. Therefore, as long as the non-otherwise-establishment of perception is not ascertained, for just that long

children.text:
nirṇayānudayaḥ satpratipakṣarūpatāṃ pratirūpayati /
taduttarakālaṃ tu kiṃ varākamanumānamityarthaḥ /
tadidamuktam-- pratyakṣamananyathāsiddhamiti /
children.translated_text: This is what has been stated: 'Perception is non-otherwise-established.'

children.text: upadarśitaprakārādanyena prakāreṇa vyavasthāpayitumaśakyam ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: it cannot be established in any other way than the way that has been shown.

children.text: anyaprakāravyavasthāpanaṃ ca viṣayasekocamātreṇa na bādhakaṃ vinā bhrāntatvenāpi /
children.translated_text: And establishment in another way, merely through restriction of scope, is not sublation, without also [establishing] it as erroneous.

children.text: tathā satyatiprasaṃgāditi //
children.translated_text: Because if so, there would be an undesirable over-extension.
the non-arising of determination simulates the form of having a valid counter-argument. But afterwards, what is that wretched inference? — this is the meaning.

children.text:
athopamānetyādi codyaṃ saṃbhāvayati gosadṛśa iti /
nanu nopamānaviruddhamiti vipratipattireva saṃpratipattirnāgarikalokasaṃpradāyenetyata āha--na bhavatītyanuṣajyate /
yodyavārttikasthamiti śeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: The remainder is: 'what is stated in the <s>vārttika</s>.'

children.text: anyathāsiddhapratyakṣāgamasamutthāpitamupamānamanumānena yadi vādhyate satpratipakṣyate vā, tadā tathābhūtau pratyakṣāgamāvevābādhitau satpratipakṣitau vā syātām /
children.translated_text: If an analogy established through non-otherwise-established perception and scripture is sublated or opposed by an inference, then those very non-sublated perception and scripture would themselves be sublated or opposed.

children.text: tathā ca sati sarvaṃ samākulamāpadyeta /
children.translated_text: And in that case, everything would become confused.

children.text: tasamād yathā tābhyāmanumānamapanudyate tathā tadutthāpitaphalaśarīreṇopamānenāpīti ṭīko pabṛṃhitasya vārttikasyārthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Therefore, just as inference is repelled by those two [perception and scripture], so too by analogy, which has a body of results established by them — this is the meaning of the <s>vārttika</s> as amplified by the <s>ṭīkā</s>.

Now he considers the objection beginning with 'analogy': 'similar to a cow.' Now, with regard to 'there is nothing contradicted by analogy,' the very disagreement is the agreement, according to the tradition of the cultured — to this he says: 'it does not occur' is to be connected.

children.text:
prayojanasvarūpeti bhrāntasyākṣepa iti vivaraṇaphalam prayojanavyākhyānāṅgamiti /
vādajalpau saprayojanāvityādibhāṣye yadyapi prayojanamaṅgatayā śrūyate tathāpyaḍgi pratyetavyam /
tenāyamartho bhāṣyasya, prayojanaṃ tāvad vādajalpau vyāpnoti, vitaṇḍāṃ tu vyāpnoti na veti cintyata iti vivaraṇārthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The purpose of the exposition is 'the nature of the purpose' — the objection of the confused one — and is auxiliary to the explanation of purpose. Although in the <s>bhāṣya</s> 'debate and disputation have a purpose' and so forth, purpose is heard as an auxiliary, nevertheless the principal is to be understood. Therefore the meaning of the <s>bhāṣya</s> is: purpose extends to debate and disputation, but whether or not it extends to cavil is to be examined — this is the purport of the exposition.

children.text: nanu vādajalpayoḥ prayojanavattvasiddhau vitaṇḍāyāstaccintyetāpi, tayoreva tu prayojanavattvaṃ kena bhāṣyeṇa pratipāditamityata āha--tatra śabdārthamiti /
children.translated_text: Now, once the purposefulness of debate and disputation is established, the purposefulness of cavil would also be examined. But by which <s>bhāṣya</s> has the purposefulness of those two been established? To this he says: 'There, the meaning of the word...'

children.text: vakṣyati hi pṛthagupadiṣṭa upalākṣaṇārtham, upalakṣitena vyavahārastattvajñānārthaṃ bhaviṣyatīti /
children.translated_text: For it will be said: 'Separately taught for the purpose of illustrative indication — the usage based on what has been indicated will serve the purpose of knowledge of truth.'

children.text: sa ca vyavahāro hetvābhāsebhyo hetovivecanalakṣaṇo 'vāntaraprayojanamapi asādhāraṇatayeha tatraśabdena bhāṣyakārasya vivakṣitamatastadeva vārttikakṛtā vyākhyātamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: And that usage, characterized by the discrimination of genuine reasons from pseudo-reasons, though also being an intermediate purpose, is intended by the <s>bhāṣyakāra</s> (commentator) with the word 'there' as being distinctive — and that very thing has been explained by the <s>vārttikakāra</s> (author of the <s>vārttika</s>) — this is the meaning.

children.text: nanu tathāpi tatra nyāye vivecayitavye iti yuktaṃ , na hi nyāyābhāsa eva viveka pradhānamityata āha--nyāyāmāsa iti tu sannidhānāditi //
children.translated_text: Now, even so, it would be proper to say 'in discriminating that <s>nyāya</s> (valid reasoning)' — for discrimination is not primarily about pseudo-reasoning — to this he says: 'But the word <s>nyāyābhāsa</s> (pseudo-reasoning) is used due to proximity.'

children.text: tadanena vicāraviṣayo vivicya darśitaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus, by this, the subject of inquiry has been discriminated and shown.

children.text: parīkṣapūrvarūpaṃ saṃśayaṃ darśayituntatkāraṇatayā vyākhyātṛvipratipattimāha--pratipakṣeti //
children.translated_text: In order to show doubt, which has the form of a preliminary to examination, he states the disagreement among expositors as its cause: 'Counter-thesis...'

children.text:
parīkṣāyā3 prayojanamāha--tatra yadīti /
pūrvapakṣaḥḥ---tatra keciditi /
siddhāntaḥ---parapakṣasādhaneti /
yadyapi parapakṣadūṣaṇenāpi prayojanena vitaṇḍāyāḥ saprayojanatva siddhacati,
children.translated_text: He states the purpose of examination: 'tatra yadi' (there if). The prima facie view (<s>pūrvapakṣa</s>): 'tatra kecid' (there some). The established conclusion (<s>siddhānta</s>): 'parapakṣasādhana' (establishment of the opponent's thesis). Although the purposefulness of <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (destructive debate) is established even by the purpose of refuting the opponent's thesis,

children.text: yamarthamadhikṛtya pravartate tatprayojanam /
children.translated_text: 'That with reference to which one proceeds is the purpose' —

children.text:
iti vacanāt, yadi ca parapakṣadūṣaṇamapi nādhikuryāt tadā vaitaṇḍika eva na syāt /
tathāpyetadeva svayaṃ kiñcidapyanabhyupagacchato na syādityataḥ pāriśeṣyādapi svapakṣasiddhim abhisaṃdadhānasyaiva pravṛttiryuktetyāśayaḥ /
nanu
children.translated_text: by this dictum; and if he did not even engage in the refutation of the opponent's thesis, then he would not even be a <s>vaitaṇḍika</s> (destructive debater). Nevertheless, since this [activity] would not exist for one who does not himself accept anything whatsoever — therefore, even by the method of elimination, the intention is that engagement is proper only for one who intends the establishment of his own thesis. Now,

children.text:
nāstyevāsau vādī yaḥ kiñcidapi nābhyupagacchet, antato narthasyaivābhyupagamāt /
tadanabhayupagame tu kiñcidapi
children.translated_text: there is no such debater who does not accept anything whatsoever, since at the very least one accepts the non-existence of the [opponent's] thesis. But if one does not accept even that, then one would not even say

children.text:
nābhyupagacchāmītyetadapi na brūyāt /
tasmāt kimanenāsadudbhāvanenetyata āha--nāstiko hīti /
nāstiko mādhyamikādiḥ /
anena hi parapakṣo nāmyupagamyate na punaḥ parapakṣapratiṣedho 'bhyupagamyata ityarthaḥ /
tadidamuktaṃ parapakṣapratiṣadhamātraprayuktaḥ pravartata iti /
tathā hi nedaṃ jagadasti, bādhyamānatvāt /
nāpi nāsti, pratīyamānatvāt /
nāpi sadasadrūpam, virodhāt /
nāpyanubhayarūpam, virodhādevāpratīteśceti /
nanu na hi yadeva pratyeti, tadevābhyupagacchati /
tathā sati prativādivacanārthaḥ pratītaścedabhyupagataḥ syādita matānujñā nigrahasthānam /
apratītaścedajñānaṃ nigrahasthānam ityāyātamityata āha--pratipattirabhyupagamaḥ /
iha vivakṣita iti śeṣaḥ /
tathāpyabhyupagamaviṣayatvādeva na pakṣastasya jñāpyatvādityata āha--yadyapīti /
children.translated_text: Even so, since [his position] is precisely the object of acceptance, it is not a thesis (<s>pakṣa</s>), because [a thesis is defined as] what is to be made known — therefore he says: 'yadyapi' (although).

children.text: tannāntarīyakatvāditi abhyupagamanāntarīyakatvāt /
children.translated_text: 'Because of being its necessary concomitant' means: because of being a necessary concomitant of acceptance.

children.text: jñāpyatāyāḥ pakṣaśabdena siddhānto 'tra vivakṣita ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Because of the to-be-made-known character — by the word '<s>pakṣa</s>' (thesis), <s>siddhānta</s> (established doctrine) is intended here. This is the meaning.

children.text: asiddhaviruddhatvādidoṣo vādyuktasādhanaviṣaya iti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: The faults of non-establishment, contradiction, and the like pertain to the proof adduced by the proponent — this is the completion.

'I do not accept anything whatsoever.' Therefore, what is the point of this baseless conjecture? — to this he says: 'nāstikaḥ hī' (for the nihilist). The nihilist (<s>nāstika</s>) is the <s>Mādhyamika</s> and the like. For by such [a person], the opponent's thesis is not accepted, but neither is the negation of the opponent's thesis accepted — this is the meaning. This is what is said: 'one who proceeds motivated merely by the negation of the opponent's thesis.' For thus: 'This world does not exist, because it is sublated. Nor does it not exist, because it is cognized. Nor does it have both the nature of existent and non-existent, because of contradiction. Nor does it have neither nature, because of contradiction and non-cognition.' Now, it is not the case that whatever one cognizes, one accepts. If it were so, then if the meaning of the opponent's statement is cognized, it would be accepted — and that would be the defeat-condition of assenting to the opponent's view. And if it is not cognized, then ignorance would be a defeat-condition — this would follow. Therefore he says: 'Cognition is acceptance — here this [sense] is intended' — the completion.

children.text:
adṛṣṭāntasyāpi sādhanavikalādeḥ pratyakṣaviṣayatvādityativyāptiḥ /
āgamādiviṣayasyāpi vyāptigrahaṇagocarasya dṛṣṭāntatvādityavyāptiḥ /
nanu tathāpyativyāptirevetyata āha--atra ceti /
saṃmugdhaṃ vārtikaṃ vivecayati--yatteṣu teṣviti /
atha lakṣaṇasūtravyāghāta eva kasmānna bhavati, yāvatā tadapi pratyakṣāpratyakṣasādhāraṇamityata
children.translated_text: Even for [a proof] without an example, because of being within the domain of perception — since it is [included in] a deficient proof — there is over-extension [of the definition]. And because what pertains to the domain of scripture and the like, being within the domain of the apprehension of <s>vyāpti</s> (universal concomitance), is also an example — there is under-extension. Now, even so there is over-extension — therefore he says: 'atra ca' (and here). He clarifies the confounded <s>Vārttika</s>: 'yatteṣu teṣu' (in those [cases]). Now, why does a contradiction with the definitional <s>sūtra</s> not arise, since that too is common to both the perceptible and the non-perceptible? — therefore

children.text: āha--na tūdāharaṇeti /
children.translated_text: he says: 'na tūdāharaṇa' (but not the illustration).

children.text: sādhāraṇaṃ viśeṣaviṣayatayāpi śakyaṃ vyākhyātumityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: What is common can also be explained as pertaining to a specific object — this is the meaning.

children.text:
tat kimidānī bhāṣyamalagnamevetyata āha--tasmāditi /
nanvanumānāt ko 'paro nyāyo yenānumānāśrayatāmuktvāpi nyāyāśrayatāṃ dṛṣṭāntasya pṛthagāha bhāṣyakāraḥ, vārtikakāro 'pi tathaivānumanyata ityata
children.translated_text: Then is the <s>Bhāṣya</s> exactly right as it stands? — therefore he says: 'tasmāt' (therefore). Now, what other <s>nyāya</s> (method of reasoning) is there apart from inference, that the author of the <s>Bhāṣya</s>, leaving aside its being based on inference, separately states the example as being based on <s>nyāya</s> — and the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> too assents to the same? — therefore

children.text:
āha--nyāyasya pañcāvayavātmakasyeti /
tathāpyāśrayatvaṃ saṃyogasamavāyābhyāṃ dṛṣṭāntasya na ghaṭate,
children.translated_text: he says: 'nyāyasya pañcāvayavātmakasya' (of the nyāya consisting of five members). Even so, the relation of the example [to the nyāya] does not work through conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) or inherence (<s>samavāya</s>),

children.text:
vākyasyākāśāśrayatvādityatta uktaṃ--mūlamiti /
tathāpyanumānāśrayatvaṃ dṛṣṭāntasyāsaṃgataṃ liṅgasya pakṣāśrayatvāt
children.translated_text: since a sentence is like space — hence it is said: 'mūla' (root). Even so, the example's being based on inference is inappropriate, because the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is located in the thesis-subject (<s>pakṣa</s>),

children.text:
tajjñānasya cāmāśrayatvāt /
ata uktam--anumānaṃ nimittatvamāheti /
pūrvapratyakṣadṛṣṭamiti yathāśrutaṃ bahvākulayatītyata āha--dṛṣṭānteti /
evaṃ ca satyanumānanimittatvāt pakṣasyāpi pṛthagabhidhānaṃ syāditi na codyam /
siddhāntābhidhānenaiva gatārthatvāditi /
nanu śabde dṛṣṭāntāpekṣā nāstyeva,
children.translated_text: and the cognition of that [mark] is located in the person — not [in the example]. Hence it is said: 'anumānaṃ nimittatvam āha' (he states that inference is the cause). The literal reading of 'previously seen through direct perception' creates much confusion — therefore he says: 'dṛṣṭānta' (example). And this being so, even the thesis-subject, being a cause of inference, should be separately stated — this objection does not arise, since the meaning is already conveyed by the statement of the <s>siddhānta</s>. Now, in the case of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>), there is simply no dependence on an example,

children.text: agniṣṭomena yajeta svargakāmaḥ
children.translated_text: 'One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>' —

children.text: ityādau tamantareṇaiva vākyārthapratīterityata āha--saṃbandhagrahaṇaviṣaya iti /
children.translated_text: since in such [cases] the meaning of the sentence is understood even without it — therefore he says: 'saṃbandhagrahaṇaviṣaya' (the domain of the apprehension of connection).

children.text: saṃbandhagrahaṇaviṣayatāmātreṇa dṛṣṭāntatvaṃ vivakṣitvedamuktam, na punarvyāptilakṣaṇasaṃbandhaviśeṣagrahaṇaviṣayatayetyabhiprāyaḥ /
