children.translated_text: While showing the <s>pramāṇa</s> for the established position, he also removes the doubt about what use the co-occurrence with the <s>sādhya</s>-word would serve: 'now, the <s>sādhya</s> portion.'

children.text: iṣṭābhyupāyatā hi neṣṭamapratītya pratyetuṃ śakyā /
children.translated_text: For being a means to what is desired cannot be understood without first understanding what is desired.

children.text: na cāpravṛttaiva sā pravartayati /
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that [the means], being merely inoperative, motivates [action].

children.text: atastāṃ viśeṣṭumiṣṭasyānuvādo 'yamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Therefore, in order to qualify that [means], this [mention of the desired end] is a reiteration (<s>anuvāda</s>) of the desired end — this is the meaning.

and so forth. Having shown the domain, he states the doubt: 'therein, what?' And the cause of doubt is the co-occurrence of the word denoting it with the injunctive word. For the one who is qualified, being one whose own word co-occurs with the injunctive word, is not the object of the injunction. And <s>agnihotra</s> and the like, being precisely of that nature, are the objects of the injunction. Therefore there is doubt regarding the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be accomplished): does heaven become an object of injunction like <s>agnihotra</s> and the like, by virtue of being a word co-occurring with the injunctive word, or does it not, like a qualified person? While showing the prima facie view itself, he states the undesirable consequence therein: 'therein, if.' Nor should one say: let violence that is accomplished by the <s>Śyena</s> sacrifice and the like be simply of purposive value, being enjoined — what harm is there? For an injunction is a motivator — that is to say, it generates effort through its own cognition, by interposing desire. And that effort cannot have the <s>sādhya</s> (end) as its object. For means are the object of effort, not the result. Therefore, by virtue of being the object of effort, it is the means-and-procedure (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) that is enjoined, not the <s>sādhya</s>, since it is not the object [of effort]. For being an injunction is not merely being an indicator, but rather being an indicator of something that is an object of desire and effort. Therefore, violence accomplished by the <s>Śyena</s> and the like, being harmful, would [wrongly] become purposive — if it were an object of injunction — so it is well stated.

children.text:
tat kimidānīmavihitamityetāvataivānarthaḥ? netyāha--na hiṃsyāditi /
nanu bhavatvevaṃ tāvat tathāpyānvīkṣikyā kimāyātamityata āha--tadiheti /
viṣayāntaramāha--evamiti /
yathā ābhikhyāyāḥ prayojakatvaṃ kṣīrahomasthāne tadviniveśanād rasādisāmyāt, vājinasyāprayojakatvamavarjanīyotpattikatvāt /
ādigrahaṇena śeṣabhāgahomavilopādayo gṛhyante /
sarvā vidyā iti vidyaśabdena taddharmān lakṣayatīti na bhāṣyavyākhyāvirodhaḥ /
vārttikakārastu dharmāṇāṃ vidyāpāratantryaṃ vivakṣanniti śeṣaḥ /
saṅkaraprasaṅga iti phalasya /
tathā ca vidyāntarulenaivāsya phalavattvaṃ na
children.translated_text: Then is merely being un-enjoined sufficient for [something to be] harmful? No, he says: 'one should not harm.' Now, let it be so for the time being — still, what has <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> contributed? To this he says: 'therefore, here.' He states another domain: 'thus.' Just as the motivating power of designation — [for instance,] the substitution [of one substance for another] at the place of a milk-oblation — [is established] due to its introduction there and due to similarity of taste and other qualities; [and] the non-motivating power of the horse — due to its being an unavoidable by-product. By the word 'and so forth,' the offerings of subsidiary portions and the omissions [of certain rites] and so forth are included. 'All disciplines' — by the word 'discipline,' he indicates their properties — therefore there is no contradiction with the commentary-explanation. But the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>, intending to express the dependence of properties on the disciplines — this is the remainder. 'The consequence of confusion' means: of the result. And thus, it is only through the other disciplines themselves that this [<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>] bears fruit — not

children.text:
punarasādhāraṇaṃ phalamasyā astītyarthaḥ /
asāṅkaryaṃ darśayituṃ tāsāmeva tāvadasādhāraṇaṃ phalamāha--vidyāntarāṇīti /
etasyā asādhāraṇaṃ phalamāha--iha tviti /
anyatrāsyāḥ pratipāditopayogavirodho mā bhūditāśayavatoktam--pramāṇādi
children.translated_text: does it have a distinctive fruit of its own — this is the meaning. To show the absence of confusion, he first states the distinctive result of those [other disciplines]: 'the other disciplines.' He states the distinctive result of this [<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>]: 'but here.' Lest there be contradiction with the utility established elsewhere for this [<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>], he says with that intention: '<s>pramāṇa</s> and the rest,

children.text: yadyapi sādhāraṇamiti /
children.translated_text: although common.'

children.text: etenaitaduktaṃ bhavati, vidyāntarulānyapi yadānvīkṣikyāmāyatante seyamūṣmasiddhirasyāḥ /
children.translated_text: By this, what is stated amounts to this: when the other disciplines also draw upon <s>ānvīkṣikī</s>, that is the incidental accomplishment [accruing to] this [discipline].

children.text: yattu pradhānamasyāḥ phalaṃ tadasaṃkīrṇameva vidyāntareṣvasaṃbhavāditi //
children.translated_text: But the principal fruit of this [<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>] is unmingled [with other disciplines], since it is impossible in the other disciplines.

children.text:
vādādīnāmiti atadguṇasaṃvijñāno bahuvrīhiḥ, vādasya parābhibhavārthamapravṛtteḥ /
jalpādayo hi madādihetavaḥ parābhibhavopāyatvāt dravyaśarīrasaṃpattivaditi prayogaḥ /
tatrāsya viruddhatvaṃ tāvadāha--tatra jalpādīnāmiti /
ayamāśayaḥ /
na tāvat pratipādyasya jalpavitaṇḍayoradhikāraḥ /
kiṃ tu pratipannasya tattvapratipattipālanārthaṃ duravaliptapratipādanārthaṃ ca tayoradhikāraḥ /
parāhaṅgāraśātanaṃ ca madamānādiviruddhameva, teṣāṃ doṣaviśeṣatvāt /
children.translated_text: 'Of <s>vāda</s> (debate) and the like' — this is a <s>bahuvrīhi</s> compound meaning 'not possessing their qualities,' since <s>vāda</s> does not operate for the purpose of defeating the opponent. For <s>jalpa</s> (sophistic debate) and the like are causes of pride and so forth, because they are means of defeating the opponent — just like the possession of wealth, body, and accomplishments — this is the argument. Against this, he first states its contradictoriness: 'therein, of <s>jalpa</s> and the like.' This is the intention: to begin with, the purpose of <s>jalpa</s> and <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil) is not for one who is being taught. Rather, their purpose is for one who has already understood — for the protection of the apprehension of truth and for teaching the arrogant. And the shattering of another's ego is itself opposed to pride, vanity, and the like, since those are particular faults.

children.text: ahaḍkāraśātanasya ca tannirodharūpatvāt /
children.translated_text: And the shattering of ego has the nature of suppressing those [faults].

children.text: na ca parābhibhāvopāyabhūtaśabdavācyatāmātreṇānumānam, vāgādīnāmapi viṣāṇitvaprasaṃgāditi //
children.translated_text: And merely because something is designated by a word denoting a means of defeating the opponent, it is not [thereby] a cause of pride — otherwise, speech and the like would also have the absurd consequence of being horns [i.e. weapons].

children.text:
syādetat /
parābhibhavopāyatvena hetunā madamānādihetutvaṃ mā saitsīt, anvayavyatirekābhyāmeva tu siddhacatvityata āha--madamānādihetutvaṃ ca heturasiddha iti /
sati ca tattvavidāṃ na saṃbhavantīti vadatā yathāśrutasya
children.translated_text: One might say this: let the causation of pride, vanity, and the like not be established by the reason 'being a means of defeating the opponent' — but let it be established simply through positive and negative concomitance — to this he says: 'and the causation of pride, vanity, and the like is an unestablished reason.' And by saying 'they are not possible for knowers of truth,' the inconclusiveness

children.text: parābhibhavopāyatvasyānaikāntikatvamapi sūcitam /
children.translated_text: of 'being a means of defeating the opponent,' as literally read, was also indicated.

children.text: ato jalpāditattvajñānavatāmapi yadi mānādayo dṛśyante, na te taddhetukāḥ, kiṃ tu balavanmithyājñānahetukā eveti sanakādyudāharaṇaphalamiti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, even if pride and the like are seen in those who know the truth of <s>jalpa</s> and the rest, they are not caused by that [knowledge], but rather by the force of powerful false cognition — this is the import of the examples of <s>Sanaka</s> and others.

children.text: etacca sphuṭamityabhiprāyeṇāha--upasaṃharatīti //1 //
children.translated_text: Since this is clear, he says with that intention: 'he concludes.' [End of] Section 1.

children.text: // pariśuddhiḥ //
children.translated_text: The Purification (<s>Pariśuddhi</s>).

children.text:
apratītasvarūpasya prayojanāmisaṃbandhasya parīkṣā na yujyate, rirāśrayatvāt /
prathamasūtraṃ tūddeśaparamevetyata āha--tadevamiti /
abhidheyasaṃbandhaprayojanaparādeva tasmāduddeśo 'pyavagataḥ /
sa cāpekṣitatvād gṛhīta ityarthaḥ /
etena parīkṣāviṣayo darśitaḥ /
ucitaṃ darśayanneva tadatikrame hetumāha--teṣāmiti /
aitena chalataḥ saṃbandhaparīkṣāyāḥ prayojanamapi
children.translated_text: Examination of the connection with the purpose is not appropriate when the intrinsic nature [of the subject] has not been understood, since it would be baseless. But the first <s>sūtra</s> is merely for the purpose of enumeration — to this he says: 'thus then.' Since the first <s>sūtra</s> is intended precisely for the referent, connection, and purpose, the enumeration too is thereby understood. And it has been accepted because it was needed — this is the meaning. By this, the subject of examination has been shown. While showing what is appropriate, he states the reason for going beyond it: 'of those.' By this, the purpose of the examination of connection, which was lurking [unexpressed], has also been

children.text:
darśitam /
abhidhānasya dvaividhyam-ubhayakoṭisaṃsparśaḥ /
samīcīnamityādyanurodhena yathā vārttikādityādāvārthaḥ kramo grāhyaḥ /
tasmādamidhānasāmānyāt abhidhānasādhargyamātrāt nirṇāyakarahitāt dṛśyamānāditi yāvat /
ubhayathā darśanācceti /
tatsahacaritobhayakoṭidarśanajasaṃskārabhuvaḥ smaraṇāditi yāvat /
etacca sūtrakārasyāptatvāvadhāraṇāt prāgiti mantavyam /
yadyapi
children.translated_text: shown. The statement has a twofold nature — touching both extremities. The meaning and order should be understood in accordance with 'correct' and so forth, as in 'from the <s>vārttika</s>' and so forth. Therefore, from the mere generality of statement, from the mere commonality of statement that is devoid of a determining factor, [arising] from what is perceived — this much is to be understood. 'And from being seen in both ways' — this much is to be understood: from recollection born of impressions produced by seeing both extremities associated with it. And this should be considered as prior to the ascertainment of the trustworthiness of the <s>sūtrakāra</s>. Although

children.text:
cātra vacana eva sākṣāt saṃśayaṃ darśayati, tathāpi taddvārā artha eva draṣṭavya iti /
saṃbandhini ca prayojane tattvajñānakāryatayā parīkṣyamāṇe saṃbandha eva kāryakāraṇabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ parokṣito bhavatīti tadeva parīkṣyatayā nirdiśyate--tat khalu vai niḥśreyasamiti /
vastutastu saṃbandhaparīkṣaiveyamityato na pratijñāsaṃśayaparīkṣāṇāṃ vaiyadhikaraṇyamiti /
tatreti /
children.translated_text: 'There' —

children.text: sūtre vyākhyātavye /
children.translated_text: in the <s>sūtra</s> to be explained.

children.text: utsūtreṇeti /
children.translated_text: 'Incidentally' —

children.text: pūrvapakṣaṃ vinā siddhāntasūtrasyāvatārābhāvāt ityāśayaḥ //
children.translated_text: the intention is: because without the prior objection, there would be no occasion for the established-conclusion <s>sūtra</s>.

here in the statement itself directly shows the doubt, nevertheless, through that, it should be seen in the object itself. And when the related purpose is examined as being an effect of the knowledge of truth, the relation itself, characterized by the causal connection, becomes the implicit subject — and so that very thing is indicated as what is to be examined: 'That indeed is the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>).' In reality, however, this is just an examination of the relation itself — and therefore thesis, doubt, and examination are not in different sections.

children.text:
nanu jīvanmuktipakṣe tadvatāmavasthānaṃ na syāditi codyamānamanavakāśamityata āha--tadatyanteti /
nanu mā bhūt
children.translated_text: Now, on the view of liberation while living (<s>jīvanmukti</s>), the continued existence of those who possess it would not be possible — when this is objected, it is without scope — to this he says: 'That absolute...' Now, let

children.text: tattvajñānānantarameva niḥśreyasam, kā no hāniḥ /
children.translated_text: the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) not occur immediately after the knowledge of truth — what harm is there to us?

children.text: na hyevaṃ pratijñātamasmābhirityata āha--tathā satīti /
children.translated_text: For we have not asserted it to be so — to this he says: 'That being the case...'

children.text: yadyapi sākṣādevaṃ na pratijñātam, tathāpi tattvajñānaniśreyasayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ sūtrakṛtā darśitaḥ, sa cānanantaryaniyama eva syāt, nāto 'nyatheti pūrvapakṣī manyata ityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Although this has not been directly asserted, nevertheless the causal relation between the knowledge of truth and the highest good has been shown by the author of the <s>sūtras</s>, and the opponent thinks that this must be a rule of immediate succession, not otherwise — this is the meaning.

children.text: tadidamuktam--mithyeti //
children.translated_text: This is what was stated: 'Falsely...'

children.text:
nanu tathāpi, tadatyantavimokṣo 'pavargaḥ /
[1.1.22] ityatāvadeva niḥśreyasamiti kena pratijñānaṃ yāvatā jīvanmuktirapi riḥśreyasaṃ bhavatyevetyata āha--na cānyaditi /
abhisandhau bījaṃ tattvajñānasyotpannasyāpavarge
children.translated_text: Now, even so, 'The absolute release from that is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation)' [1.1.22] — by this much alone the highest good is stated; by what is it asserted [to be more], since liberation while living too is indeed the highest good? To this he says: 'And not another...' The seed of the intention is: when the knowledge of truth has arisen, there is nothing further to be depended upon for effecting <s>apavarga</s>.

children.text:
kartavye 'pekṣaṇīyābhāvaḥ /
bhāve vā tadevāpavargasādhanam, na tattvajñānamiti /
tadidakukta vārttikakṛtā--satyapi tattvajñāne
children.translated_text: Or, if there is [something further], then that very thing is the means to <s>apavarga</s>, not the knowledge of truth. This was stated by the <s>Vārttikakāra</s>: 'Even when the knowledge of truth exists,

children.text: yasyābhāvānnāpavṛjyate so 'nyor'thaḥ iti sphuṭaṃ vārttikamiti ṭīkārthaḥ /
sūtrasamutthatāṃ siddhāntavārttikasya darśayituṃ sūtramavatārayati--atredamiti /
children.translated_text: In order to show the origin of the established-conclusion <s>vārttika</s> from the <s>sūtra</s>, he introduces the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Here this...'

children.text: yathāśrutaṃ vārttikaṃ na pūrvāpakṣācchādakaṃ na hyaparamapi niḥśreyasaṃ śāstrīyāt tattvajñānāt sākṣādbhavatīti, yasmācca sākṣādbhavati na tacchāstrīyamityato bhūmimaracayati--catasro hīti /
children.translated_text: The <s>vārttika</s> as literally read does not cover the prior objection — for the other highest good too does not arise directly from the scriptural knowledge of truth; and what arises directly is not scriptural — therefore he prepares the ground: 'For there are four...'

children.text: sā cānvīkṣikyāmāyatate āyattā bhavati /
children.translated_text: And that [the fourth type of cognition] extends to, i.e., depends upon, <s>ānvīkṣikī</s> (logical inquiry).

children.text: tatparikaropayogamāha--ānvīkṣikī ceti //
children.translated_text: He states its usefulness in elaboration: 'And <s>ānvīkṣikī</s>...'
that without which liberation does not occur is something else' — this is a clear <s>vārttika</s> — this is the meaning of the <s>ṭīkā</s>.

children.text:
nanu śravaṇasya tāvadākāṅkṣotthāpanenopayogo, mananasyāpyevamevetyavadhāraṇena, tat kimaparamavaśiṣyate yadarthaṃ pratipattyantaropāsanam? na hi niścayātiriktaṃ kasyacit pramāṇasya phalamityata āha--na cāyamiti /
āyamāśayaḥ /
na hi niścayo mohaḥ aupadeśikenānumānikena vā tattvaniścayena nirākartuṃ pāryate, tadupāyānuṣṭhānena tu tayorūpyogaḥ /
tasmād ye vedāntino vākyārthajñānādeva muktimicchanti, te praṣṭavyāḥ, kiṃ bhavatāṃ vastusantamupāyopeyabhāvasaṃbandhamabhyupagamya pravṛttiḥ, savṛtisantaṃ vā? ādye 'dvaitasiddhāntakṣatiḥ, kāryakāraṇabhāvasya bhedādhiṣṭhānatayā tayoḥ paramārthikatve bhedasyāpi pāramārthikatvaprasaṃgāt, dvitīye tu kimaviśeṣeṇa pravṛttiḥ, yathāsaṃvṛtivyavasthaṃ vā? ādye bhogino 'pyapavṛjyeran /
dvitīye tu na śābdādānumānikād vā tattvajñānādaindriyakavyāmohavigamaḥ /
kiṃ tarhi, sākṣātkārādeva dṛṣṭa iti tathaiva tadarthinaḥ pravṛttiryuktā /
na ca vācyaṃ vākyādevātmasākṣātkārodaya iti, tasya kevalasya sāmarthyānupalambhāt /
yadi tu svasaṃviditasvarūpatayā kiṃ tatra dhyānādikamapūrvamādhāsrūtītyucyate, tadā śruterapi vaiphalyamanenaiva nyāyena /
yadapi bhautadaśakanadīsaṃtaraṇamudāhṛtaṃ, tatrāpi na kevalenaiva vākyena sākṣātkāraḥ kiṃ tu cakṣurādinaiva /
ihāpi manasā sahakṛtena bhaviṣyatīti cet--na, anekadhā śrutaśruterapi satyapi ca paṭīyasi manasi brahmasākṣātkārābhāvāt /
tat kasya hotoḥ? bhautānāmiva svaśarīre cākṣuṣasya dṛḍhatarābhyāsasya mumukṣormānasasyātmanyabhāvāt /
tasmāt tadarthamabhyāsa eva śaraṇam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, practice alone is the refuge for that purpose.

children.text: tadidamuktaṃ lokasiddhamiti /
children.translated_text: This is what was stated: 'Established in common experience...'

children.text: lokasiddhaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvastāttviko bhavatu mā vā bhavatu sarvasya puruṣārthapravṛttasya tāvat sa eva śaraṇam /
children.translated_text: Whether the causal relation established in common experience is ultimately real or not, for everyone engaged in human goals, that alone is the refuge.

children.text: tadanādare tu puruṣārtho 'pi nādaraṇīyastulyayogakṣematvāditi //
children.translated_text: And if that is disregarded, then the human goal too need not be regarded, since they share the same status.

Now, hearing has its use in raising desire [for knowledge], and reflection too has the same use through ascertainment. What else remains for which meditation, as a further means of cognition, is needed? For no means of valid knowledge has a result beyond determination — to this he says: 'And this is not...' The intention is as follows: for neither certainty nor delusion can be removed by the determination of truth obtained through instruction or inference; but through the practice of the means of those, the two [certainty and delusion] are of use. Therefore, those <s>Vedāntins</s> who desire liberation from the knowledge of the meaning of sentences alone are to be asked: Does your activity presuppose the acceptance of a real relation of means and end? Or one that exists only conventionally? In the first case, there is damage to the doctrine of non-duality, since the causal relation, being grounded in difference, would entail the ultimate reality of difference if both [means and end] are ultimately real. In the second case, is the activity without any distinction, or according to conventional arrangement? In the first case, even worldly enjoyers would be liberated. In the second case, verbal or inferential knowledge of truth would not remove the perceptual delusion. What then? It is seen that only direct realization does so — and thus the activity of one who seeks that is proper. Nor should one say that direct realization of the Self arises from the sentence alone, since no capacity is observed in the sentence by itself. But if one says that since its nature is self-known, what unprecedented thing would meditation and the like contribute beyond the <s>śruti</s>? — then by this very reasoning the <s>śruti</s> too would be fruitless. And as for the cited example of crossing ten rivers, even there direct realization comes not from the sentence alone but from the eye and other senses themselves. If one says: here too it will come through the mind as an auxiliary — no, because even one who has heard the <s>śruti</s> many times, and even possessing a sharp mind, does not have direct realization of <s>Brahman</s>. For what reason? Because, just as in the case of physical objects and visual perception, the seeker of liberation lacks the firm and repeated mental practice regarding the Self.

children.text:
yadi nāma catasraḥ pratipattaya ātmādau prameye, prakṛte tu kimāyātamityata āha--atheti /
etaduktaṃ bhavati--yadi śrautamānumānikaṃ vā tattvajñānamādāya pūrvapakṣaḥ, tadā anabhyupagama evottaram /
na hi tasya sākṣānniḥśreyasahetutvamācakṣmahe /
kiṃ tarhi? paramparayā saiva catasro hītyādinā darśitā /
tasmāt sākṣātkāramādāya pūrvapakṣaḥ /
tasya hi sākṣādeva niḥśreyasahetutā abhyupagamyate /
children.translated_text: For it is accepted that direct realization is directly the cause of the highest good.

children.text: tatrābhayanodyaparihārārthaṃ niḥśreyasadvevidhyapratipādanamupasthāpyata iti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therein, the establishment of the twofold nature of the highest good is introduced for the purpose of removing the objection and providing the reply — this is the purport.

children.text: atha idyucyata ityantena pūrvapakṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Now, the prior objection extends up to 'thus it is said.'

children.text: pūrvaḥ pūrvo heturuttara uttarastadvāniti //
children.translated_text: Each preceding [cognition] is the cause of each succeeding one, and possesses that.

Even if there are four types of cognition with respect to objects of knowledge such as the Self, what is the relevance to the subject at hand? To this he says: 'Now...' What is stated is this: if the prior objection takes as its basis scriptural or inferential knowledge of truth, then the answer is simply non-acceptance. For we do not declare that to be a direct cause of the highest good. What then? Indirectly — as has been shown by 'For there are four...' Therefore, the prior objection must take direct realization as its basis.

children.text:
nanu sākṣātkāravāṃśca dehādimāśceti durghaṭamidam /
na hi śravaṇāderiva pare niḥśreyase kartavye sākṣātkārasyāpi kiñcit kartavyāntaramastītyata āha--na caivamiti /
codyasaṃbhāvanāya dṛṣṭāntaḥ--na ca prāyaścitteneveti /
na tāvat prāyaścittasyādhikārāpattiḥ phalam, āgamamantareṇādṛṣṭakarmaṇāṃ phalaviśeṣakalpanāyāṃ pramāṇābhāvāt śrūyamāṇaphalaparityāgaprasaṃgācca /
balavati bādhake sati nedamaniṣṭamiti cet--na, ananyathāsiddhasyāgamasya bādhakasahasreṇāpyapanetumaśakyatvāt /
śakyatve vā surāpayetvānumānamapi durnivāramiti haitukānāṃ dattaḥ svahastaḥ syāt /
ata eva na prāyaścittācaraṇaduḥkhameva brāhmahatyādīnāṃ phalam, tatphalatvenāśruteḥ, prāyaścittavidhivaiphalyaprasaṃgācca
children.translated_text: Now, that one who has direct realization also has a body and the rest — this is difficult to reconcile. For just as hearing and the rest have no further task in effecting the ultimate highest good, so too direct realization has no further task — to this he says: 'And not in this way...' An example to make the objection conceivable: 'And not by expiation alone...' To begin with, the result of expiation is not the occurrence of eligibility, since there is no authority for imagining a specific result of invisible actions (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) without scripture, and because there would follow the abandonment of the result stated in scripture. If one says that in the presence of a strong sublating cognition, this is not undesired — no, because scripture, being non-otherwise-established, cannot be removed even by a thousand sublating cognitions. Or, if it could be, then the inference 'let one drink liquor' too would be irresistible — and thus the logicians would give themselves away. Therefore, expiation-practice-suffering is not the result of sins like <s>brahmahatyā</s> (killing a Brahmin), since it is not heard as their result, and because there would follow the purposelessness of the injunction of expiation,

children.text: aviśeṣādhānācca /
children.translated_text: and because no specific assignment is made.

children.text: aniccheto 'pi karmabalādeva tatsiddheśca /
children.translated_text: And because it [the result] would be accomplished by the force of <s>karma</s> alone even for one who does not wish it.

children.text: tasmādadattaphalānyeva karmāṇi prāyaścittena kṣīyanta ityeva sādhu /
children.translated_text: Therefore, it is proper to hold that only those <s>karmas</s> that have not yet yielded their results are diminished by expiation.

children.text: tathā tadvadeva tattvasākṣātkāro 'pi kariṣyatītyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Similarly, direct realization of truth too will do likewise — this is the meaning.

children.text: atra cāgamabalapravṛttā āgamenaiva bodhayituṃ yujyanta ityāśayavānāha,
children.translated_text: Here, intending that those whose activity is driven by scripture should be instructed through scripture itself, he says:

children.text: nābhuktaṃ kṣīyate
children.translated_text: 'What has not been experienced does not perish'

children.text:
[]iti /
nanu
children.translated_text: — thus. Now,

children.text: jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi...bhasmasāt kurūte tathā /
children.translated_text: 'The fire of knowledge reduces all <s>karmas</s>... to ashes likewise.'

children.text: gītā 4.37
children.translated_text: <s>Gītā</s> 4.37

children.text:
ityevaṃ vipakṣe 'pi smṛtirasti /
tat kathaṃ nirṇayo bhaviṣyatītyata āha--antyasukheti /
syādapyevaṃ yadi nābhuktamityādismṛteranugrāhako nyāyo na syāt, asti ca tathā /
tathā ca prayogaḥ, vivādādhyāsitāni karmāṇi
children.translated_text: — thus there is <s>smṛti</s> on the opposing side too. Then how will the determination be made? To this he says: 'The final happiness...' This would be so if there were no reasoning supporting the <s>smṛti</s> 'what has not been experienced does not perish' — but there is such reasoning. And thus the argument: the <s>karmas</s> that are in dispute

children.text:
bhogādeva kṣīyante acīrṇaprayaścittakarmatvādārabdhaśarīrakarmavat /
na cātrāgamavirordhaḥ, tasyāgamāntaravirodhenānirṇāyakatvādityarthaḥ /
na cotsargasiddhāyāḥ smṛterasati bādhake 'nyathāmāvo yujyata ityāśayavānāha--autsargikasyeti /
nanu,
children.translated_text: are exhausted only through experience, because they are actions whose expiatory rites have not been performed — like <s>karmas</s> that have already begun to produce the [current] body. Nor is there here a contradiction with scripture, since that [opposing scripture], being contradicted by other scriptures, is inconclusive — this is the meaning. And it is not proper to interpret otherwise a <s>smṛti</s> that is established by the general rule, when no sublating cognition exists — with this intention he says: 'Of the general rule...' Now,

children.text: midyate hṛdayagranthiśchidyante sarvasaṃśayāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The knot of the heart is pierced, all doubts are cut asunder,

children.text: kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare //
children.translated_text: and his <s>karmas</s> are destroyed — when that supreme and immanent one is seen.'

children.text: muṇḍaka. 2.2.8
children.translated_text: <s>Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad</s> 2.2.8

children.text:
iti śrutau paripanthinyāṃ kathamucyate 'sati bādhaka iti, kathaṃ ca tadvirodhena smṛternirṇāyakatvamanumānānugraho 'pītyata āha--kṣīyanta iti /
na hīyaṃ śrutiradattaphalānāmeva karmaṇāṃ tattvajñānāt kṣayamāha, kiṃ tu kṣayamātram /
taccopabhogenāpi bhavannakiñcid virūṇaddhīti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: — when the <s>śruti</s> stands as an opponent, how can one say 'when no sublating cognition exists'? And how can the <s>smṛti</s>, through its opposition to that, be conclusive, and how can there be support from inference? To this he says: 'Are destroyed...' For this <s>śruti</s> does not state that only <s>karmas</s> that have not yielded their results are destroyed by the knowledge of truth — rather, it states mere destruction. And that can occur through experience too without creating any conflict — this is the purport.

children.text:
deheṣūpabhogo dehopabhogaḥ /
api ca viparītāpi śrutirvidyata ityāha--tāvadeveti /
asya tattvasākṣātkāravataḥ tāvadeva ciraṃ vilambaḥ /
yāvanna vimokṣa upāttakarmarāśeḥ sakāśāt phalopayogena /
atha tasmin sati saṃpatsyate kaivalyenetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Experience in bodies' means experience through the body. Moreover, there is also an opposing <s>śruti</s> — he says: 'Just so long...' For this one who possesses direct realization of truth, the delay is just so long — until liberation from the accumulated mass of <s>karma</s> through the utilization of results. And when that is accomplished, he will attain <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute liberation) — this is the meaning.

children.text: bhogena tvitare kṣapayitvā
children.translated_text: 'But having exhausted the others through experience'

children.text: []iti vākyaśeṣāt //
children.translated_text: — this is the remainder of the sentence.

children.text:
nanu bhogena prakṣayo 'nupapanna eva, karmarāśeranantatayā aniyatavipākakālatayā cetyata āha--yogarddhīti /
uktam ādivākye /
śaṅkate--na ceti /
ayamāśayaḥ--yadi tāvat karmaṇāmevāyaṃ mahimā, yadekadaiva nānāvidhadehādyavāntaravyāpāraistaistairūpabhogaḥ sādhyaḥ, kiṃ yogaprabhāvaparikalpanayā? atha naiṣa mahimā neṣām, tathāpi kva yogaprabhāvasyopayogaḥ? na hīśvaro 'pi karmaṇāṃ svabhāvaṃ viparyāsayitumarhati /
tasmāt svapratibhayā kalpanīyametat /
children.translated_text: Therefore, this must be imagined through one's own ingenuity.

children.text: evaṃ ced varamadattaphalānyeva yogaprabhāvāt kṣīyanta iti kalpyatāṃ lāghavāyeti /
children.translated_text: If so, it is better to imagine, for the sake of simplicity, that only those <s>karmas</s> that have not yielded their results are destroyed by yogic power.

children.text: pariharati--dṛṣṭānusāreṇeti /
children.translated_text: He replies: 'In accordance with what is observed...'

children.text: pramāṇānusāreṇa //
children.translated_text: In accordance with the means of valid knowledge.

Now, exhaustion through experience is untenable, since the mass of <s>karma</s> is infinite and the time of fruition is indeterminate — to this he says: 'By the supernatural powers of <s>yoga</s>...' It was stated in the initial statement. He raises an objection: 'And not...' The intention is this: if the <s>karmas</s> themselves have such greatness that in a single moment, through various intermediate operations such as multiple bodies and so forth, experience can be accomplished, what need is there for the supposition of yogic power? And if the <s>karmas</s> do not have such greatness, even then where is the use of yogic power? For not even the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) ought to reverse the nature of <s>karmas</s>.

children.text:
yathā hyupabhogādeva karmaṇāṃ kṣayaḥ, dehādiṣu satsveva copabhogaḥ, labdhavṛttibhireva karmabhirdehādisambhavaḥ, sahakārilābha eva teṣāṃ vṛttilābhaḥ, te ca sahakāriṇaḥ kvacitphalonneyāḥ yathā yugapadanekendriyopagrahe, kvacidāgamagamyā yathā vāsudevasaubhariprabhṛtīnāṃ kāyayaugapadya iti sarvatra pramāṇamasti, naivamanupabhuktakarmakṣaye /
yathā ca mahāpralaye sarvakarmaṇāmekadaiva vṛttinirodha āgamaprāmāṇyādāsthīyate, tathā yogarddhikāle 'pi sarveṣāṃ vṛttilābha āstheya āgamaprāmāṇyādeveti na kiñcit svapratibhāmātreṇa kalpitamityarthaḥ tādṛśaśca muniraparaniḥśreyasavānityarthaḥ /
kimato yadyevamityata āha--iti na vātaputrīyamiti /
children.translated_text: For just as the exhaustion of <s>karmas</s> is through experience alone, and experience occurs only when body and the rest exist, and the body and the rest come into being through <s>karmas</s> that have obtained their operation, and the obtainment of operation of those is just the obtainment of auxiliary conditions — and those auxiliary conditions are in some cases inferable from the result, as when multiple sense-organs are employed simultaneously, and in other cases knowable through scripture, as in the case of the simultaneous bodies of <s>Vāsudeva</s>, <s>Saubhari</s>, and others — there is authority everywhere, but not so for the destruction of unexperienced <s>karma</s>. And just as at the time of the great dissolution (<s>mahāpralaya</s>), the cessation of operation of all <s>karmas</s> at once is accepted on the authority of scripture, so too at the time of yogic supernatural power, the obtainment of operation of all <s>karmas</s> should be accepted on the authority of scripture alone — thus nothing has been imagined by mere ingenuity — this is the meaning. And such a sage possesses the other [type of] highest good — this is the meaning. What follows from this? To this he says: 'Thus it is not like the Vātaputrīya...'

children.text:
atha paraṃ niḥśreyasaṃ kīdṛśamityata āha--paraṃ tviti /
ityupapannaṃ niḥśreyasadvaividhyamiti /
pūrvapakṣanirākaraṇāyeti śeṣaḥ /
na sukhaduḥkhatayā manute rāgadveṣaprasavahetutvābhāvādityarthaḥ /
na hyasti sambhavo na tatra tṛṣyati tacca tasya sukhu yādṛśamajñāninaḥ tṛṣṇājanakam, na tad dveṣṭi tacca tasya duḥkhamiti yādṛśamajñānino dveṣajanakamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: For there is no possibility that one who does not crave that — and whatever generates craving in the ignorant, that is pleasure for him — and one who does not hate that — and whatever generates hatred in the ignorant, that is pain — this is the meaning.

children.text: uktaṃ tātparyamakṣarārthīkartuṃ samarthitameva śaṅkate--syādetaditi /
children.translated_text: Having articulated the stated purport, he raises the very objection that has been justified in terms of the literal meaning: 'This may be so...'

children.text: upabhogaprayatna āstheyo mokṣāya tvaramāṇenāpi kāyavyūhādāviti śeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: The effort of experience should be undertaken even by one who hastens toward liberation, through the multiplication of bodies and so forth — this is the remainder.

children.text: yastu ta tvarate yadā bhavitā karmakṣayastadā bhavitā mokṣo 'pi kiṃ tvarayā? prāptā tāvannirapāyā bhūmiriti samarthitahṛdayaḥ, tasya tu niḥśreyasadvayayaugapadyaśaḍkāpi nāstīti bhāvaḥ //
children.translated_text: But one who says 'Why the haste? When the exhaustion of <s>karma</s> comes about, liberation too will come about — and in the meantime a state free from danger has been attained' — with this established intention, for such a person there is not even the suspicion of the simultaneity of the two [types of] highest good — this is the purport.

Now, what is the nature of the ultimate highest good? To this he says: 'But the ultimate...' 'Thus the twofold nature of the highest good is established' — the remainder is: for the purpose of refuting the prior objection. It is not cognized as pleasure or pain, because there is no cause for the generation of attachment and aversion — this is the meaning.

children.text:
nanvetāvataiva sarvaṃ susthaṃ kimuttaraprabandhenetyata āha--tadevamarthagatimiti /
mithyājñānadoṣapravṛttīnāṃ pravāharūpāṇāmiti boddhavyam /
pravṛttiścātra kāraṇarūpā grāhyā, kāryarūpāyā anucchedāt /
janmaduḥkhayoḥ pravāharūpayorūcchedakramo nāsti /
children.translated_text: There is no sequential process of eliminating birth and suffering in their stream-like form.

children.text: kutaḥ? pūrvopāttasyeti /
children.translated_text: Why? 'Because of what was previously acquired' —

children.text: mūlānucchedādityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: the meaning is: because of the non-elimination of the root.

children.text: āgāmivārttikavirodhaṃ pariharannāha--idaṃ ceti //
children.translated_text: Resolving the contradiction with the forthcoming <s>Vārttika</s>, he says: 'idaṃ ca' (and this).

Now, everything is fine with just this much — what is the need for the subsequent treatise? — therefore he says: 'tadevam arthagatim' (thus the course of meaning). It should be understood that false knowledge, defects, and activity are [spoken of] in their stream-like form. And 'activity' here is to be taken in its causal form, since in its effect-form it cannot be eliminated.

children.text:
yadyapi duḥkhādīnāmekārthasamavāyalakṣaṇo 'pi yogaḥ saṃbhavati tathāpi śarīrāderjanmanaḥ sa nāsti /
kāryakāraṇabhāvastu tasyāpi sa eva grāhya ityāha--yogyatayeti /
kāraṇasya hi pūrvavartitvaṃ yujyata ityata āha--atra
children.translated_text: Although the connection of suffering and the like can also be in the form of inherence in the same substratum (<s>ekārthasamavāya</s>), nevertheless, for birth in the form of body and the like, that [connection] does not exist. But the cause-effect relation must be taken as that [connection] even for it — he says: 'yogyatayā' (by fitness). For it is appropriate that the cause precedes [the effect] — therefore he says: 'atra

children.text:
ceti /
uttarasyānantaraṃ ca pūrvameva syāt, na ca pūrvaṃ kāryamityata āha--tadanantaratvaṃ ceti /
avyavahitamavyavadhānaṃ
children.translated_text: ca' (and here). And the immediately subsequent would simply be prior [to the next], and the prior is not the effect — therefore he says: 'tadanantaratvaṃ ca' (and that immediacy). 'Avyavahita' means 'without interruption' (<s>avyavadhāna</s>) —

children.text:
tenādau pāṭho 'vyavahitādipāṭhaḥ /
mithyājñāne kāraṇe tatkāryā doṣāḥ avyavadhānenaiva ādau paṭhitā iti śeṣaḥ /
yathaitat tathānyatrāpītyata āha--evamiti /
tenāyamarthaḥ /
duḥkhādīnāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ /
teṣāmevottarottarāpāye
children.translated_text: by that, the reading at the beginning is 'avyavahitādi-reading.' The meaning is: the defects, being effects of false knowledge which is the cause, have been listed first without interruption — this is the completion. 'Just as this is so, so too elsewhere' — therefore he says: 'evam' (thus). By this, the meaning is: the cause-effect relation among suffering and the like; and through the successive removal of those very [factors],

children.text:
tadanantarābhāvādapavargaṃ iti /
dūṣayati--na hīti /
apavarga ekor'thaṃḥ /
uttarottarāpāye tadanantarābhāvāditi ca padadvayam /
children.translated_text: 'Through the successive removal, from the absence of what is immediately [prior]' — these are two phrases.

children.text: keṣāmiti duḥkhādīnāmiti ca padaṃ kiṃ bhavatīti sākāḍkṣam /
children.translated_text: 'Of which' [referring to] suffering and the like — this phrase requires completion [by asking] 'what does it become?'

children.text: tasmādekavākyatvalakṣaṇayogādekamevedaṃ vākyamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, by possessing the defining characteristic of sentence-unity, this is indeed a single sentence — this is the meaning.

children.text: yadapi vākyabhedena prayojanādhikyamabhihitam, tadapi nāstītyāha--ekanivṛttyeti //
children.translated_text: The additional purposes claimed by dividing the sentence are also non-existent — he says: 'ekanivṛttyā' (by a single cessation).
from the absence of what is immediately [prior], liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) [is attained]. He criticizes: 'na hī' (for not). '<s>Apavarga</s>' is one meaning.

children.text:
viśvatomukhatve 'pyasaṃdigdhatvaṃ prakaraṇānuvṛttyādibhirityavirodhaḥ /
sāravat prayojanavat /
anavadyaṃ śiṣṭānāmaduḥkhapratītikaram /
prakṛtatvenāstobhamiti vyācaṣṭe--astobhamiti /
yathāvyākhyāte vipratipadyamānaṃ lakṣaṇāntareṇa bodhayati--tathā hyāhuriti /
lāghavaṃ vākyeṣu padakṛtam, padeṣu svalpatvamakṣarakṛtamityapaunarūktyam /
etacca kāryakāraṇabhāvasya yogavibhāgenābhidhīyamānatvamabhyupagamyoktam /
vastutastu tenāpyasau sūcanīya eva /
na hi yogavibhāgasya etatsāmarthyam /
api tvarthādhikyasūcanamātram /
etacca vibhāge 'pi labhyata ityāha--itaretaretyādi /
nanu sūtre mithyājñānamātrameva śrūyate, tat kathamāha tatrātmādāvityata āha--yadyani sāmeti /
bhāṣyaviṣayatāṃ vārttikasya darśayati--tadeteneti /
na khalu yathā kuṇḍe badaraṃ saṃyogena paṭe vā śauklyaṃ samavāyenetyarthaḥ /
nanu na tāvat sattāmātreṇa sārūpyaṃ bhrāntāvupayujyate japākusumādisannidhānaparibhūtasitimni sphaṭhikādāvanupalabhyamānaviśeṣasmaraṇe 'pi rajatādiviparyāsābhāvāt /
tasmādupalabhyamānameva sārūpyaṃ taddheturityāstheyam /
tadapyasaṃgatam, sārūpyasya bhedādhiṣṭhānatayā tatpratibhāsane bhedasyāpi pratibhānābhedāropānavakāśāt /
children.translated_text: that too is unjustified, since resemblance, being grounded in difference, when it appears, should also make difference appear — leaving no room for the superimposition of non-difference.

children.text: tasmāt sadasatoḥ sārūpyābhāvādityāśaḍkaiveyamanupapannetyata āha--sarvatra hīti /
children.translated_text: Therefore, the doubt that 'there is no resemblance between the existent and the non-existent' is itself untenable — therefore he says: 'sarvatra hī' (for everywhere).

children.text: na hīdamane, sadṛśamiti kṛtvā sārūpyagrahaṇamiti brūmaḥ /
children.translated_text: For we do not say that the apprehension of resemblance [occurs because one thinks] 'this is the same, this is similar.'

children.text: kiṃ tarhi? rajatādau yo dharmaścakacikyādiḥ upalabdhapūrvaḥ sa eva tajjātīyo vā purovartinyupalabhyate yadi tadā bhrānti, nāto 'nyathetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: What then? When a property such as luster and the like that was previously perceived in silver and the like — that very [property] or one of its class — is perceived in what is in front, then there is error; not otherwise — this is the meaning.

Even though [the sentence] is multifaceted, the absence of ambiguity [is explained] by the continuity of the context and the like — thus there is no contradiction. '<s>Sāravat</s>' means 'having purpose.' '<s>Anavadya</s>' means 'not producing discomfort for the learned.' He explains as 'unstrained' (<s>astobha</s>) due to being the present context: 'astobham iti.' When there is disagreement about the explanation given, he instructs through another definition: 'tathā hyāhur' (for thus they say). Brevity (<s>lāghava</s>) in sentences is produced by words; in words, conciseness is produced by syllables — thus there is no redundancy. And this is stated on the assumption that the cause-effect relation is expressed through the analysis of the connection (<s>yogavibhāga</s>). But in reality, even by that [method], it should merely be indicated. For the analysis of connection does not have that capacity. Rather, it merely indicates additional meaning. And this [additional meaning] is also obtainable even with the division — he says: 'itaretara' (mutual), etc. Now, in the <s>sūtra</s> only false knowledge is heard — then how does he say 'therein, beginning with the self (<s>ātman</s>)'? — therefore he says: 'yadyapi sāma' (although common). He shows the <s>Bhāṣya</s> to be the domain of the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'tadetena' (by this). The meaning is: not like a jujube fruit in a pot, related by conjunction, or whiteness in cloth, related by inherence. Now, mere co-existence (<s>sattāmātra</s>) is not useful for resemblance (<s>sārūpya</s>) in error — since even when the proximity of <s>japākusuma</s> (hibiscus flower) and the like prevails over [the whiteness of] a crystal, and even when the distinctive [features] are not remembered, there is no error such as seeing silver [in crystal]. Therefore, only perceived resemblance should be held to be the cause of that [error] —

children.text:
anvayaṃ darśayitvā vyatirekamāha--na hīti /
yadyapi hastimaśakādāvapi yathā kathañcit sārūpyamastyeva, tathāpi vyavacdedakadharmeṇānabhibhūtaṃ sārūpyamihābhipratam /
vyavacchedakānabhibhūtatvaṃ ca tatra nāstītyataḥ sarvātmanā vā sārūpyamekadeśena vetyevamādi parāstaṃ veditavyam /
śaṅkate--asadṛśe 'pīti /
idamatra vivakṣitam, sārūpyaṃ hyāropyasyāropaviṣayeṇa cintyate, anyathā vā? anantare 'tiprasaṃgaḥ /
prathame tu na tāvata pītaguṇī śuklaguṇini śaḍkhe āropyate, pītaṃ ciravilvamidamiti pratyayānudayāt /
nāpi śuklaguṇe pītaguṇaḥ, śuklaguṇasyāpratibhāsanāt /
nāpi śuklatvasāmānyādhāre rūpasvalakṣaṇe pītaguṇaḥ, cākṣuṣapratītau śuklatvasāmānyānavabhāse tadādhārasya rūpasvalakṣaṇasya bhāsanāyogāt /
bhāsane 'pi vā dravyatvasāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na syāt /
nāpi pītatvaṃ sāmānyaṃ śuklatvasāmānyādhāre /
taddhi tadātmatayā vā āropyet, tatsaṃsargitayā vā? ādye śuklatvasāmānyādhārā vyaktiḥ pītatvasāmānyātmanā prathamānā na deśakālaniyatā syāt /
vyaktirhi deśakālaniyatā na sāmānyam /
sā cāprathitaiva /
na ca pītatvasāmānyameva śuklaguṇavyaktirūpeṇaropyata iti sāmpratam /
tathā sati pītatvaṃ na pratīyeta /
nāpi śuklatvasāmānyameva pītatvasāmānyatadātmatayā āropyeta, tathā sati śuklatvena śuklatvaṃ pratīyeta /
na hi tasyānyat kiñcid rūpamasti, yena pratītipathamavataret /
sarvathā apratītaṃ ca nāropaviṣaya ityasaṃgatirevāsya kalpasya, saṃsargitayā tu sāmānye āropyamāṇe śuklaguṇasya śuklatvenaiva pratītiḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: And what is in no way perceived is not a locus of superimposition — thus this hypothesis is altogether incoherent. But if [the universal 'yellowness'] were superimposed on the universal [whiteness] as connected with it, then the white property would be perceived merely as white,

children.text: na ca pītimapratītervinayatāratamyaṃ syāt, sāmānyasyaikarūpatvāt /
children.translated_text: and there would be no gradation of the non-perception of yellowness, since the universal is of one form.

children.text: tasmāt pītaguṇa śaṅkhe samāropyata iti vācyam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, it must be said that the yellow property is superimposed on the conch-shell.

children.text: tathā ca guṇaguṇinoḥ kva sādṛśyavārtāpītyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And thus — where is even the question of resemblance between the property and the property-bearer? — this is the meaning.

Having shown the positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>), he states the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>): 'na hī' (for not). Although in an elephant, a mosquito, and the like, resemblance of some kind does exist, nevertheless what is intended here is resemblance not overridden by a distinguishing property. And since the non-overriding by a distinguishing property does not exist there — therefore, [the objections] 'whether resemblance is total or partial' and the like should be understood as refuted. He raises a doubt: 'asadṛśe 'pi' (even in what is dissimilar). What is intended here is: is the resemblance of the superimposed [object] considered with the locus of superimposition, or otherwise? In the latter case, there is over-extension. But in the former: first, a yellow property is not superimposed on a white-propertied conch-shell, because the cognition 'this is a yellow citron tree' does not arise. Nor is a yellow property [superimposed] on a white property, because the white property does not appear [as such]. Nor is a yellow property [superimposed] on the particular form (<s>rūpa-svalakṣaṇa</s>) that is the substratum of the universal 'whiteness,' because in visual perception, since the universal 'whiteness' does not appear, the particular form that is its substratum also cannot appear. Or even if it does appear, it would not be co-extensive with the universal 'substancehood.' Nor is the universal 'yellowness' [superimposed] on the substratum of the universal 'whiteness.' For would it be superimposed as being identical with it, or as being connected with it? In the first case, the particular that is the substratum of the universal 'whiteness,' being perceived as having the nature of the universal 'yellowness,' would not be delimited by place and time. For a particular is delimited by place and time, not a universal. And that [particular] is simply not perceived [as such]. Nor is it correct that the universal 'yellowness' itself is superimposed in the form of a white-propertied particular. If so, yellowness would not be perceived. Nor would the universal 'whiteness' itself be superimposed as having the nature of the universal 'yellowness' — for in that case, whiteness would be perceived as whiteness. For there is no other form of it by which it could enter the path of cognition.

children.text:
samādhatte--na tatrāpīti, na hyatra pītaguṇa āropyo 'pi tu pītaguṇaśca śaḍkhaśca āropaviṣayau, saṃsṛṣṭasvabhāvatvaṃ tvāropyam /
tathā ca saṃsṛṣṭasvabhāvābhyāṃ guṇaguṇibhyāmanayoḥ asaṃsṛṣṭasvabhāvayoḥ sārūpyamiha prayojakam /
upadarśitaṃ ca taditi kimaprayojakena guṇisārūpyeṇa guṇasārūpyeṇa vā, satā asatā vetyarthaḥ /
asaṃbandhāgraho vaiyadhikaraṇyāgraho viṣayiṇa viṣayamupalakṣayati /
tena vyādhikaraṇagrahaṇāviṣayīkṛtatvaṃ sārūpyaṃ tayoḥ, yathā pītimācirabilvayoḥ tathaiva pītimaśaḍkhayorityuktaṃ bhavati /
ekendriyopanatasaṃbandhidvayaviṣayaṃ sārūpyamupapādyandriyadvayopanītasaṃbandhidvayaviṣayaṃ sārūpyamupapādayati--evaṃ tvagindriyeti /
na caivaṃ sati
children.translated_text: He resolves: 'na tatrāpi' (not even there). For here the yellow property is not the [sole] thing superimposed; rather, both the yellow property and the conch-shell are the loci of superimposition, while what is superimposed is the state of being of a conjoined nature. And thus, the resemblance of these two — which are of an unconjoined nature — with the property and property-bearer of a conjoined nature is what is the motivating factor here. And that [resemblance] has been shown — so what is the point of a non-motivating resemblance of the property-bearer [alone] or of the property [alone], whether existent or non-existent? — this is the meaning. 'Non-apprehension of the non-connection' or 'non-apprehension of having a different locus' — the subject (<s>viṣayin</s>) indicates the object (<s>viṣaya</s>). By this, the resemblance of those two consists in not having been made the object of the apprehension of having a different locus — just as [there is resemblance] between a yellowness-possessing citron tree [and the conch-shell], so too between a yellowness-possessing conch-shell [and the citron tree] — thus it is stated. Having established the resemblance pertaining to two related objects presented to a single sense-faculty, he establishes the resemblance pertaining to two related objects presented to two sense-faculties: 'evaṃ tvagindriya' (thus the tactile sense-faculty). And in this case,

children.text: tādātmyabhrame 'pi bhedāgraha eva sārūpyamastu, kṛtaṃ cākacikyādineti vācyam, tadantareṇa saṃskārānudbodhāt, tena ca
children.translated_text: one should not say: 'Even in the error of identity, let the non-apprehension of difference itself be the resemblance, and the luster and the like are dispensed with' — because without that [luster], the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) would not be awakened, and without that [awakening],

children.text:
vinā rajatāropaniyamānupapatteḥ /
iha tu saṃsṛṣṭatvānubhavajanitasaṃskārodbodho yāvanmātreṇa tāvadevopayuktam, saṃsargasya ca saṃsṛjyamānāveva viṣayaḥ /
tau cānubhūyamānāveveti, kiṃ tadupanāyakasādṛśyāntarāpekṣayeti sarvamavadātam /
children.translated_text: the restriction [of the superimposition] to silver would be unexplained. But here, the awakening of the <s>saṃskāra</s> produced by the experience of the conjoined state — to whatever extent that [awakening occurs], to that extent alone it is useful; and the connection has as its object precisely the two things being connected; and those two are precisely what are being experienced — so what need is there for any further resemblance to bring that about? — thus everything is clear.

children.text: nanvayamanubhavakramo 'nubhavabādhita evetyata āha--atiśīghratayeti //
children.translated_text: Now, this experiential sequence is itself contradicted by experience — therefore he says: 'atiśīghratayā' (due to extreme rapidity).

children.text:
nanu sādṛśyaṃ ced bhrāntibījamupapāditam, tarhi sarvaṃ sarvatrāropyet, asti hi kenacit kasyacit kathañcit sārūpyamityata āha--neti /
evaṃ dvicandreti /
tathāvidhāpekṣābuddhiviṣayatvaṃ dvicandrabhrame, bhedamātrārope tu nānādigdeśāvayavasaṃbandhaḥ /
prācyāṃ pratīcībhrame dakṣiṇottarānyatve sati diktvameva /
evamanyatrāpi alātacakrabhrame madhyāsaṃbandhe sati sarvadiksaṃbandhaḥ /
ādigrahaṇādagacchati gativibhrame vibhāgavaiparītyam /
asthūleṣu keśeṣu sthūlavibhrame
children.translated_text: Now, if resemblance has been established as the seed of error, then everything would be superimposed on everything — for there is some resemblance of something with something in some way — therefore he says: 'na' (no). 'Likewise the double-moon' — in the double-moon illusion, it is the being-the-object-of-such-a-required-cognition [that is the factor]; but in the mere superimposition of difference [between the two perceived moons], it is the connection with parts in different directions. In the error of east [appearing as] west, when there is the otherness of north and south, it is the mere directionality itself. Similarly elsewhere too — in the illusion of a firebrand circle, when there is non-connection with the middle, there is connection with all directions. By the word 'ādi' (etc.) — [he indicates:] in the illusion of motion, the reversal of separation [comes into play]. In the illusion of thin hairs appearing thick,

children.text:
tāvaddeśācchādakatvam /
apsu daṇḍasya vakratābhrame taraṅgavakrimadaṇḍayorasaṃsargagraha ityevaṃ neyam /
sarvatra ca tattvāgrahaḥ
children.translated_text: it is the covering of that much space. In the illusion of a stick in water appearing bent, it is the non-apprehension of the non-connection between the waves and the bent-stick [that is relevant] — it should be extended thus. And in all cases, the non-apprehension of reality

children.text: saṃplavata iti //
children.translated_text: floods in [as the common factor].

children.text:
ihātmano duḥkhahetutvena śarīrendriyādivad heyatvameva bauddhairāpāditam /
yathā hi, indriyādinā vinā nātmā duḥkhaṃ janayitumalam, evaṃ nendriyādikamapi tamantareṇa /
na hi nirāśrayaṃ duḥkha nāma /
ata ātmāpi heyaḥ /
taduktam dharmakīrtinā---
children.translated_text: Here, the Buddhists have established that the <s>ātman</s> (self) too is to be avoided (<s>heya</s>) as a cause of suffering, just like the body, sense-organs, and the like. For just as, without the sense-organs and the like, the <s>ātman</s> alone is not sufficient to produce suffering, so too the sense-organs and the like are not [sufficient] without it. For there is no suffering without a substratum. Therefore, the <s>ātman</s> too is to be avoided. Thus said <s>Dharmakīrti</s>:

children.text: na tairvinā duḥkhaheturātmā cet te 'pi tādṛśāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'If the <s>ātman</s> is not a cause of suffering without those [sense-organs etc.], then those too are of the same kind [without the ātman];

children.text: nirdeṣaṃ dvayamapyevaṃ vairāgyaṃ ca dvayostataḥ //
children.translated_text: both alike are to be pointed out [as causes], and dispassion toward both [follows] from that.' —

children.text: pra.vā.1.227
children.translated_text: <s>Pramāṇavārttika</s> 1.227

children.text: iti taccaitadasādhīyaḥ tathā hi, na tāvadātmano hānaṃ rogādivadvināśalakṣaṇam, nityatvāt /
children.translated_text: . And this is exceedingly easy [to refute]. For, first, the abandonment (<s>hāna</s>) of the <s>ātman</s> is not characterized by destruction, like [the removal of] a disease, because of its permanence.

children.text: nāpi dandaśūkadaṣṭāḍgulīvad viprayogādilakṣaṇam, nāpi sutamaraṇādivat pratipattinirodhalakṣaṇam, svasaṃvedanatvāditi vedāntinaḥ //
children.translated_text: Nor is it characterized by dissociation, like [cutting off] a finger bitten by a snake; nor is it characterized by the cessation of cognition, like [the grief at] the death of a son — because it is self-aware — thus say the <s>Vedāntins</s>.

children.text:
vayaṃ tu brūmaḥ---taddhi tadā syāt, yadi jñātasya sato duḥkhaṃ pratyātmano hetutvaṃ sutamaraṇāderiva /
na tvetadasti /
kiṃ nāma? sattāmātreṇa /
tasmādātmano heyatvavyutpādanaṃ vaiyātyamātravijṛmbhitametat /
ātmadṛṣṭestu heyatvavyutpādanaṃ manāk sadalamityāśaḍkya nirākaroti--na tviti /
abhyarhitatamam upakāryatamam /
sattvam ātma /
yadyapi rāgādinivṛttiheturnairātmadarśanamiti guḍajihvikā, vastutastu na tāvannityātmābhāvadarśanamātraṃ rāgādinivṛttihetuḥ, cārvākādīnāmeva vītarāgatvaprasaṃgāt /
ahaṅkāranivṛttiheturnairātmyadarśanam, tata eva rāgādinivṛttiriti cet? sāpi kiṃ śarīrādau, cetane vā? ādye siddhasādhanam, śarīrādavahaṅkārasya mithyātvāt /
tanmūlatvācca rāgadveṣayoḥ, tannivṛttau tayorapi nivṛttiriti ko nāma nābhyupaiti /
children.translated_text: And since attachment and aversion are rooted in that [false ego-sense], upon the cessation of that, the cessation of those two also [follows] — who would not accept this?

children.text: na ca śarīrādāvahaṅkāranivṛtternityātmadarśanaṃ virodhi, kiṃ tvanukūlameva, na hi śuktikāto rajataṃ bhedenāvyavasthāpayatastasya rajatabuddhiḥnivartate /
children.translated_text: And the perception of the permanent <s>ātman</s> does not contradict the cessation of the ego-sense with respect to the body and the like; rather, it is positively conducive. For the cognition of silver [superimposed on] nacre does not cease for one who does not discriminate the silver from the nacre as different.

children.text: atha cetanaviṣayaivāhaṅkāranivṛttī rāgādīnapanayatīti vivakṣitam? hantaivaṃ svākāre 'pīdantāvyavahāriṇāṃ pṛthagjanānāṃ vītarāgatvaprasaṃgaḥ /
children.translated_text: But if what is intended is that the cessation of the ego-sense with respect to the conscious being alone removes attachment and the like? Well then, there would follow the absurd consequence that ordinary persons — who use the expression 'I' (<s>idantā</s>) even with respect to their own bodies — would be free from attachment.

children.text: na hi te śarīrādiviviktam ahamiti pratiyanti //
children.translated_text: For they do not cognize 'I' as distinct from the body and the like.

But we say: that [argument of Dharmakīrti] would hold if the <s>ātman</s>, when known and existing, were a cause of suffering by itself — like the death of a son and the like. But this is not the case. What then? [It is a cause] merely by its existence. Therefore, the instruction that the <s>ātman</s> is to be avoided is merely a display of wantonness. Suspecting that the instruction of the avoidability of the view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>) is somewhat more plausible, he refutes: 'na tu' (but not). '<s>Abhyarhitatama</s>' means 'most deserving of respect.' '<s>Sattva</s>' means the <s>ātman</s>. Although it is a sweet morsel [for Buddhists] that the view of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) is the cause of the cessation of attachment and the like, in reality, first of all, the mere perception of the non-existence of a permanent self is not the cause of the cessation of attachment and the like — since there would follow the absurd consequence that <s>Cārvākas</s> and the like would already be free from attachment. If it is said that the perception of non-self is the cause of the cessation of the ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>), and from that the cessation of attachment and the like [follows]? Is that [ego-sense] with respect to the body and the like, or with respect to the conscious being? In the first case, what is to be proved is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>), since the ego-sense with respect to the body and the like is [already accepted as] false.

children.text:
atha bāhyābhyantaraviṣayatayāhaṅkāranivṛttirabhipretā? sāpi kiṃ sarvathā jñānābhāvādeva, cetanasyāpīdantāspadatvādeva vā, tasminneva nāstitvādhyāropād vā? na tāvadādyaḥ, adṛṣṭitvaprasaṅgāt /
na caitat prayatnaśatenāpi sidhyati /
yathā yathā dṛṣṭinirodhāya prayatnaḥ, tathā tathā dṛṣṭeḥ pratyāpatteḥ /
na cādṛṣṭereva rāgādayo vinivartante, yugasahāstramapi suptasya punarjāgarāvasthāyāṃ rāgādidarśanāt, nāpi dvitīyaḥ, ahamabhāve satīdamo 'pyabhāvāt, ātmāni sati parasaṃjñeti tvayaivoktaṃ yataḥ /
nāpi tṛtīyaḥ, grahaṇāgrahaṇayorūbhayorapi asaṃbhavāt /
yadi hyahamāspadaṃ cetano gṛhītaḥ, kathaṃ nāstitādhyāropaḥ? na gṛhītaścet kutra nāstitādhyāropaḥ? na ca prathamaṃ grahaḥ
children.translated_text: Now, is the cessation of the ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>) intended with respect to both external and internal objects? And is that [cessation] due to the complete absence of cognition, or due to the fact that even the conscious being is merely a locus of 'this' [rather than 'I'], or due to the superimposition of non-existence upon that very [self]? Not the first, since it would entail the absurd consequence of non-perception. And this cannot be accomplished even with a hundred efforts. For the more one strives to suppress perception, the more perception rebounds. And it is not the case that passions (<s>rāga</s>) and the like cease merely from non-perception, since even one who has slept for a thousand ages is seen to have passions and the like in the waking state. Nor the second, because in the absence of 'I,' 'this' too would be absent — for you yourself have stated that 'when the self exists, there is the cognition of other [things].' Nor the third, because neither of the two [options] — apprehension and non-apprehension — is possible. For if the conscious being as the locus of 'I' has been apprehended, how can non-existence be superimposed? And if it has not been apprehended, upon what is non-existence superimposed? Nor can you say that first there is apprehension

children.text:
paścādāropa iti tvayā vaktuṃ śakyate /
na cāparispharati niṣedhye niṣedhasaṃbhavaḥ /
svapratipaṣṭhajñānamātreṇeti cet--na, jñānasya svapratiṣṭhatādhrauvye 'pi rāgādidarśanāt /
tattabdahirūpaplavavirahe satīti cet? tarhi bahirūpaplavavirahe svātmapratiṣṭhaṃ jñānaṃ rāgādinivṛttiheturityevaṃbhūtayātdṛṣṭyā kimaparāddham, yena tāṃ nirasya nairātmyadṛṣṭirūpādīyate? audāsīnyadṛṣṭireva nairātmyadṛṣṭiriti cet? kimidamaudāsīnyam? śūnyatvamiti cet? evaṃ tarhi svātmadṛṣṭirapi dṛṣṭirna syādityadṛṣṭitvaprasaṃgaḥ /
anālambanatayā niḥsaṃbandhitvamaudāsīnyamiti cet? tarhi nirātmīyatādṛṣṭiṃ vadan kuto nairātmyadṛṣṭiṃ supta iva pralapasīti /
evaṃ pretyabhāvābhāvajñānasyeti paramaṃ nidānamiti anuṣajyate /
tathā ca
children.translated_text: and then superimposition. And there is no possibility of negation without the negated [object] being present [in cognition]. If [one says] 'merely through a self-established cognition' — no, because passions and the like are observed even when cognition is permanently self-established. If [one says] 'when the external fluctuations are absent' — then, when external fluctuations are absent, cognition established in its own self is the cause of the cessation of passions and the like — what fault has this kind of view [committed], that one should reject it and adopt the view of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>)? If [one says] 'the view of indifference is itself the view of non-self' — then what is this indifference? If [one says] 'emptiness (<s>śūnyatva</s>)' — then even the perception of one's own self would not be a perception, leading to the absurd consequence of non-perception. If [one says] 'indifference is the absence of relation, due to having no object (<s>anālambana</s>)' — then, speaking of the view that [the self is] without possessions, from where do you babble about the view of non-self, like one talking in sleep? Thus, 'the knowledge of the non-existence of afterlife existence' is connected as 'the supreme source.' And thus

children.text:
ityapi guḍajihvikā /
vastutastu nāsti karma, nāsti karmaphalam, nāsti pretyabhāva iti /
children.translated_text: this too is a sugar-coated [poison]. In reality, [for such a person] there is no <s>karma</s> (action), there is no fruit of <s>karma</s>, there is no afterlife existence.

children.text: yāvajjīvet sukhaṃ jīvennāsti mṛtyoragocaraḥ
children.translated_text: 'As long as one lives, let one live pleasantly; there is nothing beyond death' —

children.text:
iti nyāyamālambamānena prāṇivadhādattādānādāveva ghaṭitavyam /
sādhīyaścaivamasya kaivalyamiti /
na ca
children.translated_text: following this principle, one must engage in the killing of living beings, theft, and the like. And thus, <s>kaivalya</s> (liberation) becomes more readily [available] for such a person. Nor should

children.text: santānamādāya pretyabhāvādidṛṣṭirūpapatsyata iti vācyam, tadā hi tamādāya sopapadyeta, yadi taddṛṣṭiranarthānnivartayet
children.translated_text: one say that the view of afterlife existence and the like will be justified by adopting [the doctrine of] the continuum (<s>saṃtāna</s>). For that [continuum-based view] would be justified only if that view would turn [one] away from harm

children.text: arthācca pravartayet pravṛttinivṛttī ca saiva dṛṣṭiḥ karoti yā rāgadveṣau prasūte, tanmūlatvāt tayoḥ /
tathā ca tādṛśī saṃtānadṛṣṭirapi heyaiva /
children.translated_text: And thus, such a view based on the continuum is also to be abandoned.

children.text: na tādṛśī cennāstikatvameva nirvāhayet /
children.translated_text: If [the view] is not of such a nature, then it would simply sustain nihilism (<s>nāstikatva</s>).

children.text: tadidamuktam--so 'yaṃ vṛścikabhiyeti /
children.translated_text: This is what is said: 'This is [like one who flees from] the fear of a scorpion...'

children.text: tasmād yaḥ paralokārtho tasya paralokinamātmānamaḍgīkṛtyaiva svarge 'paparge vā prayatnaḥ, yastu nityamātmānaṃ nābhyupaiti tasya cārvākasya iva svargāpavargāveva na staḥ, kutastadarthā pravṛttirityāśayavānāha--seyamiti //
children.translated_text: Therefore, one who desires the fruits of the other world must, having accepted the self as an entity that transmigrates, make effort toward heaven (<s>svarga</s>) or liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). But one who does not accept a permanent self — for him, like the <s>Cārvāka</s> [materialist], neither heaven nor liberation exists at all. Whence, then, activity directed toward that end? — with this intention he says: 'This very...'

and impel [one] toward benefit. And the very view that produces attachment (<s>rāga</s>) and aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) is what causes engagement and disengagement, since both [engagement and disengagement] are rooted in that [attachment and aversion].

children.text: yattūktam--ātmānamabhyarhitaṃ paśyanniti so 'yaṃ kasya prasaṅgaḥ? kiṃ sarvaduḥkhopaśamamupakāramapaśyataḥ, paśyato
children.translated_text: Now, what was said — 'seeing oneself as worthy' — this [constitutes] a <s>prasaṅga</s> (reductio) against whom? Is it against one who does not see the complete cessation of all suffering as beneficial, or against one who does

children.text:
vā? ādyaścedevametat /
na hyevaṃbhūtasya nairātmyadṛṣṭirabhyupapadyate /
na hyātmocchedameva kaścidupakāratvena manute, api tu duḥkhaṃ jihāsamāna ātmānaṃ jahāti, ātmānamanapahāya duḥkhasya hātumaśakyatvāditi manyamānastasmād duḥkhamajihāsataḥ sukhaṃ copādātumicchato nairātmyadṛṣṭerasaṃbhava eva /
tathā ca tathābhūtasya nairātmyadarśino nityātmadarśino vā tulyaḥ saṃsāraḥ /
dvitīyastu kalpo 'saṃgata eva /
children.translated_text: The second alternative, however, is entirely inconsistent.

children.text: na hi sarvaduḥkhocchedam evopakāraṃ paśyati sukhāya tadupakārāya ca ghaṭata iti /
children.translated_text: For one who sees the complete cessation of all suffering as beneficial does not strive for happiness or for the means to it.

children.text: sarvaduḥkhocchedaśca sukhaṃ ceti vipratiṣiddhametat /
children.translated_text: And 'the complete cessation of all suffering' and 'happiness' — these two are mutually contradictory.

children.text: evaṃ sarvaduḥkhocchedamicchati paraṃ cāpakarotītyetadapyasaṃgatam, na hi parāpakāraḥ sarvaduḥkhocchedanidānamiti hṛdi nidhāyāha--abhyarhitatā ceti //
children.translated_text: Similarly, 'he desires the complete cessation of all suffering' and 'he harms others' — this too is inconsistent. For harming others is not the cause of the complete cessation of all suffering — keeping this in mind, he says: 'And the worthiness...'

see [it as beneficial]? If the first, then this is so [i.e., the reductio applies]. For the view of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>) is not tenable for one of such a nature. For no one considers the annihilation of the self itself as beneficial. Rather, one who desires to abandon suffering abandons the self [only] because, thinking 'suffering cannot be abandoned without abandoning the self,' he [then] abandons the self. Therefore, for one who does not desire to abandon suffering but wishes to acquire happiness, the view of non-self is simply impossible. And thus, for one who holds such a [non-self] view, and for one who holds the view of an eternal self, <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of transmigration) is the same.

children.text:
sāmānyadharmo 'haṅkārāspadatvam /
ahamiti kartṛpadaviṣayatvam, anena tatpravṛttinimittasya kartṛtvasyaikadeśamupalakṣayati /
tenāyamarthaḥ, itarakārakaprayoktṛtvam bāhyakārakaprayojyatāṃ ca dṛṣṭvā bhedāgrahe sati śarīrādau kartṛtvamāropyātmatvena viparyasyatīti tadidamuktam--tāṃ khalviti /
evaṃ siddhaṃ kṛtvā viparyayam anyathākhyātirūpamiti śeṣaḥ /
saṃprati sandihāno viśeṣata iti śeṣaḥ /
nanu sthāṇāvevāyaṃ mama corapratyayo vṛtta ityāgāpālāṅganaṃ prasiddhamiti tadatra saṃśaya eva nāstītyata āha--parīkṣakāṇāmiti /
pratipattuḥ pratyayāt pratyetavyāt /
avyatirekāt abhedādityarthaḥ /
nanvidaṃ rajatamityatra dvayaṃ pratibhāti, jñānasyātmā, purovarti dravyaṃ ca /
tatra purovartino rajatatve pratiṣiddhe, arthādāpadyate jñānasyeti, tadanyeṣāṃ tu pratipattyanārohādeva nāvakārśaḥ /
tat kathamucyate vaṇigvīthyādāviti, ata āha--āntaratvaṃ tvasyānupalabdhacaraṃ katastyam? yaddhi yasya kadācidavagatam, tadanyatra pratiṣedhe pāriśeṣyāt tatra gamyate, na tu pratītipathamavatīrṇayoranyataratra pratiṣedhe pāriśeṣyāditaratrāsaṃbhāvitamapi, tathā sati nedaṃ rajatamiti śuktikāyāṃ rajatatvapratiṣedhe tadekajñānasaṃsargiṇo bhūtakāderapi rajatatvaṃ vidadhyāt /
na caivam /
tat kasya hetoḥ? tasya rajatatvaṃ kadācidapi nopalabdhacaraṃ /
yataḥ, tathā
children.translated_text: The common property is being the locus of the ego-sense (<s>ahaṅkāra</s>). 'I' — being the referent of the agent-word (<s>kartṛpada</s>); by this he illustratively indicates a part of agency, which is the ground for the activity [denoted by the agent-word]. Therefore, the meaning is: having observed [on the one hand] the instigation of other <s>kārakas</s> and [on the other hand] the fact that the external <s>kārakas</s> are instigated, when the distinction [between the self and the body] is not grasped, one superimposes agency upon the body and the like, and erroneously [takes it] as the self — this is what is said: 'That indeed...' Having thus established [the error], the completion is: the error is of the nature of <s>anyathākhyāti</s> (apprehension as other than what [it is]). 'Now, the one who doubts, specifically' — this is the completion. Now, it is well-known that 'this very cognition of a thief arose in me regarding the post' [is said by] the guard's embrace — so there is no doubt here at all — therefore he says: 'For examiners...' 'From the cognition of the apprehender' — from that which is to be ascertained. 'Due to non-difference' — the meaning is: due to identity. Now, in 'this is silver,' two things appear: the self of the cognition, and the substance in front. Therein, when the silver-nature of what is in front is denied, it follows by implication that [silver-nature] belongs to the cognition — but for those others [i.e., the Naiyāyikas], since [internal silver-nature] does not even enter their understanding, there is no scope [for this]. So how can one say 'in the merchants' quarter' and so forth? — therefore he says: 'But the internality of this — when has it been apprehended and by whom?' For whatever has been known to belong to something at some time — when denied elsewhere, is understood to belong there by elimination. But when one of two [things that are] both within the domain of cognition is denied in one [of them], what has not even been suspected in the other [is not thereby established]. Otherwise, when 'this is not silver' denies silver-nature in the mother-of-pearl, it would [absurdly] establish silver-nature even in the elements and the like that are co-present in that single cognition. But this is not so. Why? Because the silver-nature of those [elements] has never been within the range of apprehension. Since, in the same way,

children.text:
svātmāno 'pi rajatātmatvaṃ na kasyacidupalabdhigocaraḥ kadācit svapne 'pi /
atha dṛṣṭameva satyarajatajñāne rajatākāratvamātmana ityāśayaḥ? so 'yaṃ svapnāyate, tatrāpi hi purovartini rajate anubhūyamāne svātmano rajatākāratvaṃ
children.translated_text: the silver-nature of one's own self is never within the range of anyone's apprehension, not even in dreams. If [one says] 'the intention is that the silver-form of oneself is indeed observed in the veridical cognition of silver' — this [objection] is itself dreaming. For even there, when silver that is in front is being experienced, the silver-form of one's own self —

children.text:
kasya pramāṇasya gocara iti /
tadanena svākārasya bāhyatve sādhakapramāṇābhāvo darśitaḥ /
bādhakamapi sūcitam /
yathā hi nedaṃ rajatamiti bādhakabalena purovartino rajatatvapratiṣedhaḥ, tathā nāhaṃ rajatamityapi bādhakaṃ sphuṭameva /
ayameva bhrama iti cet? evaṃ tarhi na rajatatvamāropyate bāhye, kiṃ tu tasminnevāhamāspade bāhyatvamāropyate ityāśayaḥ /
tathā sati bādhakapratyayena tadevāpaneyam, tasmiścāpanīte 'haṃ rajatamiti syāt /
evaṃ ca satīdaṃ rajatamiti kor'thaḥ? nāhaṃ rajatamiti /
children.translated_text: And that being so, what is the meaning of 'this is silver'? [It would mean] 'I am not silver.'

children.text: nedaṃ rajatamiti kor'thaḥ? ahaṃ rajatamiti /
children.translated_text: What is the meaning of 'this is not silver'? [It would mean] 'I am silver.'

children.text: tataśca yathedaṃ nedamahaṃ nāhamityanayorvirodhāt samuccayābhimāno 'pi nāsti, tathā nedaṃ rajataṃ nāhaṃ rajatamityanayorapi virodhāt samuccayābhimāno 'pi na syāt /
children.translated_text: And just as 'this' and 'not-this,' and 'I' and 'not-I' — these are contradictory, so that the notion of their co-existence does not arise — so too 'this is not silver' and 'I am not silver' — these being contradictory, the notion of their co-existence should not arise either.

children.text: asti ca, tasmādubhayorapi rajatatvapratiṣedho 'nyasya rajatatvaṃ vyavasthāpayatīti pāṣāṇarekheyaṃ na durūttarapāṃsupūraṇamātreṇāpanetuṃ śakyate //
children.translated_text: But it does arise. Therefore, the denial of silver-nature in both [the external object and the cognition] establishes silver-nature in the other [i.e., a third reality] — this is a line inscribed in stone, which cannot be erased by merely filling it with easily-refuted dust.

of what <s>pramāṇa</s> is it the object? By this, the absence of a probative <s>pramāṇa</s> for the externality of one's own form [i.e., for the view that the form in cognition is external] has been shown. A refuting [argument] is also indicated. For just as 'this is not silver' denies the silver-nature of what is in front by the force of the sublating [cognition], so too 'I am not silver' is also clearly a sublating [cognition]. If [one says] 'this very thing is the error' — then silver-nature is not superimposed on the external [object]. Rather, externality is superimposed on that very locus of 'I.' In that case, the sublating cognition should remove that very [externality], and when that is removed, 'I am silver' should remain.

children.text:
sāmarthyātiśayaḥ svabhāvātiśayaḥ /
atiśayastu viṣayajanyajñānāpekṣayā /
santamiveti satyajñānābhiprāyaṃ svarūpābhiprāyaṃ vā /
viṣayasāmarthyamiti sāmarthyaṃ kāraṇatvam, tabhdāvasiddheḥ /
ata eveti kṛtvā vedāntyekadeśinaḥ api
children.translated_text: The 'surplus of capacity' is the surplus of intrinsic nature. And the surplus is relative to cognition produced by [ordinary] objects. 'As if existent' — with the intention [of referring to] veridical cognition, or with the intention [of referring to] [the object's] own form. 'The capacity of the object' — capacity means causality; because the other [interpretations] are unestablished. For this very reason, even the approval of the one-sided <s>Vedāntin</s>s,

children.text:
nirākārabauddhamatānumatirdarśitā /
sadasattvena gṛhṇātīti na vikalpitamatinirdalatvāt /
pravṛttyaupayiko hyarthaḥ prakṛte prakāśate, na tu sadasattvena gṛhītvā pravṛttirūpapadyate /
asadeva rajataṃ prakāśate /
purovartibhedagrahācca śukto
children.translated_text: the agreement with the <s>nirākāra</s> (formless) Buddhist position is shown. 'Apprehends as existent and non-existent' — this does not demolish [our position], because of the demolition of the conceptual view. For the object that is useful for activity appears in the present context, but activity is not justified by apprehending [something] as existent or non-existent. What appears is non-existent silver. And due to the apprehension of non-difference from what is in front, from the mother-of-pearl —

children.text: pravṛttirnānyatretyādi nāśaḍkitam, prābhākarapakṣeṇa tulyayogakṣematvādapohe nirākariṣyamātvācca //
children.translated_text: activity is not [directed] elsewhere — and so forth is not to be suspected, because this is equally applicable to the <s>Prābhākara</s> position, and because [the <s>apoha</s> theory] will be refuted in the [section on] exclusion (<s>apoha</s>).

children.text:
anirvacanīyakhyātimanubhavavirodhena nirākaroti---na ceti /
ta thāhi kimidam anirvacanīyatvam, kiṃ nirūktiviraha eva, āhosvinnirūktinimittaviraha eva? na tāvadādyaḥ, idaṃ rajataṃ nedaṃ rajatamiti
children.translated_text: He refutes the <s>anirvacanīyakhyāti</s> (the doctrine of indescribable error) by [showing its] contradiction with experience: 'Nor...' For what is this indescribability (<s>anirvacanīyatva</s>)? Is it merely the absence of explanation, or the absence of the ground for explanation? Not the first, because explanation — 'this is silver,' 'this is not silver' —

children.text:
nirūkteranubhūyamānatvāt /
nāpi dvitīyaḥ, nirūktinimittaṃ jñānaṃ vā syāt viṣayo vā? na tāvadādyasya virahaḥ, khyāteḥ svayamavābhyupagamāt /
nāpi dvitīyaḥ, viṣayo 'pi kiṃ bhāvarūpo 'bhāvarūpo vā? ādye asatkhyātyabhyupagamaprasaṅgaḥ /
dvitīye tu satkhyātireva /
ubhau na sta iti cet? atha bhāvābhāvaśabdena lokapratītisiddhāvevobhāvabhipretau, viparītau vā? ādye tāvad
children.translated_text: is experienced. Nor the second. Is the ground for explanation a cognition or an object? Not [the absence of] the first, because [this theory's proponent] himself accepts the appearance (<s>khyāti</s>). Nor the second. Is the object of the nature of a positive entity or of the nature of a non-entity? In the first case, the absurd consequence is the acceptance of <s>asatkhyāti</s> (error of the non-existent). In the second case, it is simply <s>satkhyāti</s> (error of the existent). If [one says] 'neither of the two exists' — do the words 'positive entity' and 'non-entity' refer to what is established by ordinary cognition, or to the opposite?  In the first case,

children.text:
yathābhayorvidhirnāsti, tathā pratiṣedho 'pi, parasparavidhiniṣedhayovi dhiniṣedhanāntarīyakatvāt /
dvitīye tu na kācit kṣatiḥ /
na hyalaukikaviṣayasahasranivṛttāvapi satyajñānaviṣayanivṛttistannirūktinivṛttirveti /
athāpi niḥsvabhāvatvamanirvacanīyatvam? atrāpi nisaḥpratiṣedhārthatvena svabhāvaśabdasyāpi bhāvābhāvayoranyatarārthatve pūrvavat prasaṃgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Or, if indescribability means being without intrinsic nature (<s>niḥsvabhāvatva</s>)?
