abhāvajñānotpattāvindriyārthasannikarṣo na kāraṇaṃ vyabhicārāditi vādinam utthāpayati---nanu svarūpeti /
tadiyamiti /
children.translated_text: 'This then' —

children.text: pramāṇāntaraṃ tu tena saṃbhavatītyabhimānaḥ parasyetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: the opponent's presumption is that another <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible through that [non-apprehension].

children.text: seyamanupalabdhiḥ sattāmātraiṇābhāvaṃ gamayeta, svajñānena vā? na tāvadādyaḥ, tadānīṃ gehasya viprakṛṣṭasya vyavahitatvena yogyānupalabdherasattvāt /
children.translated_text: Would this non-apprehension indicate absence by its mere existence, or by a cognition of itself? Not the first, to begin with — since at that time, there is no fit non-apprehension (<s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>) of a remote or obstructed house, because of the remoteness or obstruction.

children.text: na dvitīyaḥ, anavasthāprasaḍgāt, anupalabdherapyabhāvarūpatayā anupalabdhyantarasādhanīyatvāt //
children.translated_text: Not the second [alternative], because of the consequence of infinite regress — since non-apprehension too, being of the nature of absence, would require establishment through yet another non-apprehension.

Raising and instructing the verbal quibbler (<s>vākchalavādin</s>) regarding the phrase 'recollection of the counter-positive': 'and not the recollection of sound and the like.' Raising the opponent who says 'sense-object contact is not a cause in the generation of absence-cognition, because of deviation': 'now, the intrinsic nature.'

children.text:
yogyasya smaraṇābhāvastāvadastīti cet---na, abhāve viparyayasaṃśayābhāvaprasaṃgāt /
bhavati hi kadācit pratiyogyadhikaraṇayoḥ smaraṇe 'pyasato 'pi sabhdāvapratītiḥ, sato 'bhāvapratyayaḥ, kathamanyathā nāstītyuktvā jhaṭiti saṃjātavādhaḥ prāha, na hi na hi bhrānto 'smi, dṛṣṭa evāsau tatra mayeti, astīti vā prathamamuktvā paścānnāstīti /
kimāsīnnaveti nāvadhārayāmīti veti /
na hi pratiyoginamadhikaraṇaṃ vānupalabdhamevānyathākāraṃ smarati /
na ca svarasasiddhasya smaraṇasyānupalabhyamānasyaiva viparyayaḥ saṃbhavati /
iyatī ca sāmāgrī yaduta pratiyogyadhikaraṇasmaraṇaṃ tattāsmaraṇaṃ ceti /
na vā sādhāraṇaṃ pramākaraṇamadūṣayanta eva doṣā viparyayahetavaḥ, sarvatrānāśvāsaprasaḍgāt /
tvayāpyetat samarthanīyamiti cet---na, yogyāsmaraṇasya mayā liṅgatveneṣṭatvāt /
liṅgaviparyayasaṃśayābhyāṃ ca tallaiḍgikasaṃśayaviparyayayoḥ sulabhatvāt /
yadā tu sunipuṇaikajñānagrahaṇayogyasya caitrasya gehasmaraṇai'pyasmaraṇalakṣaṇaṃ liṅgamavadhāryate, tadā liḍgipratītiraviparītā bhavatyeva /
ata eva kṣaṇaṃ dhyātvetyāha /
anyathā dhyānamapyanupapannam /
asmaraṇamātrasya hi vyabhicāram upalabhya tadanādṛtya viśiṣṭāsmaraṇaṃ jñātukāmasya praṇidhānamupapadyate /
children.translated_text: For having observed the deviation of mere non-memory, disregarding it, the focused attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) of one who desires to know the qualified non-memory is justified.

children.text: tasmāt liṅgatvenaiva asmaraṇamupayujyate /
children.translated_text: Therefore, non-memory is useful precisely as an inferential mark.

children.text: kiṃ tu tadapi kathaṃ jñātavyamityavaśiṣyate? tatrāha---naitaditi /
children.translated_text: However, how even that is to be known — this remains [to be addressed]. To that he says: 'na etad' (not this).

children.text: vyadhikaraṇatāṃ parihartuṃ prayogaṃ darśayati---tathā hīti //
children.translated_text: To resolve the [problem of] having a different locus, he shows the formulation: 'tathā hī' (for thus).

If it is said: 'the absence of memory of what is fit [to be perceived] does at least exist' — no, because in the [case of] absence, there would follow the absence of error and doubt. For sometimes, even when the counterpositive and the locus are remembered, there is the cognition of the existence of something non-existent, and the cognition of the absence of something existent. How else [could one explain that] one who says 'it does not exist' suddenly, having been contradicted, says 'No, no, I was mistaken! I myself saw it there!' — or, having first said 'it exists,' later [says] 'it does not exist,' or 'was it there or not? I cannot determine!' For one does not remember the counterpositive or the locus in a form other than what was [actually] perceived. Nor is it possible for the error of a spontaneously established memory to occur only when [the object] is not perceived. And the totality of conditions is just this: the memory of the counterpositive and the locus, and the non-memory of that [object]. Nor are the defects that are causes of error — while not vitiating the common instrument of valid cognition — [an explanation], because there would follow the absurd consequence of unreliability everywhere. If it is said: 'you too must justify this' — no, because the non-memory of what is fit [to be perceived] is accepted by me as an inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>). And since from the doubt and error of the mark, the doubt and error of the inferred [conclusion] are easily obtained. But when, for <s>Caitra</s> who is capable of grasping [something] through a single precise cognition, the inferential mark characterized by non-memory [is ascertained] even through the memory of the house, then the cognition of the inferred [conclusion] is indeed non-erroneous. For this very reason, [the text] says 'having reflected for a moment.' Otherwise, even reflection would be untenable.

children.text:
na cāvacchedyāvacchedakayorvaiyadhikaraṇyaṃ doṣaḥ, viśeṣaṇa eva tanniyamāt, atra tūpalakṣaṇatvāt, vaiyadhikaraṇye 'pyupalakṣaṇatvāvirodhāt, na[?]atāvanmātreṇaivopayogāt /
upalakṣitaṃ tu sādhyasamānādhikaraṇameva /
ata evānutpannapādavihārasya acalacakṣuṣa ityādi vyadhikaraṇameva darśayati sma vārttikakāraḥ /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, even the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> was showing precisely examples with different loci: 'of one who has not arisen and walked about,' 'with unmoving eyes,' and the like.

children.text: ṭīkākāro 'pi tathā anumene, yato nānyathākṛtavān /
children.translated_text: The author of the <s>Ṭīkā</s> too assented to the same, since he did not alter it.

children.text: parairapi yadyadā yajjānanasamarthamiti vadabhdiḥ svīkṛtamevaitat /
children.translated_text: Even by others, this has been accepted by saying 'whatever, whenever, has the capacity to cognize whatever.'

children.text: tat kasya hetoḥ? tathaiva pratibandhasiddheḥ //
children.translated_text: For what reason? Because the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) is established precisely in that way.

Nor is the difference of locus between the delimited and the delimiter a fault — because the restriction pertains only to the qualifier. But here, because of being an indicative marker (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>), and because the indicative marker is not contradicted even when the loci are different, and because the usefulness is not exhausted by just that much. But what is indicated is always co-extensive with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved).

children.text:
nanvindriyārthasannikarṣavyabhicārastadavastha ityata āha---na ca yaditi /
sākṣātkāriṇī hi
children.translated_text: Now, the deviation of the contact of sense-organ and object is in the same condition [as before] — therefore he says: 'na ca yad' (and not that which). For the direct

children.text: pratītirasmadādīnāmindriyārthasannikarṣaṃ na vyabhicarati, iyaṃ tvānumānikī pārokṣyavatī tasmānna kvacid vyabhicāraśaḍkā /
children.translated_text: cognition of people like us does not deviate from the contact of sense-organ and object; but this [cognition of absence] is inferential, having indirectness — therefore there is no suspicion of deviation anywhere.

children.text: yadyanumānagamyo 'bhāvaḥ, kathaṃ pratyakṣasya tatra pravṛtti? anayorasaḍkīrṇaviṣayatvāditi tu kadācid brūyāt /
children.translated_text: If absence is cognized through inference, how does perception operate with respect to it? One might sometimes say: because these two have non-overlapping domains.

children.text: tacca saṃplavavyavasthāpanayaiva samāhitamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And that has been settled by the very establishment of the flooding [of non-apprehension into perception] — this is the meaning.

children.text: na tarhi ityādibhāṣyeṇa kaḥ sūtrāvayavo vyākhyāta iti śaḍkāmapanayanneva vārttikamavatārayati---saṃpratīti /
children.translated_text: Dispelling the doubt about which component of the <s>sūtra</s> is being explained by the <s>Bhāṣya</s> [passage] 'na tarhi' (not then) and so forth, he introduces the <s>Vārttika</s>: 'saṃprati' (now).

children.text: nanu lakṣaṇaṃ tathāpyaduṣṭamityata āha---pratyakṣakāraṇeti /
children.translated_text: Now, the definition is nevertheless not faulty — therefore he says: 'pratyakṣakāraṇa' (the cause of perception).

children.text: kāraṇāvadhāraṇābhimāninaścodyamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: The meaning is: [this is] the objection of one who claims to ascertain the cause [of perception].

children.text: viṣayasaṃyogicakṣurālokaśceti vadatā viṣayasaṃyogenaivālokavyāpāro na tvagindriyādhiṣṭhānasaṃyogenetyuktam //
children.translated_text: By saying 'the eye-light that is conjoined with the object,' it is stated that the operation of light is through conjunction with the object, not through conjunction with the substratum of the tactile sense-organ.

children.text:
etaccāndhakāramadhyavartināpyālokamadhyavartiviṣayopalabdherālokamadhyavartināpi cāndhakāramadhyasthānupalabdherūnneyam /
nanu mahattvānekadravyavattvayoḥ parasparāvinābhūtayoragṛhyamāṇaviśeṣatvenobhayorapi cākṣaṣatvaṃ prati kāraṇatvāt samuccaya eva /
viśeṣe vā ekasyaiva kāraṇatvam, kuto vikalpaḥ? parasparavyabhicāriṇo hyarthakriyāyāṃ vikalpasambhavo na tvime tathā /
tasmāccākṣuṣadravyalakṣaṇe kartavye 'nayorvikalpopanyāsaḥ kartavyaḥ /
children.translated_text: And this is to be inferred from the fact that even one situated in darkness perceives objects situated in light, and even one situated in light does not perceive [objects] situated in the midst of darkness. Now, since largeness and being-composed-of-many-substances — these two being mutually inseparable, and since both, being of the nature of undiscriminated distinguishing features, are causes of visual perceptibility — therefore there is simply aggregation [of conditions]. Or [if] only one is the cause with respect to a specific [object], whence the alternative? For those that deviate from each other with respect to causal efficacy admit of alternatives, but these are not so. Therefore, when formulating the definition of visually perceptible substance, the alternative presentation of these two must be made.

children.text:
ubhayopādāne cāsamarthaviśeṣaṇaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ bhavedityarthaḥ /
ata evāgre satyapyevaṃ lakṣaṇakatva ityāha uktasāmagrīsambhave 'pi cakṣuravayavino na pratyakṣatā, ata uktaṃ vārttikakṛtā upalabdhiphalaḥ saṃskāra iti /
sa ca durnirūpaḥ /
tathāhi guṇidharmo vāsau syāt, guṇadharmo vā syāt? tatra guṇidharmatve tabdale rūpasparśayoraviśeṣeṇa grahaṇam, na tu kvacid grahaṇam agrahaṇaṃ ca kvaciditi /
tadekārthasamavetayorgrahaṇameveti cet---na, niśi nidāghasamaye tejaḥ-sparśagrahe 'pi rūpāgrahāt, candrātaparūpagrahe 'pi sparśāgrahāt, guṇadharmastvanityo na bhavatyeva, nityastu sāmānyarūpo na saṃskāraśabdavācyo nāpyupalabdhiphalaḥ, tasya
children.translated_text: But if both are included, the definition would have a powerless qualifier — this is the meaning. For this very reason, even though such a definition exists, [the author] says ahead: 'even when the stated totality of conditions is present, a composite [substance] does not have perceptibility to the eye.' Therefore the author of the <s>Vārttika</s> said: '<s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) has apprehension as its result.' And that is difficult to analyze. For is it a property of the property-bearer, or a property of the property? In the case of its being a property of the property-bearer, then on the surface, form and touch would be apprehended without distinction, not apprehended in some cases and not in others. If it is said: 'what is inherent in the same substratum is apprehended' — no, because at night in the hot season, even when touch of heat is apprehended, form is not; and when the form of the moon and the like is apprehended, touch is not. But a property of the property cannot be non-eternal; and a permanent [property] having the nature of a universal is not denotable by the word '<s>saṃskāra</s>,' nor does it have apprehension as its result, since that [universal]

children.text:
svepalabdheranyatrānimittatvādityata āha--dharmādharmanimitta ubhdavasamākhyāta iti /
rūpādīnā svakāraṇavaśādeva sa svabhāvabhedo jāyate keṣāñcit, yatrobhdavatvaṃ nāma sāmānyaviśeṣaḥ samavaiti /
sa ca dharmādharmajanyatayā saṃskāra ityucyate, upalabdhiphalaśca bhavatītyarthaḥ /
pratyakṣalakṣaṇatayā tatkāraṇamuktam, na tu kāraṇatayaiva /
na ca kāraṇaṃ lakṣaṇamityekam /
utpattivyavasthāpakaṃ hi lakṣaṇamalakṣaṇaṃ vā, kāraṇasvarūpavyavasthāpakaṃ tu kārakamakārakaṃ vā lakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: For a definition either establishes the arising [of the definiendum] or not; a causal factor either establishes the intrinsic nature of the cause or not — [these are] the definitions [respectively].

children.text: na caivamālokādayaḥ, teṣāmativyāpakatayā avyāpakatayā ca pratyakṣasvarūpāvyavasthāpakatvāt /
children.translated_text: And light and the like are not [definitions] in this way — because, by their over-extension and under-extension, they do not establish the intrinsic nature of perception.

children.text: utpattivyavasthāpakāḥ punarete bhavanti /
children.translated_text: But these [factors] do establish the arising [of perception].

children.text: teṣāmanyatamāpāye 'pi pratyakṣānupapatterityāśayavān parihāraṃ vyācaṣṭe---pratyakṣalakṣaṇeti //
children.translated_text: Because without any one of these, perception would be impossible — with this intention he explains the resolution: 'pratyakṣalakṣaṇa' (the definition of perception).

is not the cause [of anything] elsewhere, by virtue of its own apprehension — therefore he says: 'dharmādharma-nimitta' (caused by merit and demerit), 'called ubhaya (both).' It is a specific difference of intrinsic nature in form and the like that arises from their respective causes in certain [substances], where a specific universal called 'manifestness' (<s>ubhayatva</s>) inheres. And that, being produced by <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), is called <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), and has apprehension as its result — this is the meaning. It is stated as the definition of perception — not as a cause by itself. And being a cause and being a definition are not one and the same.

children.text: nanu yadyapi svarūpataḥ santānato vā indriyābhedādindriyamanaḥsannikarṣābhedo yathāyathaṃ saṃbhavati, tathāpi vijñānābhedo vyaktikṛto jātikṛto vā syāt /
children.translated_text: Now, although the non-difference of sense-organ — whether in its intrinsic nature or in its continuum — and the non-difference of sense-organ-mind contact, as the case may be, are possible, nevertheless, the non-difference of cognition may be due to the individual [instance] or due to the class (<s>jāti</s>).

children.text: pūrvasminnindriyārthasannikarṣābhede 'pi dhārāvāhikavijñānāni bhidyante /
children.translated_text: In the former [case], even when there is non-difference of sense-organ-object contact, stream-like cognitions do differ.

children.text: uttaratra tu indriyārthasannikarṣabhede pyabheda eva, sarveṣāṃ sākṣātkārijātīyatvāditi /
children.translated_text: But in the latter [case], even when there is difference of sense-organ-object contact, there is indeed non-difference [of cognition], since all [such cognitions] belong to the class of direct perception.

children.text: tat ekadeśiparihāro garbhastrāveṇaiva gata upanyāsayogyo 'pi na bhavatītyāśayavānāha---yadā hīti //
children.translated_text: That [response] is a partial resolution that has already been rendered defunct even in its preliminary formulation and is not worthy of being presented — with this intention he says: 'yadā hī' (for when).

children.text:
asti hi svarūpajātikṛtabhedātirikto viṣayakṛto viśeṣo buddhīnām /
sa cendriyārthasannikarṣabhedādeva dṛṣṭaḥ, nendriyamanaḥsannikarṣabhedāt /
yatra tu dhārāvāhijñāne nendriyārthasannikarṣo bhidyate, tatra jñānasyāpi na viṣayakṛto bheda ityarthaḥ /
tadidamuktam---kramavanti hāstikāśvīyādivijñānānīti /
children.translated_text: This is what is said: 'The cognitions of elephants, horses, and the like are sequential.'

children.text: nirākaraṇe 'pyetadanurūpamudāharati---yadā iti /
children.translated_text: Even in the refutation, he cites an example in accordance with this: 'yadā' (when).

children.text: tasyaiva goścakṣuṣā saṃyogena tatraiva gavi samavāyena prathamaṃ śuklaguṇajñānaṃ paścād gamanakarmajñānamiti bhede 'bhedāditi /
children.translated_text: For that very cow, through conjunction with the eye, through inherence in that very cow — first [arises] the cognition of the white property, then the cognition of the action of going — thus from non-difference [of the object], [the cognitions arise] in difference.

children.text: samānamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'Samānam' — the meaning is: the same.

For there is indeed a distinction in cognitions, produced by the object, that is over and above the distinction produced by intrinsic nature and class. And that [distinction] has been observed only from the difference of sense-organ-object contact, not from the difference of sense-organ-mind contact. But where, in stream-like cognition, the sense-organ-object contact does not differ, there too the cognition has no object-produced difference — this is the meaning.

children.text: yadyapyaprasiddhatvamavyapadeśakatvavyāpakatvāt tadabhidhānenaiva labdham, tathāpyālokaviṣayasannikarṣo 'vyapadeśakatve 'pi prasiddhaḥ, indriyamanaḥsannikarṣastvavyapadeśako 'prasiddhaśca ityetāvatā prakārāntaratvam //
children.translated_text: Although being-unestablished is obtained through the pervasion of being-non-designative, nevertheless the contact of light and object, though non-designative, is well-known; but the contact of sense-organ and mind is both non-designative and not well-known — to this extent, it is a different mode [of the argument].

children.text: nanvanyatarātīndriyādhāratvamindriyārthasannikarṣasyāpyasti, ubhayātīndriyādhāratā tu ātmamanaḥsannikarṣasyāpi nāstītyata āha--ātmā tu yadyapīti //
children.translated_text: Now, even the contact of sense-organ and object has the feature of one of the two [relata] being supersensible; but the contact of <s>ātman</s> and mind does not even have the feature of both [relata] being supersensible — therefore he says: 'ātmā tu yadyapi' (but although the ātman).

children.text:
nanu viśiṣṭakarmābhinirvartitatvena prasannāndhānandhakṛṣṇasārāṇāṃ na kaścidviśeṣaḥ, na hi rūpopabhogānarthinaḥ kṛṣṇasāre tṛṣṇā tatkarmasaṃbhavaḥ /
asaṃbhave ca kathamasyotpattiriti? ataḥ kārye 'pi karmaṇaḥ sahakāritāmāha--etaduktaṃ bhavatīti /
karmakṣayāt ityupalakṣaṇam, pratibandhāt, sahakārivirahāccetyapi draṣṭavyam /
yadi hi rathādisaṃyogānāṃ nabhovyāpakatvaṃ bhavet tadā tatkāryasyapi śabdasya sarvatrotpādaprasaḍgeḥ /
asamavāyikāraṇaprādeśikatvānurodhena hi
children.translated_text: Now, there is no distinction among the clear-eyed, the blind, and the black-antelope — [all being produced] by specific <s>karma</s> — for one who does not desire the enjoyment of form does not have craving for the black-antelope; and [if] the <s>karma</s> for it is impossible, how can it arise? Therefore, he states the auxiliary role of <s>karma</s> even with respect to the effect: 'etaduktaṃ bhavati' (this is what is stated). 'From the exhaustion of <s>karma</s>' is merely indicative — 'from obstruction, and from the absence of auxiliary causes' should also be understood. For if the conjunctions of chariots and the like had the pervasiveness of space, then their effect — sound — would have the absurd consequence of arising everywhere. For in accordance with the localness of the non-inherent cause,

children.text: vyāpakaguṇāḥ pradeśāvacchedena jāyante /
children.translated_text: qualities that pervade [their substrata] arise with spatial delimitation.

children.text: iha tu tadabhāvādanavacchinnadeśataiva syāt /
children.translated_text: But here, in the absence of that [spatial delimitation of the non-inherent cause], there would be [pervasion] in undelimited space itself.

children.text: tataśca taddvāreṇopalamyamānā rathādayastatsaṃyogāśca na niyatadeśatayā pratīyerannityāśayavānāha---mā bhūtasarvatreti //
children.translated_text: And thus, chariots and the like, and their conjunctions, being perceived through that [space], would not be perceived as in a determinate place — with this intention he says: 'mā bhūt sarvatra' (lest [it be] everywhere).

children.text:
nanvākāśapratyakṣatāpakṣaḥ kimiti nāśaḍkita iti pariharatnāha--nāsmākamiti /
tvagādibhiriti tatra tvagudāhaṇamuktam /
rasanodāharaṇaṃ tu tiktatvābhāvaviśiṣṭo madhurataro guḍaḥ /
tathā ghrāṇodāharaṇaṃ pūtigrandhābhāvaviśiṣṭā surabhitarā kastūriketyato bahuvacanāvirodhaḥ /
bauddhasiddhānte ca guṇaguṇinorabhedād guṇimūrtatvameva guṇamūrtatvam /
guṇagrāhakamevendriyaṃ guṇigrāhakam /
guṇābhāva eva ca guṇyabhāvaḥ /
ato mūrtābhāvaviśiṣṭagrahe udāharaṇīye
children.translated_text: Now, why was the position that space (<s>ākāśa</s>) is perceptible not even suspected? — while resolving this he says: 'nāsmākam' (not for us). 'By touch (<s>tvak</s>) and the like' — there the example of touch has been stated. The example of taste is: jaggery (<s>guḍa</s>), which is sweeter [precisely] because it is qualified by the absence of bitterness. Similarly, the example of smell is: musk (<s>kastūrikā</s>), which is more fragrant because it is qualified by the absence of foul odor — hence the use of the plural [in the original text] is not contradicted. And in the Buddhist system, since there is no difference between property and property-bearer, the corporeality of the property-bearer is itself the corporeality of the property. The very sense-organ that apprehends the property also apprehends the property-bearer. And the very absence of the property is the absence of the property-bearer. Therefore, when citing an example of apprehending [an object] qualified by the absence of corporeal [qualities],

children.text: alpābhāvaviśiṣṭagrahamāheti //
children.translated_text: he mentions the apprehension [of an object] qualified by the absence of a minor [quality].

children.text:
nanu mā bhūt sahāntareṇa grahaṇaṃ sāntara iti vā grahaṇaṃ hetvarthaḥ, śarīrendriyādhiṣṭhānāsambandhasya grahaṇamartho bhaviṣyati /
na hyayamanyathāsiddhaḥ, etasyaivottaropādhitvena prayojakatvādityata āha---indriyasambandho bhavatu mā veti /
yaccharīrasambddhaṃ tadavaśyamindriyasambaddhamiti /
yadindriyasambaddhaṃ tadavaśyaṃ śarīrasambaddhamiti vā na pramāṇamasti,
children.translated_text: Now, let the intended meaning of the inferential mark not be 'apprehension without an intermediary' or 'apprehension with an intermediary,' but rather the apprehension of the non-connection with the body-sense-organ-substratum. For this is not otherwise established, since this very [body-connection] serves as the qualifying condition in what follows — therefore he says: 'indriyasambandho bhavatu mā vā' (let there be connection with the sense-organ or not). For there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> [for the rule] that whatever is connected with the body is necessarily connected with the sense-organ, or that whatever is connected with the sense-organ is necessarily connected with the body,

children.text: tayorvibhinnatvāt, vibhinnāśrayatvācca /
children.translated_text: because the two are different, and because they have different substrata.

children.text: na hyasti niyamo yat pradīpena sambaṇsate tadavaśyaṃ mallimayāpi yad vā mallimayā tadavaśyaṃ pradīpenāpi /
children.translated_text: For there is no rule that whatever is connected with a lamp is necessarily connected with a jasmine [pot], or that whatever is connected with a jasmine [pot] is necessarily connected with a lamp.

children.text: tasmāt tatra sādhākabādhakapramāṇābhāvāt sandeha evetyarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, in the absence of both probative and sublating <s>pramāṇas</s> there, there is simply doubt — this is the meaning.

children.text: tasmāt tadanyathāsiddhirevetyasiddhivyavacchedārthaṃ sajalasatejaḥpaṭādigrāhiṇā prāpyakāriṇā tvagindriyeṇa viruddhamapi sahāntareṇa grahaṇaṃ draṣṭavyam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, that [supposed non-connection] is indeed otherwise established. And for the purpose of excluding [the fault of] non-establishment, it should be observed that apprehension without an intermediary — even though contradicted by the tactile sense-organ, which reaches [its object] and which apprehends things that are wet, luminous, or cloth-like — is [nevertheless the correct understanding].

children.text: āvaraṇānupapattirūpasya tarkasyopaskurvāṇaḥ prayogeṇa pramāṇamāha--prayogastviti //
children.translated_text: Augmenting the <s>tarka</s> (reasoning) in the form of the impossibility of obstruction, he states the <s>pramāṇa</s> through a formulation: 'prayogastu' (but the formulation).

children.text:
iha dvividhaḥ sambandhaḥ prāptilakṣaṇo yathā, ālokādīnāṃ ghaṭādibhiḥ /
tadviparītaśca yathā, abhidhānajñānādīnāmabhidhayajñeyādibhaḥ /
tatra svaviṣayaṃ prāpyeti siddhasādhanavyudāsārtham /
janakatvādityukte śabdādibhiraprāptasvaviṣayapratipattyādijanakairanaikāntikamatastadaprāptāvajanakatvāditi /
etāvanmātreṇa tu sarvathā
children.translated_text: Here, the connection is of two kinds: characterized by contact (<s>prāpti</s>) — as of light and the like with pots and the like; and the opposite of that — as of designation, cognition, and the like with the designated, the cognizable, and the like. Among these, 'reaching its own object' is for the purpose of excluding what is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>). If 'because of being a generator' were said [alone], then [the mark] would be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) because of generators like sound and the like that produce cognition of objects they have not reached — therefore 'in the case of their non-reaching, because of being a non-generator.' But by just this much, in every way

children.text: ajanakairanaikāntikamato janakatve satīti /
children.translated_text: it is inconclusive because of non-generators [in general] — therefore 'when generating does occur.'

children.text: yuktyantaram tarkāntaram, dūrāntikānanuvidhānaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Another reasoning — another <s>tarka</s> — [leads to] the absurd consequence of non-conformity with distance and proximity.

children.text: asyāpi viparyayeṇa prayogo draṣṭavyaḥ //
children.translated_text: The application of this [argument] too, in reverse, should be understood.

children.text: nanu prāptatvāviśeṣe sūryamaṇḍalavanmerūpṛṣṭhamadhyandinolkāprakāśāvapi gṛhṇīyāt /
children.translated_text: Now, if there is no difference in contact, one should also apprehend the light of the midday meteor on the summit of <s>Meru</s> just as [one apprehends] the solar disc.

children.text: athānubhdūtābhibhūtatayā na sūrasadanādīnāṃ grahaṇam, ubhdūtānabhibhūtatvāt sūryamaṇḍalaṃ gṛhyata iti, evaṃ tarhi viṣaya eva sa kaścit tādṛśo yo gṛhyate netara ityabhyupeyatām, kiṃ vyabhicāriprāptiparigrahegotyata āha---prāptau tviti /
children.translated_text: If [one says] that the sun's abode and the like are not apprehended because they are overpowered by what has arisen, while the solar disc is apprehended because what has arisen is not overpowered — then let it be accepted that only that particular object that is apprehended is of such a nature, and not the other. Why embrace a contact that is deviant [i.e., unreliable]? — therefore he says: 'But in contact...'

children.text: viṣayamāhātmyaṃ hi prāptisahakāri, na tu svatantram /
children.translated_text: For the excellence of the object is an auxiliary to contact, not independent.

children.text: na hi sparśarasādayo grahaṇayogyā ityaprāptaireva tvagādibhirgṛhyante, prāpyakāritvād vā tairanubhdūtābhibhūtā api te prāptatvamātreṇa gṛhyanta ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: For touch, taste, and the like, [which are] fit for apprehension, are not apprehended by the skin and the like without contact. Or, because [the skin and the like] operate through contact, even those [objects] that have arisen and are not overpowered are [still only] apprehended by the mere fact of being in contact — that is the meaning.

children.text: yadyapi kṣaṇabhaṅgapariṇāmanaye 'pi prāptānāmeva parasparaṃ kartṛkaraṇakarmaṇāṃ kāryajananam, na tvaprāptānāmapi, na hi parasparamapratyāsīdantaḥ sahakāripratyayā bhāvānatiśāyayanto dṛśyante /
pratyāsattistu nirantarotpāda eva teṣām /
children.translated_text: their proximity, however, is nothing but uninterrupted origination.

children.text: saiva ca svarūpyogyatā /
children.translated_text: And that alone is intrinsic fitness (<s>svarūpayogyatā</s>).

children.text: tathā ca svarūpayogyatāmindriyārthayobruvatā nirantarotpāda eva vaktavyaḥ, na punarvyavahitaviprakṛṣṭotpannānāṃ kvacidapi svarūpayogyatā nāma /
children.translated_text: And thus, one who speaks of intrinsic fitness between the sense-organ and the object must speak only of uninterrupted origination; there is no such thing as 'intrinsic fitness' for things that have originated in a separated and remote manner.

children.text: tasmāt prāptau svarūpātiriktāyāṃ vipratipadyeta, na tu nirantarotpāde 'pi tatrādhikāprāptiḥ sādhanamarhatītyāśayavānāha---niṣetsyete hīti //
children.translated_text: Therefore, one may disagree about contact as something over and above intrinsic nature, but even with uninterrupted origination, additional contact deserves to be proved — with this intention he says: 'For it will be denied...'

Although even in the doctrine of momentary destruction and transformation, it is only for [things that are] in mutual contact — [viz.] agent, instrument, and object — that the production of the effect [occurs], and not for those not in contact; for auxiliary conditions that do not approach each other and that do not enhance entities are never observed —

children.text: evaṃ nivāritābhimānaḥ paradarśane 'pi pramāṇamapaśyan sandigdha iti //
children.translated_text: Thus, one whose presumption has been refuted, not seeing a <s>pramāṇa</s> even in the opposing view, is in doubt.

children.text:
nanu janakatve satīti nirṇayahetuṃ paśyan kathaṃ nāma sandigdha ityata āha---ayamabhisandhiriti /
adṛśyamānaprāptāvayaskānte 'pi dṛṣṭatvādanaikāntikasyābhimanyate para ityarthaḥ /
tvagādīnāṃ daṇḍādīnāṃ ca prāptānāmeva kāryajanakatvaṃ paśyan kathamiva sarvatra vipratipadyata ityato vipratipattibījamāha---yogyatayaiveti /
children.translated_text: Seeing that the skin and the like, and sticks and the like, produce effects only when in contact — how can one disagree in every case? — Therefore he states the seed of disagreement: 'By mere fitness...'

children.text: nanvayaskāntasyāprāpyakāritve hetvantare 'pi kaḥ pratīkāra ityata āha---ayaskāntamaṇeriti /
children.translated_text: Now, even if the magnet operates without contact, what remedy is there through another reason [for proving contact]? — therefore he says: 'Of the magnet...'

children.text: nanu tasya vṛttibhedaḥ anupalambhabādhita ityata uktam---cakṣuṣa iveti /
children.translated_text: Now, the different mode of operation of that [magnet] is contradicted by non-apprehension — therefore it is said: 'Just as of the eye...'

children.text: tulyayogakṣematvādityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: because of equal standing [i.e., the same argument applies to both].

Now, seeing the determining reason 'when there is productivity' — how can one be in doubt? — therefore he says: 'This is the intention.' The meaning is: the opponent considers [the reason] to be inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), since [productivity] is observed even in the case of the magnet, where contact is not visible.

children.text: vyavadhānaviprakarṣau hi anirantarotpādo vā syādaprāptirvā, svarūpayogyatā vā? tatrānirantarotpādābhāvo
children.translated_text: Now, are obstruction and remoteness [identical to] non-uninterrupted origination, or [to] non-contact, or [to] intrinsic unfitness? In the first case, the absence of non-uninterrupted origination

children.text:
nirantarotpādaḥ syāt /
na ca kṛṣpāsārasyārthena maṇervā lohena nirantarotpādaḥ saṃbhavati /
aprāptyabhāvastu prāptireva, tathā ca kaḥ pratikūlo 'nukūlamācarati? ayogyatābhāvastu yogyataiva /
sa ca bauddhanaye kāraṇajātīyasya nirantarotpādānna bhidyata ityuktam /
tasmāt sthiranaye kāryaṃ janayanti kāraṇāni parasparaprāptiṃ vā vyabhicaranti,
children.translated_text: would be uninterrupted origination. And uninterrupted origination is not possible between a piece of iron and a magnet. But the absence of non-contact is contact itself — and so, who that is hostile behaves favorably? And the absence of unfitness is fitness itself. And that, in the Buddhist system, is said not to differ from uninterrupted origination of something of the same causal class. Therefore, in the system of permanent [entities], either causes produce effects while deviating from mutual contact,

children.text: prāptirvā svarūpayogyatāprayuktāṃ vyāptimupajīvatītyavaśiṣyate /
children.translated_text: or contact depends on the <s>vyāpti</s> (invariable concomitance) that is brought about by intrinsic fitness — this remains.

children.text: tatrāha---prāptereveti //
children.translated_text: Regarding that he says: 'Of contact itself...'

children.text:
nanu lakṣaṇāntareṇa vyavasthite lakṣye kathamanyonyāśrayatvamityata āha---agatirveti /
taddhi lakṣyasāpekṣamanapekṣaṃ vā? ādye anyonyāśrayatvadoṣādevāgatiḥ /
uttaratra tu avagate lakṣye tatsāpekṣeṇa lakṣaṇena kiṃ gamayitavyamityagatirevetyarthaḥ /
asti hīti /
yadi vijñānābhinnahetujatvāt sukhaṃ vijñānajātīyaṃ syāt sukhābhinnahetujatvāt tadapi sukhajātīyaṃ bhavet /
vijñānaṃ na sukhenābhinnahetujamiti cet? evaṃ tarhi kathaṃ sukhamapi vijñānenābhinnahetujamityarthaḥ /
nanu jñānahetvanugamaḥ sukhe 'pyasti, na tu sukhahetvanugamo jñāne, ato yatkāraṇānugamo
children.translated_text: Now, when the characterized thing is established through another definition, how can there be mutual dependence? — therefore he says: 'There is no [other] recourse...' Is that [definition] dependent on the characterized thing or not? In the first case, the difficulty arises from the very fault of mutual dependence. In the second case, when the characterized thing is already known, what is to be made known by a definition dependent on it? — the meaning is: there is no recourse. 'For indeed...' — if pleasure were of the same class as consciousness because it arises from causes not different from those of consciousness, then [consciousness] too, because it arises from causes not different from those of pleasure, would be of the same class as pleasure. If [one says] 'consciousness does not arise from causes not different from those of pleasure' — then how does pleasure also arise from causes not different from those of consciousness? — that is the meaning. Now, the conformity with the causes of cognition exists in pleasure too, but the conformity with the causes of pleasure does not exist in cognition — therefore whatever has the conformity with the causes of whatever

children.text:
yatra tajjātīyatvaṃ tatrāstu /
yathāḍkuramātrakāraṇānugame yavāḍkurasyāpyaḍkurajātīyatvam /
na tu sarvasya yavāḍkuratvam tatkāraṇānugamābhāvādityāśayavān āśaṅkate---avāntareti /
na hyasti niyamo yajjātīyakāryahetucakrānagamo yatra tatra tajjātīyatvamiti /
bījajātīyakāryahetucakrānugame 'pyaḍkurasya bījājātīyatvāditi sāmānyopasaṃhāre 'naikāntikatvam, viśeṣopasaṃhāre tu
children.translated_text: is of the same class as that. For example, when there is conformity with the causes of sprouts in general, a barley-sprout too is of the sprout-class. But not everything is a barley-sprout, due to the absence of conformity with the causes of that — with this intention he raises the objection: 'subsidiary...' For there is no rule that whatever has the conformity with the causal complex of the effect of a certain class, is of that class wherever [such conformity exists]. For even a sprout, despite having conformity with the causal complex of the seed-class effect, is not of the seed-class. Thus, when applied to the general case, the [reason is] inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>); when applied to the specific case,

children.text: sandigdhānaikāntikatvamāha---na kiñciditi //
children.translated_text: he states [that it is] doubtfully inconclusive: 'Nothing...'

children.text:
ākasmikatvaprasaṅgabhayāddhi kāryabhedopapattaye sakalakāraṇabhedamanusaran prayasyati bhavān, sa ca kāryabhedaḥ kiñcitkāraṇabhedenaiva bījāḍkurādivat jñānasukhādāvapyanākasmika ityarthaḥ /
tadidamuktaṃ tadarthatvācceti /
nanu rūparasagandhasparśānāṃ hi upādānabhedābhedamātrānuviddhaṃ tajjātīyātajjātīyatvam /
na hyasti saṃbhavo rūpādyupādānaṃ cārūpādikaṃ ceti /
ato jñānopādānatve sukhaṃ jñānajātīyameva syāt /
ajñānatve vā na jñānopādānatvamiti yadi pratyavatiṣṭhate tatrāha---na ceti /
children.translated_text: Or if [pleasure] is not cognition, then [cognition is] not its material cause — if one insists on this, he responds: 'Nor...'

children.text: yadi hyekajātīyopādānatayaikajātīyatvaṃ bhavet, avāntaraikajātīyamapi kiṃ na syāt? tathā caikasmāt samanantarapratyayādanekāvāntarajātīnayānutpādaprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: For if being of the same class were due to having the same material cause as something of one class, would it not also be of the same sub-class? And thus, the absurd consequence would be that from a single immediately preceding condition (<s>samanantarapratyaya</s>), there would be no production of many sub-classes.

children.text: dṛśyate ca rūpajñānād rūpajñānaṃ rasajñānādijātīyaṃ ca /
children.translated_text: And we observe that from a cognition of form arises [another] cognition of form, and [also one] of the class of taste-cognition and the like.

children.text: sākṣātkāriṇaḥ sākṣātkāraścāsākṣātkaraścetyādi //
children.translated_text: And from direct perception arises both direct perception and non-direct perception — and so forth.

For, out of fear of the absurd consequence of randomness, you strive to account for the diversity of effects through the diversity of the entire causal complex. But that diversity of effects is non-random even through the diversity of just some causes, as in the case of seeds and sprouts — the same [applies] to cognition and pleasure and the like — that is the meaning. This is what is said by: 'because of being for that purpose.' Now, form, taste, smell, and touch have their same-class and different-class nature pervaded solely by the sameness or difference of their material cause (<s>upādāna</s>). For the possibility does not exist that the material cause of form and the like is also non-form. Therefore, if pleasure has cognition as its material cause, it would necessarily be of the same class as cognition.

children.text: atha vilakṣaṇānekasahakāripraveśādanekāvāntarajātīyakāryakaraṇasvabhāvasya kasyanacidevotpādaniyama upapādya /
children.translated_text: Now, the restriction of production to just something [specific] by a [cause] whose nature is to produce effects of many sub-classes, due to the entry of many dissimilar auxiliary [causes], is to be justified.

children.text: evamavāntarajātibhedopapādanavadvivakṣitaikajātīyopādānatve 'pi vilakṣaṇānekasahakāripraveśād vivakṣitānekajātīyakāryakaraṇasvabhāvasya kasyacidevotpādaniyama upapatsyata ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Similarly, even when the material cause of the desired single class is accepted, due to the entry of many dissimilar auxiliary [causes], the restriction of production to just something [specific] by a [cause] whose nature is to produce effects of the desired many classes will be justified — that is the meaning.

children.text:
so 'yamekopādānakatve 'pyavāntarajātibhedābhyupagamaḥ pareṣāṃ dṛṣṭāntārthamubhdāvitaḥ api cetyādyubhdāvitaṃ sandigdhavyāvṛttikatvaṃ sphuṭhayitumato nāsaṅgatamiti /
tadetat sakalaṃ bauddhasiddhāntābhyupagamenoktam /
paramārthatastu yadupādānavat tatsajātīyaṃ yadvyāpakopādānavat tadguṇajātīyamiti niyamaḥ /
ataḥ paramaniyamaḥ /
tadyadi sattayā guṇatvena vā sukhajñānayorekajātīyatvaṃ sādhyate, tadā siddhasādhanam /
anyatrāniyame 'saḍkīrṇamudāharaṇam āha---ata eveti /
ekopādānatve 'pi rūpādīnāṃ na vyaktikṛto bhedaḥ, nāpyavāntara jātikṛtaḥ nāpi guṇatayā piṭharopādānatve 'pi karmaṇo 'guṇatvāt /
children.translated_text: Even when [they have] a single material cause, the difference of form and the like is not due to individuals, nor due to sub-classes, nor is action a quality even when it has a pot as its material cause [as qualities do].

children.text: atropādānamātrabalena yathā dravyaguṇakarmaṇāmasatāmeva sattvaṃ bahiḥ, tathā āntaramapi jñānasukhādīnām /
children.translated_text: Here, just as the existence of substance, quality, and action — which are non-existent [before production] — is [brought about] externally by the mere force of the material cause, so too [is] the internal [existence] of cognition, pleasure, and the like.

children.text: yathā ca teṣābhavāntarakāraṇabhedād dravyatvaṃ pṛthivyādīnām, guṇtvaṃ rūpādīnām, karmatvamutkṣepaṇādīnām, tathāvāntarakāraṇabhedād darśanasparśanasmaraṇādīnāṃ jñānatvaṃ nirūpādhyanukūlānūkūlatarādīnāṃ sukhatvamityādi /
children.translated_text: And just as the substance-hood of earth and the like, the quality-hood of form and the like, and the action-hood of throwing and the like [arise] from the diversity of subsidiary causes, so too from the diversity of subsidiary causes [arise] the cognition-hood of seeing, touching, remembering, and the like, and the pleasure-hood of the unconditionally favorable, more favorable, and the like — and so forth.

children.text: ekamavāntarāsādhāraṇanimittādibhedād yathā pṛthivyā ghaṭādibhedo, rūpasya śuklādibhedaḥ, utkṣepaṇasya ca pāṭavādibhedastathā jñānasyāpi darśanādibhedaḥ sukhasyāpi tāratamyādibhedo bhaviṣyatītyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Just as from the diversity of uncommon particular causes within a single [genus], there is the difference of pot and the like in earth, the difference of white and the like in form, and the difference of lightness and the like in throwing — so too there will be the difference of seeing and the like in cognition, and the difference of degrees and the like in pleasure — that is the meaning.

This very acceptance of sub-class diversity even when there is a single material cause has been raised by the opponents as an example. And [the argument] raised by 'moreover' and so forth — [namely] the doubtful exclusion — is clarified [by the phrase] 'therefore it is not irrelevant.' All this has been stated according to the Buddhist doctrinal acceptance. But in reality, the rule is: what has the same material cause is of the same class; what has the same pervading material cause is of the sub-class of a quality. Beyond that, there is no further rule. Therefore, if the same-class nature of pleasure and cognition is proved through existence (<s>sattā</s>) or through quality-hood (<s>guṇatva</s>), then what is to be proved is already established (<s>siddhasādhana</s>). Where there is no [further] rule, he states an uncontaminated example: 'For this very reason...'

children.text:
syādetat, ajñānarūpatāyāṃ punaḥ kiṃ pramāṇamityata upasaṃhāravyājenāha---tasmāditi /
yadyapi vijñānasukhādīnāṃ bhinnajātīyatvamanubhavasiddham /
na hi candanamahaṃ jānāmītyatra sukhaṃ parisphurati tadāhaṃ sukhīti syāt /
nāpi sukhyahamityatra jñānaṃ parisphurati tadā jānāmīti syāt, na caitadasti /
jñānaviśeṣaḥ sukhaṃ tathāvidhe ca sukhabuddhirbhavatyeveti cet---hanta bhostasya jñānaviśeṣasya viṣayaviśeṣo 'pyasti na vā? nāsti cet? nirviṣayajñānaṃ sukhamiti prāptam /
na caitad dṛṣṭamiṣṭaṃ śakayaṃ vā sādhayitum /
asti cet? bāhya ābhyantaro vā? na tāvad bāhyaḥ kaścid viṣayabhedo 'sti /
yadeva hi rāgavatā gītamanubhūyate tadeva vītarāgeṇāpi /
children.translated_text: For the very song that is experienced by one who has passion is [also experienced] by one free from passion.

children.text: tadeva gītam, paraṃ rāgavatā anukūlatayā, vītarāgeṇa tu tadviparītatayeti cet? kimanukūlatvamasya nirūpādhikam, sopādhikaṃ vā? kathaṃ kañcit prati, sopādhikatve sa evocyatām /
children.translated_text: If [one says] 'it is the same song, but [experienced] as agreeable by one with passion, and as the opposite by one free from passion' — is this agreeableness unconditional, or conditional? How [can it be unconditional] toward some [and not others]? If conditional, let that [condition] be stated.

children.text: icchaivopādhiriti cet---na, itaretarāśrayatvaprasaḍgāt /
children.translated_text: If [one says] 'desire itself is the condition' — no, because of the absurd consequence of mutual dependence.

children.text: iṣyamāṇatvādanukūlatvam, tena ceṣyamāṇatvamiti //
children.translated_text: For [it would mean]: agreeableness comes from being desired, and being desired comes from agreeableness.

Now, what is the <s>pramāṇa</s> for [pleasure's] nature as non-cognition? — therefore, under the guise of a conclusion, he says: 'Therefore...' Although the different-class nature of consciousness, pleasure, and the like is established by experience — for in 'I know sandalwood,' pleasure does not shine forth, otherwise 'I am happy' would [follow]; nor in 'I am happy' does cognition shine forth, otherwise 'I know' would [follow] — but this is not so. If [one says] 'pleasure is a specific kind of cognition, and in such [a cognition] the cognition of pleasure indeed arises' — well then, sir! Does that specific kind of cognition have a specific object or not? If not, then it follows that pleasure is an objectless cognition. And this is neither observed, nor accepted, nor capable of being proved. If it does? Is [that object] external or internal? Not an external specific object, to begin with.

children.text: tasmāt tasya jñānaviśeṣasya sukhatvenābhimatasyābhyantara eva viṣayaviśeṣo nisargānukūlasvabhāva eṣṭavyaḥ, yaddhetutayā bāhyo viṣayo 'nukūlatayābhimatatveneṣyamāṇo bhavati sa evoktarūpo viṣayaḥ sukhamityucyate /
tathāpi mūḍhadhiyāṃ vyavahārārthaṃ samānāsamānajātīyavyavacchedakā dharmā jñānādīnāmuktāḥ /
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, for the practical usage of the confused-minded, the properties that distinguish [these categories] from the same-class and different-class [members] — of cognition and the like — have been stated.

children.text: tatrārthapravaṇatvaṃ jñānasyārthanirūpaṇādhīnanirūpaṇatvamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therein, 'being directed toward an object' as the [definition] of cognition means having its determination dependent on the determination of an object — that is the meaning.

children.text: tadapravaṇatvamajñānalakṣaṇam /
children.translated_text: Not being directed toward [an object] in that way is the definition of non-cognition.

children.text: tatrāpyanukūlavedanīyatvaṃ sukhalakṣaṇam, pratikūlavedanīyatvaṃ duḥkhasyetyevamādi samānatantrānusādeṇa boddhavyamityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: And therein, being experienced as agreeable is the definition of pleasure; being experienced as disagreeable is [the definition] of pain — and so forth should be understood following the same system — that is the meaning.

Therefore, the specific object of that specific kind of cognition accepted as pleasure must be sought internally — of a nature that is inherently agreeable — [namely,] that very object of such a form, by virtue of which an external object is desired as being accepted as agreeable, is what is called 'pleasure.'

children.text:
nanvajñānātmakatve ghaṭādivadavaśyasaṃvedyāḥ sukhādayo na bhaveyuḥ /
avaśyasaṃvedyāśca te /
na hyasaṃvidite
children.translated_text: Now, if [pleasure is] not of the nature of cognition, then pleasure and the like would not be necessarily self-aware, just like a pot and the like. But they are necessarily self-aware. For there is no other <s>pramāṇa</s> for pleasure that is not

children.text: sukhe pramāṇamanyadasti /
tadetad jñānātmatve paramupapadyate svasaṃvedanatvādityata āha---tīvrasaṃvegitayeti /
children.translated_text: And this is tenable only when [pleasure] is of the nature of cognition, because of being self-aware (<s>svasaṃvedana</s>) — therefore he says: 'Due to being intensely impelled...'

children.text: santi hi padārthāḥ svakarmopārjitatvāviśeṣe 'pi kecidadhyakṣā eva, yathā svaśarīrādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: For there are entities that, despite no difference in being produced by one's own <s>karma</s>, are some directly perceptible — like one's own body and the like.

children.text: kecit tu parokṣā eva, yathā tadantargatanāḍīsaṃsthānādayaḥ /
children.translated_text: And some are only non-perceptible — like the configuration of the channels (<s>nāḍī</s>) inside that [body] and the like.

children.text: evamajñānatvāviśeṣe 'pi kāraṇalabdhasvabhāvabhedāḥ kecit avaśyasaṃvedyāḥ sukhādayaḥ kecidanyathetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Similarly, despite no difference in being non-cognition, [entities that are] differentiated in nature due to [different] causes — some, like pleasure and the like, are necessarily self-aware; and some are otherwise — that is the meaning.
cognized [by itself].

children.text:
sagotramutthāpayati---syādetaditi /
tathāpi jāgarāvasthāyāṃ tāvadanubhavajananadvārā sukhotpattāvindriyārthasannikarṣa upayujyate /
anyathā sukhavadanubhavo 'pi tena vinaiva syāt /
children.translated_text: Otherwise, even experience, like pleasure, would arise without that [contact].

children.text: na ca sākṣātkāraṇameva kāraṇam, tathā sati vyāpāriṇa udāsīnāḥ prasajyeran /
children.translated_text: And it is not the case that only the direct cause is a cause; for in that case, the intermediary [causes] would absurdly become indifferent [i.e., non-causal].

children.text: vyāpārāvyavadhāyakatvavādastvatrāpi tulya ityata āha---indriyārthasannikarṣasya tviti /
children.translated_text: The argument that [the intermediary] does not obstruct the operation [of the direct cause] is equally applicable here too — therefore he says: 'But of the sense-object contact...'

children.text: jñānamātramavyāpārībhūtaṃ tatra upayogādityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: The meaning is: mere cognition, without being operative [as a cause], is useful there [in the production of pleasure].

He raises a related [objection]: 'It may be that...' Even so, in the waking state at least, the sense-object contact is useful for the production of pleasure through the door of generating experience.

children.text:
ayamāśayaḥ /
bhavedevaṃ yadīndriyārthasannikarṣasya jñānaṃ vyāpāraḥ syāt /
sahi kāryāsavāno vyāpāryavyabhicārī bhavati /
jñānaṃ punaḥ kāryāvasānamapi indriyārthasannikarṣam atipatatyeva svapnāntike /
anyathā tu vyāpārakalpanāyāmaniyamaprasaṅgaḥ iti /
pariharati---tadayuktamiti asiddherapratīteḥ /
pramāṇābhāvāditi śeṣaḥ /
nanu mānasaḥ atrānubhavaḥ pramāṇamityata āha---tadjñānasyeti /
kuto mithyātvāvagatirityata āha---yathā hīti /
ālambnaṃ tvasya viparyāsasya yathā pūrvānubhūtā smaraṇārhā kāminītyevaṃ tajjānmapūrvānubhūtaṃ smaraṇārhaṃ sukhameva /
viparyāsatvaṃ punaretāvataivāsya yat viprakṛṣṭadeśakālayoḥ kāminītajjanyasukhayoḥ sannikṛṣṭadeśakālatayāvabhāsaḥ /
na punarakāminyasukhayoḥ kāminīsukhatvena pratibhānam /
tathā sati kāminītvasukhatvaniṣedhenānyasya kasyacit pratibhāsanaṃ bādhakaṃ bhavet /
na ca vācyam yadi na svapnāntike sukhamutpadyate na
children.translated_text: The intention is as follows. It would be so if the operation of sense-object contact were cognition. For that [cognition], being the terminal stage of the effect, would deviate from the operator. But cognition, even though it is the terminal stage of the effect, transgresses sense-object contact in the case of dreams. Otherwise, in the supposition of [another] operation, there would follow the consequence of indeterminacy. He refutes: 'That is untenable' — because of non-establishment, i.e., non-cognition. The remainder is: due to the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s>. Now, mental experience is the <s>pramāṇa</s> here — to this he says: 'Of that cognition...' Whence is the falsity known? To this he says: 'For just as...' The object of this error is, just as a woman previously experienced and worthy of being remembered, so too pleasure previously experienced in that birth and worthy of being remembered. And the error consists in just this: that the woman and the pleasure caused by her, which are remote in place and time, appear as if near in place and time. It is not that something that is not a woman and not pleasure appears as a woman and pleasure. For if so, the sublation — 'this is not a woman, this is not pleasure' — by negating womanhood and pleasantness, would establish the appearance of something else. Nor should one say: if pleasure does not arise in a dream, then no one

children.text: nasmai ghirahī spṛhayediti, mohādasādhane 'pi pravṛttidarśanāt /
children.translated_text: would yearn for it even in a dream — because activity toward what is not a means is seen even from delusion,

children.text: śītāpanuttaye guñjāpuñja iva markaṭānām /
children.translated_text: like [the activity of] monkeys toward a heap of <s>guñjā</s> berries for the removal of cold.

children.text: tadidamuktam---smaraṇaviparyāsa iti /
children.translated_text: This is what was stated: 'memory-error...'

children.text: smaraṇe prāpte viparyāsaḥ smaraṇaviparyāsaḥ anubhavalakṣaṇastadviṣaya evetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: 'Memory-error' means: when memory is expected, an error occurs — an error of the nature of experience regarding the very object of memory — this is the meaning.

children.text:
nanu sukhaduḥkhotpādaprayojanau dharmādharmau yadasukhaduḥkhārūpān dehādīn utpādayataḥ tattadarthatayaiva, evaṃ tayoḥ sarvotpattimatāṃ nimittatvaṃ nirvahati /
idaṃ tu svapnajñānaṃ na sukharūpam, saṃkhasādhanamapi yadi na syāt, na tarhi dharmanimittakam /
nāpyadharmanimittakamaduḥkhatvādataddhetukatvācca /
tataścādṛṣṭanirapekṣotpattirasya ca bahvākulayedityata āha---sukheti /
sukhādyupabhogo hyadṛṣṭasya pradhānaṃ prayojanam /
children.translated_text: For the experience of pleasure and the like is the principal purpose of unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).

children.text: na ca sukhādi svarūpataḥ upabhogaḥ, kiṃ tu tadanubhavaḥ /
children.translated_text: And pleasure and the like are not themselves experience in their essential nature — rather, the experience of them is [the experience].

children.text: sa ca pratyutpannasukhādyanālambanatve 'pi pūrvotpannam ālambya jāyamānaḥ sarvaṃ samañjasayati /
children.translated_text: And that [experience], even when not taking present pleasure and the like as its object, arising with reference to what was previously produced, makes everything consistent.

children.text: na ca sarvatraivamastu sāmagrīvaicitryāt, satyamithyāpratyayavibhāgavyavasthāpanāt //
children.translated_text: Nor should this [explanation] apply everywhere — because of the variety of the causal complex, and because of the establishment of the distinction between true and false cognitions.

Now, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, whose purpose is the production of pleasure and pain, when they produce bodies and the like that are not of the nature of pleasure and pain, do so for the sake of those very [pleasure and pain] — and thus their being the occasional cause of all things that arise is maintained. But this dream-cognition is not of the nature of pleasure; even if it were not a means to a chain [of further experiences], then it would not be caused by <s>dharma</s>. Nor is it caused by <s>adharma</s>, since it is not of the nature of pain and is not caused by that. And thus its arising independent of unseen merit would cause much difficulty — to this he says: 'Pleasure...'

children.text:
na hyekadopalabdharajataviṣayasaṃskāravaśādarajate 'pi rajatapratyayaḥ iti sarvadaivamevāstviti vaktumucitam /
yastu manyate svapne tāvatsukhādikamanubhūyata ityavivādam /
tatra tu bādhakaṃ bhavad dvirūpaṃ bhavet---asukhametaditi vā, nāsīt sukhamiti vā /
na caitadasti /
jāgarāvasthāyāṃ tu nāsīt kāminīti yujyate bādhakaṃ sthiratvāt /
sahasāpasaraṇasyāpyasaṃbhavāt /
tatkāryāṇāṃ ca daśananakhakṣatādīnāmananuvṛtteḥ /
caramadhātuvisargādīnāṃ cānuvṛttāvapyatatkāryatvāt /
tatkāryatvena tadanuvṛttāvanyeṣāmapi tatkāryāṇām anuvṛttiprasaḍgāt /
nāstīdānīṃ sukhamiti tvidānīntarasukhasya bādho na prāktanasya, kṣaṇikatvāt tasya /
tatkāryāṇāṃ ca harṣāśrupulakādīnāmanuvartamānānāmupalambhādanyathā āśutaravināśināṃ kṣaṇāntare 'darśanāt tadanubhavānāmaprāmāṇikatvameva syāt /
tasmātabādhitānubhavasiddhatvādasti svapnāntike sukhamiti taṃ pratyāha---na cāsatīti /
yadyapi svapnāntikasukhasya jāgarāvasthāyāmāhatya bādhakaṃ nāsti, tathāpi svapnāntika eva tatkāraṇatvena pratītānāṃ candanavanitādīnāmasti bādhakam /
kāraṇe ca bādhite kāryaṃ bādhitameva yathā svapnāntikadṛṣṭapayodapaṭalabādhe
children.translated_text: For it is not proper to say: 'Just as a cognition of silver arises even in non-silver due to the force of latent impressions from silver perceived on a previous occasion, so let it always be thus.' But one who thinks: 'In a dream, at least, pleasure and the like are experienced — this is undisputed.' Now, the sublating cognition there would be of two forms: either 'this is not pleasure,' or 'there was no pleasure.' But neither of these exists. In the waking state, however, 'there was no woman' is a tenable sublating cognition, due to the stability [of the waking state], and because sudden disappearance is impossible, and because the effects of that [woman] — such as bite and scratch marks — do not persist. And even though the final discharge of bodily fluids and the like do persist, they are not effects of that [dream-woman]. For if they persisted as effects of that, then other effects of that too would have to persist. 'There is no pleasure now' — but this is a sublation of present pleasure, not of past pleasure, since that is momentary. And since the effects of that [pleasure] — such as tears of joy, horripilation, and the like — are observed to persist; otherwise, because of the non-observation in a subsequent moment of things that perish more quickly, the experience of those too would be invalid. Therefore, since it is established through unsublated experience, there is pleasure in dreams — to that person he says: 'And not when it does not exist...' Although there is no striking sublating cognition against dream-pleasure in the waking state, nevertheless, there is a sublating cognition against sandalwood, butter, and the like that were cognized in the dream as causes of that pleasure. And when the cause is sublated, the effect is sublated too — just as when the cloud-mass seen in a dream is sublated,

children.text: tadāśrayo vidyududyotaḥ /
children.translated_text: the flash of lightning that rested on it [is also sublated].

children.text: harṣāśruprabhṛtayastu na sukhakāryāḥ kiṃ tu sukhajñānakāryā iti na tāvanmātreṇa tatsaṃbhavopapattiḥ /
children.translated_text: But tears of joy and the like are not effects of pleasure — rather, they are effects of the cognition of pleasure. Therefore, from their mere presence, the occurrence of pleasure is not established.

children.text: tasmāt svapnāntikodāharaṇabalena jñānamātrakāryato sukhasya sidhyatīti manorathādyudāhṛtya parihṛtam //
children.translated_text: Therefore, by the force of the dream example, pleasure is established as being merely an effect of cognition — citing daydream and so forth, it has been refuted.

children.text:
caturdhā khalu saṃsāriṇāṃ sukhamutpadyate /
kiñcidabhyāsād yathā mṛgayādiṣu ; kiñcidabhimānād yathā candanādiṣu ; kiñcita viṣayasaṃbhogād yathā surabhimadhuragauragāndhārādiṣu ; kiñcinmanorathādisaṃpratyayamātrād yathā bhaviṣyatputrādijanmadinamahotsavānucintanādiṣu /
te cāmī svarūpabhedavanto 'nubhūyante /
na hi yathā manoratheṣu sukhaṃ tathā viṣayasaṃbhoge /
tathā sati tatparityāgenānyopādānavaiyarthyāt /
tāvadeva hi bubhukṣito modakān manorathayati
children.translated_text: Pleasure arises in four ways for beings in <s>saṃsāra</s>: some from habituation, as in hunting and the like; some from conceit, as with sandalwood and the like; some from the enjoyment of objects, as with fragrant, sweet, fair <s>gāndhāra</s> melodies and the like; and some from mere mental fancy and the like, as in the contemplation of the future birthday celebration of a son and the like. And these are experienced as having differences of essential nature. For the pleasure in fantasies is not like that in the actual enjoyment of objects. If it were, the abandonment of the latter and the adoption of the former would be pointless. For a hungry person fantasizes about sweets only so long as

children.text: yāvadamī nāsya paramārthataḥ sannidhīyante /
children.translated_text: those are not actually present before him.

children.text: atha manorathavyasanamapahāya tatraiva niyamataḥ pravartate, tadekajātīyatve sarvamasamañjasaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: And when, abandoning the obsession with fantasy, one invariably engages in that [actual enjoyment] — if they were of the same type, everything would be inconsistent.

children.text: jātibhede tu kāraṇabhedo 'vaśyābhyupetavya ityarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: But if there is a difference of type, a difference of cause must necessarily be accepted — this is the meaning.

children.text:
tadatrendriyārthasannikarṣasya sattvamanuvidhatve sukhotpattiriti siddhāntino vivakṣitam /
taccānyathāsiddhamiti manvānaḥ punaḥ pūrvoktaṃ smārayati---jñānamātrameveti /
nātra tatsattvānuvidhānamātraṃ vivakṣitam /
kiṃ nāma? jātibhedaḥ
children.translated_text: Here, the intention of the proponent is that pleasure arises in conformity with the existence of sense-object contact. Thinking that to be otherwise-established, the [opponent] reminds of what was said earlier: 'Mere cognition alone...' What is intended here is not merely the conformity to the existence of that [contact]. What then? The difference of type

children.text: kāraṇabhedamākṣipati /
sa ca kāraṇabhedo 'nuvihitabhāvābhāva eva sidhyatītyatra vivakṣitamiti pratipipādayiṣuruktam evānubhāṣate /
children.translated_text: And that difference of cause is established precisely through the conformity of presence and absence — wishing to demonstrate that this is what is intended here, he repeats what was already said.

children.text: na, viṣayāsannidhāna iti /
children.translated_text: 'No — when the object is not present.'

children.text: tadidamuktam---tādṛśasya sukhabhedasya anutpādāditi /
children.translated_text: This is what was stated: 'Because such a type of pleasure does not arise...'

children.text: yādṛśa indriyārthasannikarṣādutpadyata iti śeṣaḥ //
children.translated_text: The remainder is: such as arises from sense-object contact.
entails a difference of cause.

children.text:
śaṅkate--viṣayeti /
jñānābhede hi bhinnajātīyaṃ sukhaṃ kāraṇāntaraṃ bhinnamākṣipet /
iha tu jñānameva bhinnajātīyamityarthaḥ /
pariharati--hanteśvarasyāpīti /
nanu viṣayasākṣātkāro 'pīṣṭopalabdhilakṣaṇaḥ sukhahetuḥ /
sa ca tādṛśo nāstīśvare tasya bubhukṣāvirahāt , kathaṃ tasya sukhotpādaprasaṅga ityata āha--yogarddhisampannānāmiti /
nanu te 'pyalaṃpratyayavantaḥ kathamiva sukhabhājo bhaveyurityata āha--asatyāmiti /
children.translated_text: He raises an objection: 'The object...' For if there is no difference in cognition, pleasure of a different type would entail a different cause that is other [than cognition]. But here, it is the cognition itself that is of a different type — this is the meaning. He refutes: 'Alas, even for the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>)...' Now, the direct realization of objects too, characterized by the apprehension of the desired, is a cause of pleasure. And such [direct realization] does not exist in the Lord, since He is free from hunger [i.e., desire]. How then would pleasure arise for Him? To this he says: 'For those endowed with yogic supernatural powers...' Now, they too are free from desire for anything — how could they experience pleasure? To this he says: 'When there is no...'

children.text: na hi te sarvadaiva pratipakṣadhāraṇāvanto mā bhūdamīṣāṃ sarvadā bhogavirahād dharmādharmapracayatādavasthyam /
children.translated_text: For they do not always maintain the counter-practice [against desire] — lest there be a constant state of neither accumulation of <s>dharma</s> nor <s>adharma</s> for them due to constant absence of enjoyment.

children.text: tasmād yadā pratipakṣadhāraṇā nāsti tadā viṣayasākṣātkāramātrādeva teṣāṃ sukhaṃ prasajyetetyarthaḥ //
children.translated_text: Therefore, when the counter-practice is not maintained, pleasure would arise for them from the mere direct realization of objects — this is the meaning.

children.text:
na ca vācyam, yadi bhavedevaṃ kīdṛśo doṣa iti /
kāyavyūhe śarīrendriyanirmāṇavaiyarthyaprasaḍgāt /
iṣṭāniṣṭasākṣātkārasya ekasminneva śarīre manasaiva siddhatvāt /
na cendriyāṇāmarthānāṃ ca parasparamasannikṛṣṭānāmeva sattāmātraiṇa kvacidātmadharmasamutpāde sāmarthyamadhigatam, tasmād yogarddhimatāṃ satyapi viṣayasākṣātkāre indriyārthasannikarṣābhāvāt sukhaṃ nāstītyabhipretyopasaṃharati--tasmāditi /
children.translated_text: Nor should one say: 'If it were so, what fault would there be?' — because there would follow the consequence of the purposelessness of the creation of body and sense-organs in the multiplication of bodies. Since the direct realization of the desired and the undesired is accomplished in a single body through the mind alone. And the capacity for the arising of properties of the Self by the mere existence of sense-organs and objects that are not mutually in contact has not been ascertained anywhere. Therefore, intending that for those possessed of yogic powers, even when there is direct realization of objects, there is no pleasure due to the absence of sense-object contact, he concludes: 'Therefore...'

children.text: tadayaṃ pramāṇārthaḥ, yogarddhīnīndriyāṇi sukhaduḥkhasamutpādaprayojanāni, sukhaduḥkhatabdodhānyatve satyanyatrācāritārthatvāt,
children.translated_text: This then is the meaning of the argument: the sense-organs of those with yogic powers serve the purpose of producing pleasure and pain — since, when pleasure and pain are not produced through them, their purpose is already served elsewhere,

children.text:
iṣṭāniṣṭopalabdhivat /
na cāyamasiddhaḥ /
anyatra hi caritārthatvaṃ sākṣātkāre saṃbhāvyeta, sa tu yogajadharmasahakṛtena manasaiva janitaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the serving of purpose elsewhere is conceivable with regard to direct realization, and that [direct realization] is produced by the mind alone aided by the <s>dharma</s> born of <s>yoga</s>.

children.text: te ca sukhaduḥkhe sannikṛṣṭairevendriyairjanyete, bāhyendriyajanyatve satyātmagharmatvāt, asmādādiviṣayasākṣātkāravaditi /
children.translated_text: And those pleasures and pains are produced only by sense-organs that are in contact, since they are properties of the Self when produced by external sense-organs — like our own direct realization of objects.

children.text: so 'yaṃ sannikarṣo yadā nāsti tadā teṣāmapi na sukhādikamiti /
children.translated_text: When that contact does not exist, even for them there is no pleasure and the like.

children.text: tadidamuktam--sa ceti //
children.translated_text: This is what was stated: 'And that...'
just as with the apprehension of the desired and the undesired. And this [argument] is not unestablished.

children.text:
nanvindriyārthasannikarṣajanmā viṣayasākṣātkāraḥ sukhādihetuḥ, na ca tathā siddhānāmasti, ato na teṣāṃ sukhotpādaprasaṅga ityata āha--api ceti /
na tāvadindriyajanyājanyayoḥ sākṣātkārayoḥ kaścidājānato viśeṣaḥ, kiṃ tu indriyārthasannikarṣarūpakāraṇasambandha eva viśeṣaḥ /
sa ca yadi kārye vivakṣitaḥ, kathaṃ na tasya kāraṇatā sukhādikaṃ prati? avivakṣitaścet, siddhānāmapi tadutpādaprasaḍgo durvāraḥ, tulyayogakṣematvāt /
tasmāt caramabhāvinyeva sākṣātkāre sati kimindriyeṇetyahṛdayasyābhiprāyaḥ avaśiṣyate /
tatra cātiprasaṅga ityarthaḥ /
atraivārthe vṛddhasaṃmatimāha--sragādīti /
atra sragādīti kāraṇacakrakathanam /
yadutpadyata ityanukūlapravedanīyaṃ svarūpam /
anugrahādīti kāryam /
children.translated_text: 'Gratification and the like' is the effect.

children.text: anugraho bhogāparanāmā sukhapratyayaḥ /
children.translated_text: Gratification, also called enjoyment, is the cognition of pleasure.

children.text: abhiṣvaṅgaḥ punaḥ punaḥ sukhapravāhasyāvicchedecchā /
children.translated_text: <s>Abhiṣvaṅga</s> (attachment) is the desire for the non-interruption of the continuous flow of pleasure.

children.text: prasādaḥ sukhaviṣayagrahaṇapāṭavamiti //
children.translated_text: <s>Prasāda</s> (serenity) is the adeptness in apprehending the object of pleasure.

Now, the direct realization of objects born of sense-object contact is the cause of pleasure and the like, and for those who are accomplished [in yoga], such [contact-born realization] does not exist — therefore there is no consequence of the arising of pleasure for them — to this he says: 'Moreover...' To begin with, one who examines finds no difference between direct realizations that are sense-generated and those that are not. Rather, the difference lies only in the causal connection in the form of sense-object contact. And if that [difference in causal connection] is intended to be present in the effect, how can it not be a cause with regard to pleasure and the like? But if not intended, then even for the accomplished ones the consequence of the arising of that [pleasure] is irresistible, since they share the same status. Therefore, the intention of the heartless one who says 'What need is there for the sense-organ when direct realization is already present in the final stage?' remains. And therein lies the undesirable over-extension — this is the meaning. On this very point he cites the view of the elders: 'Garlands and so forth...' Here, 'garlands and so forth' is the statement of the causal complex. 'That which arises' is the essential nature, which is what is to be agreeably experienced.

children.text: nanvavyapadeśyavyavasāyātmakapadayoḥ saṃgrāhyaṃ vyavacchedyaṃ vā na paśyāmḥ pratyuta parasparaviruddhayoranayorekasmin pratyakṣe 'samāveśa evetyata āha--iha dvayīti /
saṃgṛhītāpi svaśabdenopāttā kimiti cediti śaḍkāśeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Even though included, why is it taken up by its own word?' — this is the remainder of the doubt.

children.text: uttaram--tatra vipratipatteḥ /
children.translated_text: The answer: 'Because there is disagreement regarding that.'

children.text: yatastatra vipratipattistatastāṃ niṣeddhumityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Since there is disagreement regarding that, therefore, in order to negate it — this is the meaning.

children.text: vyapadiśyate vyavacchidyate 'neneti vyapadeśaḥ, sā ca vyavacchittirvyāvṛttipratītirūbhābhyāṃ kriyata iti tadubhayamāha--viśeṣaṇamiti //
children.translated_text: 'That by which one designates, i.e., distinguishes, is designation (<s>vyapadeśa</s>)' — and that distinguishing, in the form of cognition of exclusion, is done by both [indeterminate and determinate perception] — so he states both: 'qualifier...'

Now, we do not see what is to be included or excluded by the two terms 'indeterminate' (<s>avyapadeśya</s>) and 'of the nature of determination' (<s>vyavasāyātmaka</s>). On the contrary, these two, being mutually contradictory, simply cannot co-exist in a single perception — to this he says: 'Here, a twofold...'

children.text:
tatra samānādhikaraṇaṃ vyavacchedakaṃ viśeṣaṇam /
vyadhikaraṇaṃ tūpalakṣaṇam /
yathā daṇḍī devadatto jaṭābhistātasa iti /
na tu sedava viśeṣaṇam, ativyāpakatayā alakṣaṇatvāt /
lakṣaṇaviśeṣaṇametaditi cet? atha lakṣaṇaṃ kim? svoparaktapratītijanakatvamiti cet? etadeva kimuktaṃ syāt avacchedakatvamanyadvā? na tāvadādyaḥ, upalakṣaṇasyāpyavacchedakatvāt /
ata eva saditi viśeṣaṇamiti cet--na, sato 'pi kasyacidupalakṣaṇatveneṣṭatvāt /
anyuttu samānādhikaraṇavyavacchedakatvānnānyat /
tasmāt sad vā asad vā samānādhikaraṇaṃ vyavacchedakaṃ viśeṣaṇaṃ viparītamupalakṣaṇamiti /
ata eva viśeṣaṇamātramudāharannopalakṣaṇam, tat kasya hotoḥ? tadeva vyādhikaraṇatayopalakṣaṇa
children.translated_text: There, a co-referential distinguisher is a qualifier (<s>viśeṣaṇa</s>). But one in a different locus is an indicatory mark (<s>upalakṣaṇa</s>). As in 'the staff-bearing <s>Devadatta</s>' or 'the one with matted hair is his father.' But existence (<s>sat</s>) is not a qualifier in the same way, because of being a non-definition due to over-extension. If one says 'it is a qualifier of the definition' — then what is a definition? If one says 'the capacity to generate a cognition colored by itself' — would this amount to the stated 'being a distinguisher' or something else? Not the first, since even an indicatory mark has the capacity to distinguish. For this very reason, if one says 'existence is a qualifier' — no, since something existing too is accepted as an indicatory mark. But something other [than being a distinguisher] is nothing but being a co-referential distinguisher. Therefore, whether existent or non-existent, a co-referential distinguisher is a qualifier; the opposite is an indicatory mark. For this very reason, when only a qualifier is cited as an example, [it is used as] an indicatory mark — for what reason? That very thing, by being in a different locus, is an indicatory mark.

children.text:
yataḥ /
vyapadeśyaṃ viśeṣyamiti yāvaditi /
vyavacchedyamiti yāvadityarthaḥ /
evamuttaratrāpi /
nāmadheyānvitāḥ nāmadheyātmāna ityarthaḥ /
etadeva vyatirekato darśayati--nāstīti /
nāmadheyena saha viyujyate vibhidyata ityarthaḥ /
tairityatra kāraṇatābhramo mā bhūdityetadarthamupetadenāpūrya vyācaṣṭe--arthā hīti /
tadayaṃ samudāyārthaḥ /
nāmadheyātmānor'thāstatsāmānādhikaraṇyena pratīyamānatvāt /
yat punaryadātmakaṃ na bhavati na tat tatsāmānādhikaraṇyena
children.translated_text: Because. "The designable is the qualificand" — this is what is meant. "What is to be excluded" — this is the meaning. Similarly in what follows as well. "Conjoined with names" means "having names as their nature" — that is the meaning. He shows this very point through negative concomitance: "There is not..." "Is dissociated from, is distinguished from the name" — that is the meaning. Lest there be confusion about causality in [the word] "by them," he fills in the meaning with what is accepted and explains: "For the objects..." The overall meaning is this: the objects are cognized through <s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s> (co-referentiality) with the name, because they have names as their nature. Now, what is not of the nature of something is not

children.text: pratīyate /
children.translated_text: cognized through co-referentiality with that.

children.text: yathā goraśvasāmānādhikaraṇyena /
children.translated_text: Just as a cow is not cognized through co-referentiality with a horse.

children.text: pratīyante cārthāḥ śabdasāmānādhikaraṇyena tasmāt tadātmāna iti //
children.translated_text: But objects are cognized through co-referentiality with words; therefore they are of the nature of those [words].

children.text: nanu gavāśvādīnāṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyavyāvṛtti kimabhedavyāvṛtterūta tatpratītyorūpāyopeyabhāvavyāvṛtteriti saṃdihyata ityata āha--na ceti /
children.translated_text: Now, the question arises whether the exclusion of co-referentiality between cow, horse, and the like is due to the exclusion of non-difference, or due to the exclusion of the means-end relation of that [co-referentiality] and its cognition — therefore he says: "Nor..."

children.text: api ca yadi śabdārthayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇye upāyopeyabhāva upādhiḥ syāt, upāyatvanivṛttāveva tadapi nivarteta, na ca nivartata ityata āha--api ceti //
children.translated_text: Moreover, if the means-end relation were a limiting condition (<s>upādhi</s>) of the co-referentiality of word and meaning, then upon the cessation of means-hood, that [co-referentiality] too would cease — but it does not cease — therefore he says: "Moreover..."

children.text:
hetvantaramāha--kiṃ ceti /
utkarṣaḥ prāśastyam /
upakarṣo 'prāśastyam /
na cedaṃ vyavahāramātram /
śabdanibandhano
children.translated_text: He states another reason: "Furthermore..." <s>Utkarṣa</s> (superiority) means excellence. <s>Upakarṣa</s> (inferiority) means lack of excellence. And this is not mere conventional practice. For the conventional practice of superiority and inferiority based on words

children.text:
hyutkarṣāpakarṣavyavahāraḥ tathābhūtavastupratyayādeva bhaviṣyati /
yathā ṣaḍjādyutkarṣāpakarṣavyavahāranibandhano mayūrādyutkarṣāpakarṣavyavahāra iti dṛṣṭāntārthaṃ ṣaḍjādiṣvityuktam /
anyathā nāmadheyatādātmyaprasādhanaprastāve kimanena /
children.translated_text: Otherwise, what is the relevance of this in the context of establishing the identity of name [and referent]?

children.text: ata eva siddhānte saṃjñāniveśanamityāha /
children.translated_text: For this very reason, he says the established conclusion is the placement of the convention (<s>saṃjñā</s>).

children.text: prayogastu nāmadheyātmānor'thā tadutkarṣāpakarṣānuvidhāyitvāt /
children.translated_text: The argument is: objects have names as their nature, because they conform to the superiority and inferiority of those [names].

children.text: yat punaryadātmakaṃ na bhavati na tat tadutkarṣādyanuvidhāyi, yathā gauraśvasyeti //
children.translated_text: But what is not of the nature of something does not conform to the superiority and the like of that, just as a cow [does not conform to the superiority of] a horse.

will arise only from a cognition of reality that is of such a nature. Just as the conventional practice of superiority and inferiority of the peacock and the like is grounded in the conventional practice of superiority and inferiority of <s>ṣaḍja</s> (the first note of the musical scale) and the like — [the mention of] "in <s>ṣaḍja</s> and the like" is for the purpose of illustration.

children.text:
nanu yadyarthapratyayo nāmadheyotkārṣādyavidhatte tat tasyaiva tādātmyamastu, kimāyātamarthasyetyata āha--pratyayasyeti /
sākṣādanabhidhāne 'pi guṇaguṇyāderapi yogyatayā sapakṣatvena tadgatasāmānādhikaraṇyena virodha ubhdāvayituṃ na śakyata iti tadupekṣyānyathā śaṅkate--astīti /
asti hi śuklabhāsvaratvādibhiḥ yuktikāgatai rajatatvasya sāmānādhikaraṇyapratyayo natu tādātmyaṃ parasparaṃ dharmiṇorityarthaḥ /
punaruktabhramo mā bhūdityetadartham āha--uktamapi vyapadeśamiti /
vyākhyānasya caitat prayojanam, yaddhetvantarasūcanam, tathā ca prayogaḥ, rūpādyarthaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ rūpādiśabdaviṣayam, niyamatastena vyapadiśyamānatvāt, yat tu yadviṣayaṃ na bhavati, na tanniyamatastena vyapadiśyate yathā rūpavijñānaṃ raseneti /
anuviddhatā saṃśleṣalakṣaṇārthenaiva vijñānasya nāsti, kutastarāṃ tadātmanāpi śabdena bhaviṣyatītyata uktamiveti /
yathā hyartho jñānāntarniviṣṭa iva viṣayatayā
children.translated_text: Now, if the cognition of the object conforms to the superiority and the like of the name, let that identity belong to the cognition itself — what has the object got to do with it? — therefore he says: "Of the cognition..." Even without direct denotation, one cannot raise a contradiction through the co-referentiality pertaining to quality and qualified and the like, since they are in the same class by [mere] fitness — setting that aside, he raises the objection differently: "There is..." For there is the cognition of co-referentiality of silverness with [properties] such as whiteness, brilliance, and the like, which are obtained by reasoning — but there is no identity of the two subjects with each other — that is the meaning. Lest there be a confusion of repetition, he says: "Even the designation that has been stated..."
